<meta>Continuing from the entry on page 976, numbered 80, this page transitions to the decorative binding elements of the volume.</meta>

->**Decorative Marbled Endpaper**<-

The entirety of this page is covered in a decorative marbled paper pattern. It features distinct blue "spots" or "stones" set against a warm, brownish-tan background. 

<note>This specific style, often called "stone marbling," was a hallmark of bookbinding in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. To create this effect, a craftsman would drop pigments onto a bath of thickened liquid (called "size"), where they would spread into circular shapes. A sheet of paper was then carefully lowered onto the surface to "pick up" the floating design.</note>

<term>Marbled paper: A decorative paper produced through a water-surface design process, often used to line the inside covers of books.</term>

<term>Endpaper: The sheets of paper used by a bookbinder to attach the body of the book to its covers; these were often made of high-quality or decorative paper to protect the manuscript and provide a beautiful opening to the reader.</term>

<summary>This page displays a well-preserved example of "stone" marbled paper, a common decorative feature in early modern bookbinding. It serves as an endpaper, reflecting the material history and craftsmanship of the manuscript's physical construction.</summary>

<keywords>marbled paper, bookbinding, endpaper, stone pattern, decorative arts, 18th-century craft</keywords>

<meta>This page is the formal dedication of the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili," following the title page (Cat. Inc. 74). It establishes the fictional framework of the book: a letter from the lover Poliphilus to his beloved Polia.</meta>

# POLIPHILUS SENDS MANY GREETINGS TO POLIA.
<note>original: "S. P. D." stands for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a formal Latin greeting.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring intricate interlaced strapwork or knotwork patterns within a rectangular border.</image-desc>

MANY TIMES, POLIA, REFLECTING HOW
the ancient authors dedicated their works to princes and high-minded men—some for reward, others for favor, and some for praise—I found no prince more worthy for me to dedicate this, my <term>Hypnerotomachia</term><note>A title combining the Greek words for Sleep, Love, and Struggle; literally "The Strife of Love in a Dream."</note>, than to you, my high Empress. Your extraordinary condition, your incredible beauty, your venerable and greatest virtue, and your most illustrious manners—holding dominion over any Nymph of our age—have excessively inflamed, burned, and consumed me with your noble love. Receive, then, this little gift, radiant with beauty, adorned with every grace, and distinguished by your illustrious presence. You yourself have skillfully fashioned and created this work, for you have painted it within my loving heart with golden arrows and marked it with your own angelic image; thus, you possess it as its sole Patroness. I thereafter commit this gift to your diligent and ingenious judgment, having left behind my original style to translate it into this one at your insistence. Therefore, if any fault appears, or if you find it in any part sterile or lacking in your elegant dignity, you shall be the one accused—for you are the supreme maker and the sole key-bearer of my mind and my heart. For the reward of my great talent and effort, I value and desire nothing else especially but your gracious love and your benign favor.

->Farewell.<-

<insert>
<note>This is a handwritten addition in Spanish, likely from the late 16th or early 17th century, quoting a famous literary critic of the time.</note>
Antonio Agustín in the eleventh dialogue on ancient medals:
"A book called *Poliphilus*, whose title is *Hypnerotomachia*. 
**B.** In what language? Greek, Latin, or Italian? 
**A.** In all languages, and in none of them. 
**B.** How so? 
**A.** Because it seems he wanted to write his dreams and loves in Italian, but he mixes in so many Greek and Latin words, and sought such obscurity and a mixture of these three languages, that we can say he wrote in none of them. 
**B.** Now I remember having seen it in the French language, which it seems a curious man translated as if on a wager. 
**A.** Unfortunate was he to lose his time on such a book, etc."
</insert>

<summary>This page contains the dedication of the book to "Polia" by the fictional narrator Poliphilus, followed by a handwritten 16th-century Spanish note criticizing the book's notoriously difficult "macaronic" language—a mix of Italian, Latin, and Greek.</summary>

<keywords>Poliphilus, Polia, dedication, Renaissance literature, Antonio Agustín, linguistic style, macaronic, book history</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative introduction. Poliphilo describes his sleepless night spent lamenting his unrequited love for Polia before finally succumbing to a deep, visionary sleep. This transition from wakeful suffering to a dream-state is a classic trope of medieval and Renaissance "Dream Allegory" literature.</meta>

...to the desiring shores, where the painful and ungrateful death of the swimming Leander <note>A youth from Greek mythology who drowned while swimming across the Hellespont to visit his lover, Hero.</note> was warmly sighed for. I, Poliphilo, lying upon my bed—that opportune friend of a weary body—with no one present in my familiar chamber except my dear wakeful companion **Agrypnia** <note>original: "Agrypnia" (Greek for sleeplessness/wakefulness). Here personified as his only companion during the night.</note>. After she had held various consoling conversations with me, and after I had revealed to her the cause and the origin of my deep sighs, she piteously tried to persuade me to temper such distress. And perceiving that the hour had come when I should finally sleep, she took her leave.

Thus, left alone with my high thoughts of love, consuming the long and tedious sleepless night—all disconsolate and sighing because of my sterile fortune and my adverse and hostile star—and weeping for my troublesome and unsuccessful love, I reconsidered point by point what an unequal thing love is. I wondered how one can aptly love someone who does not love in return, and with what protection the fluctuating soul, besieged by unusual and frequent attacks and surrounded by hostile battle, can resist while so unarmed—especially since this seditious battle is internal, and one is constantly ensnared by anxious, unstable, and new thoughts.

Having grieved bitterly for a long time over such a miserable state, my wandering spirits were finally exhausted from useless thinking and from feeding on a false and feigned pleasure. But, truly and without fail, this pleasure was not of a mortal object, but rather of the divine Polia, whose venerable **Idea** <note>In the Platonic sense, an eternal and perfect form.</note> remains deeply impressed within me, and is most intimately sculpted there as a living occupant.

And already the trembling and flickering stars were beginning to grow pale in their splendor, when my tongue fell silent. That desired enemy <note>Referring to Cupid or the personification of Love.</note>, from whom this great and unceasing struggle proceeds, was impatiently troubling my wounded heart, calling out to it tirelessly for some profitable and effective remedy. This was nothing other than a cruel renewal of my torment, without any pause.

I meditated on the quality of wretched lovers: by what condition they choose to die sweetly to please others, while living badly to please themselves, feeding their sword-like desire with nothing but laborious and sighable imaginations. Therefore, like any man weary after long daily labors, I had barely settled my painful outward weeping and shut off the flow of dewy tears that had carved furrows of amorous languor into my cheeks, when I finally desired my natural and opportune rest.

Now my moist eyes were closed a little between my reddened eyelids. Lingering between a bitter life and a sweet death, that part of me <note>The body/senses.</note> was invaded and occupied and oppressed by a sweet sleep—the part which is not united with the mind nor shares in such high operations alongside the loving and ever-watchful spirits.

O thundering Jupiter! Shall I call this unusual vision happy, or marvelous, or terrifying? For there is not an atom in me that does not tremble and burn as I think of it. To me

<meta>This page continues from the previous leaf, where Poliphilo, exhausted by his unrequited love for Polia and a night of tossing and turning, finally falls into a deep sleep. This folio marks the beginning of his dream-vision, a standard literary device where the narrator's subconscious creates a symbolic landscape.</meta>

...it seemed that I was in a spacious plain <note>original: "planitie"</note>, which appeared all green and very much adorned, being painted with many various flowers. And with gentle breezes, there was a certain silence there. Not even to the readiest ears did any noise or any formed voice reach. But with the gracious rays of the sun, the temperate weather passed.

In which place I, a lonely stranger with timid wonder, said to myself: "Here no human presence appears to my longing gaze, nor even any wild creature, nor wood-dweller, nor wood-nymph <note>original: "silvia"</note>, nor domestic beast. No rustic house, nor any country hut, nor shepherd's roof, nor Libyan huts <note>original: "Magalia," a term used by ancient Roman poets to describe the dwellings of Carthaginian nomads.</note> are seen." Similarly, in the grassy places, I saw no shepherd <term>Opilione<gloss>A Latinate term for a shepherd of sheep.</gloss></term>, nor goatherd <term>Epolo<gloss>Derived from the Latin 'aipolos,' meaning one who tends goats.</gloss></term>, nor cowherd <term>Buſequa<gloss>One who tends cattle.</gloss></term>, nor horse-handler <term>Equiſio<gloss>From the Latin 'equis,' meaning one who manages horses.</gloss></term>, nor wandering flock or herd with their double-piped rustic reed-flutes <note>original: "Syringe"</note>, nor with their sounding pipes of bark <note>original: "Tibie"</note>. But emboldened by the quiet plain and the kindness of the place, and proceeding as if feeling safe, I looked here and there, seeing the tender leaves resting motionless, perceiving no other activity. And so, facing a thick forest, I directed my unknown journey. Having entered it a little way, I did not notice that I had—I know not how—incautiously left the proper path. A sudden fear immediately invaded my anxious heart, spreading through my pale limbs, and with a rapid beating of the heart, my cheeks became bloodless in color. This was because my eyes were not permitted to see any trace of a path or any fork in the road. Instead, in the thorny forest, nothing appeared except dense thickets, stinging brambles, the wild ash tree—hated by vipers <note>A piece of Renaissance folklore suggesting that snakes would rather jump into a fire than pass through the shadow of an ash tree.</note>—rough elms, pleasing to the fertile vines <note>Elms were traditionally used as supports or "husbands" for grapevines in ancient and Renaissance agriculture.</note>, cork-trees <note>original: "Subderi"</note> with thick bark—a suitable material for women's footwear <note>A reference to "choppines" or platform shoes, which were often made with thick cork soles.</note>—hard Turkey oaks, strong English oaks, and acorn-bearing oaks and holm-oaks, so abundant with branches that they did not permit the rays of the gracious sun to reach the dewy ground entirely. But as if covered by a vaulted roof of dense foliage, the nourishing light did not penetrate. And in this way, I found myself in the cool shade, humid air, and the dark woodland <note>original: "Nemorale"</note>.

<meta>This page continues from Poliphilo’s entry into a thick, dark forest, leaving the sunlit, silent plain behind. The dream-vision shifts from a peaceful landscape to a site of growing anxiety and physical struggle.</meta>

Because of this, I then began reasonably to suspect and believe I had arrived in the vast <term>Hercynian Forest<gloss>A legendary primeval forest mentioned by ancient Roman authors such as Julius Caesar and Tacitus; to a Renaissance reader, it symbolized a terrifying and impenetrable wilderness.</gloss></term>. And there was nothing else there but the hiding places <note>original: "latibuli"</note> of harmful beasts, and the dens of noxious animals and savage creatures. And therefore, with the greatest terror, I feared being without any defense, and—without realizing it—being torn apart by a bristly and tusked <term>Boar<gloss>original: "Apro."</gloss></term>, like <term>Charidemus<gloss>A figure from Greek history or myth associated with being killed by a wild boar.</gloss></term>, or by a raging and hungry <term>Aurochs<gloss>original: "Vro." An extinct species of large wild cattle that lived in Europe.</gloss></term>, or by a hissing serpent. I feared that howling, attacking wolves would miserably dismember and devour my flesh.

Terrified by these doubts, I resolved (condemning any further laziness) to linger there no longer, but to find an exit and escape the looming dangers, and to quicken my already hesitant and disordered steps. I frequently stumbled over large roots uncovered by the earth; wandering here and there, now to the right side and now to the left, sometimes moving backward and sometimes forward. Unknowing and not certain where I was traveling, I arrived in a <term>woodland glade<gloss>original: "Salto."</gloss></term> and a <term>thicket<gloss>original: "dumeto."</gloss></term>, a thorny place where I was all scratched by the branches and by prickly plum-bushes, my face battered by unpalatable fruit. My gown was torn and caught by the pointed thistle-beds and other thorns, which slowed my attempted flight. 

Beyond this, seeing no sign of helpful footprints nor any worn path, and being more than a little confused and doubtful, I hurried even more anxiously. Because of these swift steps, as well as the midday <term>heat<gloss>original: "æsto."</gloss></term> which made my body grow hot, I was entirely soaked with sweat, and the [cold] <note>The page ends here with the catchword "fredo" (cold), suggesting the next page describes the sweat turning cold from fear.</note>

...I bathed my cold breast. Not knowing what to do anymore, I kept my mind bound and intent only on terrible thoughts. And so, in the end, only Echo, that mimic of the voice, offered herself in response to my sighing words. My resounding sighs were dispersed alongside the hoarse chirping of the cicada <note>original: "mante"</note> of the dewy Aurora, and with the shrill crickets. Finally, in these rough and trackless woods, I believed in and desired only the help of the Piteous <term>Ariadne<gloss>In Greek mythology, Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to help him find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth.</gloss></term>. She, aware of the plan to kill her monstrous brother, gave the skillful and guiding thread to the deceitful <term>Theseus<gloss>The hero who escaped the labyrinth but later abandoned Ariadne.</gloss></term> to find his way out of the treacherous labyrinth. And I desired the same to escape this dark forest.

## POLIPHILO, FEARING THE PERIL OF THE DARK WOOD, OFFERED A PRAYER TO <term>DIESPITER<gloss>An archaic Latin name for Jupiter, meaning "Father of Light" or "Father of Days."</gloss></term>; HE CAME FORTH ANXIOUS AND THIRSTY, AND WISHING TO REFRESH HIMSELF WITH WATER, HE HEARS A SWEET SINGING. FOLLOWING THIS, HE REJECTED THE WATERS AND FELL INTO GREATER ANXIETY.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' featuring classical foliate and floral scrolling patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>My intellect having already begun to be obscured—so that I could no longer recognize things—and my senses being clouded as to which option I should choose, whether to seek a hateful death or to hope for salvation while wavering in this shadowy and opaque grove. Running here and there, I applied all my strength and effort to find an exit. But the further I persuasively penetrated into it, the darker it became. And having already become weak from great fear, I waited in doubt for some most cruel and attacking beast to begin devouring me. Or perhaps I feared stumbling blindly and falling into an abyssal pit or ditch, or plunging into some vast chasm in the earth. I feared ending my weary life like <term>Amphiaraus<gloss>A legendary seer swallowed up by the earth during the war of the Seven against Thebes.</gloss></term> or <term>Curtius<gloss>Marcus Curtius, a Roman hero who sacrificed himself by leaping into a chasm that opened in the Roman Forum.</gloss></term>, swallowed by a foul-smelling <note>original: "mephitica"</note> terrestrial vortex, or falling from a greater height than the foolish <term>Pyreneus<gloss>A king who attempted to capture the Muses; he fell to his death from a tower while trying to follow them as they flew away.</gloss></term>. In this way, almost without hope, my mind was troubled on all sides, yet I still attempted a pathless exit, wandering without direction. Wherefore, more trembling than the shifting leaves in the wine-rich Autumn when the thieving North Winds <note>original: "Aquili"</note> blow—leaves lacking their green vigor and the heavy weight of their moisture—I said to myself in prayer: "O <term>Diespiter<gloss>Jupiter</gloss></term>, Greatest, Best, and Omnipotent, and Helper. <meta>The previous page concluded with Poliphilo entering a state of total despair within the dark wood, praying to Jupiter (Diespiter) for deliverance from the labyrinthine thicket.</meta>

...humanity, through just prayers, deserves support and ought to be heard. At present, grieving for every frail offense, I suppliantly invoke you, supreme father of the celestials, eternal ruler of the highest, middle, and lowest realms <note>original: "Medio ximi, & inferi æterno rectore"</note>, that it might please your immense Deity to liberate me from these mortal perils and this present horror, and to end this doubtful life of mine by some other, better end.

And here, like the trembling <term>Achaemenides<gloss>A character from Virgil’s "Aeneid" who was accidentally left behind on the island of the Cyclops by Odysseus and was later rescued by Aeneas.</gloss></term> who pleaded with Aeneas with an anxious and precarious voice to escape the horrific Cyclops—desiring rather to die at the hands of human enemies than by such a horrendous death—I prayed in the same manner. 

Hardly had I finished these devout prayers sincerely, with a unified heart, contrite and agitated, and bathed in tears—firmly believing that the Gods assist a good mind—than without delay I found myself outside that narrow, rough, and thorny wood <note>original: "nemore"</note> without even realizing it. It was as if I had emerged into a new day from the humid night. My shaded eyes could not for a while endure the lovely light. 

Completely filthy, mournful, and anxious, it seemed to me that I had reached the desired light no less than one who might come out of a "blind prison," freed from heavy and troublesome chains and emerged from murky darkness. Entirely thirsty and torn, my face and hands bloodied and blistered by stinging nettles <note>original: "Vrtica"</note>, feeling myself faint, I yet considered nothing as an obstacle to the gracious light. I was so thirsty that the fresh breezes could not refresh me, nor could they adequately satisfy my parched heart. I was most greedy to swallow even the hollow saliva that had dried up within me. 

But after I was somewhat reassured, and a little bit of spirit was recalled into me—though my chest was dried out by frequent sighs, anxiety of spirit, and physical fatigue—I decided by every means to extinguish my parched thirst. Therefore, exploring that region curiously to find some water, and seeking it while very exhausted, a most pleasant fountain opportunely offered itself to me with a thick vein of freshly rising water. Its location was revealed to me by marshy <term>Sweet Flag<gloss>original: "Achori"; a wetland plant often used in perfumes and medicines.</gloss></term>, the <term>Woodruff<gloss>original: "barba Siluana"; a low-growing woodland plant.</gloss></term>, the flowering <term>Loosestrife<gloss>original: "Lisimachia"</gloss></term>, and the musky <term>Masterwort<gloss>original: "Imperatoria"; a medicinal alpine plant.</gloss></term>. 

From this fountain was born a most clear stream which, with wandering rivulets through the middle of the deserted forest, flowed on with a colorful and winding bed, growing larger as it took in many other liquid channels. Against the obstructing stones and ruined trunks, the current and sounding waves rose up. And then, it received a great increase from impetuous and wave-sounding torrents of melted snow falling from the alpine and frozen mountains—which appeared not too far distant, whitened in the icy majesty of <term>Pan<gloss>The god of the wild; here used to personify the rugged, snowy mountain landscape.</gloss></term>. Having arrived at this stream many times during my fearful flight, I found a bit of dim light through the tall trees, a little in the

<meta>The previous page concluded with Poliphilo emerging from a dark, thorny wood into the light, though he remained exhausted, thirsty, and physically wounded from his ordeal.</meta>

...lopped at the peaks, above the muddy river, where I saw the sky torn by the obstructing leafy branches and dried ones alike; a horrific place for a man to find himself alone without any crossing. Furthermore, the far banks appeared even more obscure and intricate than the near ones. Here was my terror: to hear from there, at times, the whistling ruin of trees, a crashing of branches, and a crackling splitting of wood, with a doubled and hair-raising noise <note>original: "horriſono ſtrepito"</note>, echoing through a long stretch of the tree-density and the trapped air.

Therefore, I, Poliphilo, terrified and afflicted, having escaped such horror and wishing to draw the desired waters from the green banks, knelt upon my knees <note>original: "popliti"</note> and, bringing my fingers together to form a hollowed cup of my palms, I made a most welcome vessel for drinking. This I dipped into the spring and filled with water to offer to my parched and panting mouth, and to refresh the dryness of my burning breast. It was more pleasing to me then than the <term>Hyphasis<gloss>A river in India, now known as the Beas; one of the rivers encountered by Alexander the Great.</gloss></term> and the Ganges are to the Indians, or the Tigris and Euphrates to the Armenians; nor is the Nile so pleasing to the Ethiopian people—or to the Egyptians when its flooding soaks the parched earth. Nor was the <term>Eridanus<gloss>The ancient name for the River Po in Italy.</gloss></term> so dear to the Ligurian people as these most welcome and fresh banks were offered to me. Nor was the spring shown by the fleeing Ram to <term>Father Liber<gloss>Another name for Bacchus (Dionysus), the god of wine. Legend says a ram led him and his thirsty army to a hidden spring in the Libyan desert.</gloss></term> so delightful.

It happened that no sooner were the expected and desirable waters, held within the enclosure of my cupped hand, about to reach my open mouth, than in that instant I heard a **Dorian song**—I am convinced that not even <term>Thamyris the Thracian<gloss>A legendary singer of Greek mythology who was so proud of his skill that he challenged the Muses to a contest.</gloss></term> could have invented it—penetrating through my hollowed ears and passing into my restless heart with such smooth sweetness and harmony. It was a voice not of this earth, with such harmony, such incredible resonance, and such unusual proportion. Oh, how much more than could ever be imagined! 

For without doubt, this thing exceeds the power of narration. Its sweetness and delight provided me with far more pleasure than the little drink being offered. So much so that, while the water drawn into the enclosure between the gaps of my fingers remained, my intellect was almost insensible and already stupefied, and my appetite was soothed; with no strength left to resist, my fingers unclasped their knots, and the water scattered upon the damp earth.

Now, like an animal that does not perceive the hidden trap because of the sweet bait—setting aside its natural needs—I went without delay, hurrying along the path with vehemence toward that inhuman note <note>original: "inhumana nota"; referring to a sound or melody that does not seem to be made by a person.</note>. When I reasonably thought I had reached it, I would hear it in another place; and when I had arrived at that location by rushing toward it, it seemed to be fixed elsewhere. And just as it changed locations, it likewise changed its sweet and delightful voice with heavenly harmonies <note>original: "cœleſti concenti"</note>. Therefore, due to this futile effort <note>original: "inane fatica"</note> and having run so much with a troublesome thirst, I became so weakened that I could hardly sustain my weary body. And my gasping spirits no longer being able to sustain my heavily fatigued body—partly due to the past terror, partly the urgent thirst, the long and wandering search, the heavy anxiety, and the heat of the hour—having lost and been abandoned by my own strength, I desired or craved nothing at all except quiet rest for my weakened limbs. Marveling at the accidental occurrence, stunned by the honey-sweet voice <note>original: "melliflua uoce"</note>, and much more by finding myself in an unknown and wild region, though it was a very pleasant country <note>original: "amœno paeſe"</note>. Besides this, it pained me greatly that the liquid spring, found with such labor and sought with such careful inquiry, was now taken away and lost from my eyes. Because of all these things, I stood with my mind entangled in ambiguity and very pensive. Finally, overcome by such great weariness, my whole body growing cold <note>The text ends with the fragment "frigeſcen-", likely continuing as "frigeſcente" (growing cold), describing Poliphilo falling into a deep, death-like sleep.</note>

...faint and languid. Beneath a rough and **very old oak** <note>original: "ueterrima quercia"</note>, heavy with cup-shaped or tufted acorns—the kind despised by those in fertile **Chaonia** <note>original: "Chaonia"; a region in Greece famous for the ancient prophetic oak groves of Dodona. The author suggests these acorns are so common they are undervalued there.</note>—in the middle of a spacious and grassy meadow, its thick branches spreading wide to cast a fresh shade, I laid myself down upon the dewy grass beside its hollow trunk. Lying there restfully on my left side, I drew in the cool breezes with my thinning breath, more and more frequently with trembling lips. 

I was like a weary **Stag** <note>original: "Ceruo"</note> that has been hunted and bitten on its flanks by fierce, snapping dogs, wounded in the chest by an arrow, leaning its heavy head and branching antlers against its weak back; finally, unable to stand any longer, it collapses, exhausted and dying, upon its failing knees. 

As I lay there in a similar state of agony, I turned over in my mind the most intricate misfortunes of hellish fate and the enchantments of the wicked **Circe**, wondering if I had perhaps been ensnared by her verses or if the **magic wheel** <note>original: "Rhombo"; a spinning tool used in ancient Greek sorcery to cast spells or restore lost love.</note> had been used against me. Amidst these many mounting terrors, I cried out, "Alas! Where could I find the medicinal **Moly of Mercury** <note>original: "Mercuriale Moly"; the magical herb with a black root given by the god Hermes to Odysseus to protect him from Circe’s magic.</note> here among these various plants to serve as my aid and remedy?" Then I said to myself, "This is not that. What is this, then, if not a malignant delay of my longed-for death?"

Staying thus in these ruinous agitations, my strengths were fading bit by bit. I could think of no other salvation than to frequently and diligently drink in the fresh air, warming it in my chest where a tiny spark of vital heat still beat, and then exhaling it from my parched throat. Finding myself in no other state than half-dead, I took up the damp, dew-covered leaves sheltered beneath the leafy oak as a final refreshment. I pressed them to my pale and rough lips with the utmost greed, licking the moisture from them to quench my thirst and cool my parched throat <note>original: "siticuloſa uuea"; literally "thirsty uvula."</note> a little. 

I wished then for **Hypsipyle** <note>original: "Hypsipyle"; in mythology, she guided the thirsty Greek army to the spring of Langia.</note> to appear and show me a spring, as she once did with the fountain of Langia for the Greeks. For I anxiously suspected that perhaps, while wandering unawares in the vast forest, I had been bitten by the **Dipsas serpent** <note>original: "ſerpa Dipſa"; a mythical snake whose bite was said to cause an unquenchable, fatal thirst.</note>, so unbearable was my craving for water. 

Finally, having renounced and given up on my tedious life, and resigning myself to whatever might happen, I was stunned and alienated by these heavy thoughts, wavering as if in a daze. Once again, beneath the shade of this oak—luxuriant with the wide darkness of its branches—I was oppressed by a heavy sleep. As a sweet slumber spread through my limbs, it seemed to me that I fell asleep once more.

This place was not surrounded by dreadful mountains and craggy rocks, nor was it carved with swollen ridges. Instead, it was harmoniously composed of pleasant little hills of modest height. At the sight of this <note>likely referring to a wolf mentioned in the preceding text, which startled the narrator</note>, my hair immediately stood on end, and though I wished to cry out, I had no voice. The creature suddenly fled. And I, having then somewhat returned to myself, lifting my eyes toward that part where the wooded hills appeared to join together, I saw in the far distance an incredible height in the shape of a tower, or rather a very high lookout-tower. Nearby, a great building was also appearing, though as yet imperfectly, which was clearly a work of ancient structure. Where the graceful little hills of the valley rose ever higher toward this building, I saw them joined with the aforementioned structure. It served as a closure between one mountain and the other, creating a valley-closure <term>valliclusio; an architectural barrier blocking a valley</term>. Shrewdly judging this sight to be most worthy of investigation, I eagerly redirected my already anxious journey toward it without delay. And the more I subsequently approached it, the more I discovered a work both immense and magnificent, and my desire to gaze upon it multiplied. For it no longer appeared as a sublime lookout-tower, but proved to be an exalted **Obelisk**, founded upon a vast mass of stones.

The height of this structure incomparably exceeded the summit of the surrounding mountains, even if they had been the famous mountains I judged to be Olympus, Caucasus, or Cyllene <note>Cyllene is a mountain in Greece, the birthplace of Hermes</note>. Having come eagerly to this deserted place, surrounded by an unthought-of pleasure, I quietly stopped myself to gaze freely at such an extraordinary display of the building art, and the immense structure, and its stupendous height. I stood gazing at and considering the entire solid mass and the thickness of this fragmented and half-ruined structure made of white Parian marble <note>original: "marmo de Paro"; a fine-grained, semi-translucent pure white marble from the Greek island of Paros</note>. The squares and quadrangles were fitted together without any glue of cement, and were equally placed and located, so polished, and their edges so exquisitely marked out as could ever possibly be done. So much so that between one edge and another, or between the joints, even a needle-like thinness, however much one might try to insert it, would not have been able to penetrate even a little. Here, then, I found such noble colonnades of every shape, design, and material as anyone could ever imagine—some broken, some in their proper place, and others preserved unharmed—along with the architraves <term>Epistyli</term> and capitals, which were excellent in their design and sharp carving. There were cornices, friezes <term>Zophori</term>—or Phrygian work—and arched beams. I saw huge fragments of statues, with many of their precise bronze limbs lopped off. There were basins <note>original: "Scaphe"</note>, shells <note>original: "Conche"</note>, and vases, made of Numidian stone <note>a yellow marble also known as Giallo Antico</note>, of Porphyry <note>a hard purple igneous rock</note>, and of various other marbles and ornaments. There were large wash-basins, aqueducts, and almost infinite other fragments of noble sculpture, though they were totally deprived of the knowledge of what they were when whole, and were almost reduced to their first raw state. They lay collapsed and cast down here and there upon the earth. Above...

And among those rugged ruins many wild saplings had sprouted, especially the non-quivering bean trefoil <note>original: *Anagyro non quassabondo*; the stinking bean trefoil, known for its unpleasant odor</note> with its pod-filled husks, and both types of Mastic-tree <note>original: *Lentisco*</note>, and Bear’s-foot <note>original: *Vngula ursi*; likely Acanthus mollis, a plant often depicted in Corinthian capitals</note>, and Snapdragon <note>original: *Cynocephalo*</note>, and Stinking Iris <note>original: *Spatula fetida*</note>, and the rough Bindweed <note>original: *Smylace*</note>, and Centaury, and many others sprouting among the fallen stones. Among these, some lizard-like creatures slithered, and they also crawled over the vine-covered walls, frequently in those deserted and silent places causing no small horror in me at their first movement, for I stood there entirely in suspense.

In many parts there were great pieces of flat circular stones, and of Serpentine <note>original: *Ophites*; a green, snake-patterned marble</note>, and Porphyry <note>original: *Porphyrite*; a deep purple-red rock</note>, and coral-colored stone, and many other pleasing colors. Therefore, having approached the middle front of the great and illustrious work, I saw an intact portal, marvelous and conspicuous, and perfectly proportioned to the whole building.

I saw this structure placed continuously between the slopes of two mountains, which I could roughly guess to be twenty paces wide and six stadia long. The slopes of these mountains were leveled perpendicularly from the summit down to the base area. Because of this, I stood deep in thought, wondering with what iron tools, and with how much wear on men’s hands, and with what great number of people such a massive work had been violently carried out, for it was a labor beyond belief and must have cost a great wasting of time. Here, then, this admirable structure joined with both mountains in a conscious bond. By this conjunction, as said above, the valley was fortified with a closure, so that no one could leave from there, nor return back, nor enter except through this wide-open gate. 

Now, atop this so huge work of masonry—the height of which could easily be guessed to be a fifth of a stadium from the highest crown down to the pedestal and the base platform <term>original: *Areobate*; the solid base upon which a building or colonnade stands</term>—was founded a pyramid, peaked like a diamond and most portentous. Therefore I reasonably judged that never, without inestimable expense, time, and a maximum multitude of mortals, could such an incredible artifice have been devised and erected. Wherefore, if I deservedly deemed the contemplation of its excess to be an unthinkable thing beyond belief—for gazing upon it tired my visual power in no small way and weakened my other spiritual senses—how much more would the reality of it? Thus, so that the grasp of my intellect may be provided to me at least in some part, I now briefly describe it in this manner.

Each face of the square base of the structure <note>original: *meta*; literally a turning post in a racecourse, here referring to the pyramid's shape</note>, beneath the start of the stairs of this admirable Pyramid, situated atop the aforementioned building, was six stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of length, approximately 185 meters</note> in longitudinal extension. Multiplied by four for its perimeter, the base occupied twenty-four stadia in its equilateral foundation. In height, from each corner, the lines rose with such measure—the same as the base line of the plinth—until all four met together at the central summit, forming a perfect pyramidal figure. This immense and terrifying Pyramid, rising by steps with admirable and exquisite symmetry in diamond-like hardness, contained one thousand, four hundred and ten grades, or steps, of stone casing. Ten steps were removed at the top to appropriately end the tapering. Let us return, then, to the vast **Pyramid**, beneath which lay a huge and solid *Plinth*, or broad stone, or square foundation, fourteen paces in height, and six stadia in its extension or length. This formed the foundation for the lowest level of the massive **Pyramid**. And I skillfully judged <note>original: "ſolerteméte arbitraua"</note> that it had not been brought here from elsewhere, but was carved out of the mountain itself by human labor into that figure and shape, and reduced to such a mass in its own place. The rest of the steps were built up from individual pieces.

This immense square did not touch the neighboring mountains of the valley, but was separated from them on each side by a gap of ten paces. On the right side, as I walked, was the aforementioned *Plinth*, in the center of which the snaky head of the terrifying **Medusa** was perfectly carved, in a raging, shouting, and snarling expression. With terrifying eyes, sunken beneath suppressed brows, a wrinkled forehead, and a wide, gaping mouth. This mouth, hollowed out with a straight passage and a vaulted ceiling, penetrated to the center—or rather, to the median perpendicular line of the highest *Catillo* <note>The flat, square platform at the top of the pyramid that serves as the base for the obelisk</note> of the wondrous **Pyramid**—and served as a very large entrance and passage. To this opening of the mouth, one ascended by her tangled hair, expressed with unimaginable intellectual subtlety, art, and the heavy thought of the craftsman. It was designed with such order that the steps for climbing were aptly formed leading to the open mouth. And in place of the curls <note>original: "trece capreolate"</note>, I gazed in amazement at the vipers and twisted serpents with their lively and huge coils. Around the monstrous head, they were confusedly involving themselves with the quickest turnings. Those faces and the scaly, fighting serpents were so distinctly feigned in their workmanship that they struck me with no small horror and fear. In their eyes, very bright stones were most conveniently set, so that if I had not been certain the material was marble, I would not have dared to approach so easily.

The aforementioned path, carved into the solid rock, led to where the stairs were, with a winding passage through spiral turnings <note>original: "amfraƈti coclei"</note>. By these, one ascended to the highest summit of the **Pyramid**, onto the surface of the square *Catillo*. Upon this, the eminent **Obelisk** was founded. upper lighting. The upper part was illuminated by means of the **descending shafts** <note>original: "catabaſſi"</note>. With some reflection from the opposite surfaces, they provided sufficient light. Such was the calculated rule of the exquisite arrangement of the ingenious mathematician on the three faces—East, South, and West—that at every hour of the day, the winding staircase was bright and clear. These air-holes <note>original: "ſpiracoli"</note> were symmetrically defined and dispersedly distributed in various locations of the enormous **Pyramid**.

To the part of the aforementioned mouth-opening I arrived by climbing another solid and direct staircase, which was hollowed out within the stone itself at the foundation level of the building, towards the right side adjacent to the **hewn mountain** <note>original: "mōte delumbato"</note>, where there was a gap of ten paces. By this way—certainly more out of curiosity than was perhaps permitted—I climbed. Having reached the entrance to the staircase through the mouth, I finally ascended through innumerable steps, or rungs, not without heavy labor and dizziness of the head, circling up over such an unimaginable height <note>original: "celſitudine"</note>. My eyes could not properly bear to look down at the ground. So much so, that everything below appeared to me as small and imperfect. And because of this, I did not dare to move away from the middle of the platform. And here, in the circuit of the circular and highest exit—the end of the twisting staircase and opening—many cast metal posts <note>original: "ſtipiti fuſatili"</note> were polished and fixed in a circle. The space between them <note>original: "īterlocatiõe"</note>, measuring from center to center, was one foot, and they were half a pace in height. They were encircled at the top with a small wavy crown of the same cast material, which surrounded and fenced the lip of the opening and the gap of the upper exit of the said staircase, except for that part through which one exited onto the surface, by a wise design. This was so that no one, through lack of caution, might plunge into the opening of the winding cavern. For indeed, the immoderate height induced a staggering sensation. Beneath the level base of the **Obelisk**, a bronze tablet was set in lead, facing upward, with ancient writing in our own characters, as well as in Greek and Arabic, through which I fully understood that the structure was dedicated to the **Supreme Sun**. The entire measurement of the great structure was also fully noted and described there. And the name of the architect was noted in Greek upon the **Obelisk**.

It seemed to lack only the breath of life, being of wonderful carving and excellently sculpted. With its movements and with such readiness—

[multi]tude of the giant bodies, more than one could ever tell. The artist, as an **imitation and rival of nature**, expressed them so accurately that the eyes and feet together grew weary, violently forced to rush greedily now to one part, now to another. No less detail appeared in the lifelike horses. Some were thrown down, some stumbling as they fell. Many, wounded and struck, indicated that their graceful life was breathing its last. Their hooves were placed poorly upon the fallen bodies, furious and unrestrained. And the giants, their armor crushed, were strictly embracing one another. Some were carried away with their feet caught in the foot-straps <note>original: "subsolea"</note>. Others were crushed under their own bodies. And some plunged down with their wounded horses. Many were girded with <term>parazonii</term> <note>small daggers worn by military officers</note> and sword-belts, and with ancient Persian swords, and multiple instruments of deadly shape. Some were clad in breastplates and helmets, marked with various crests; others were naked, appearing to leap with lively courage, intent on death, some wearing cuirasses and decorated with various and most noble military ornaments. Many had fearsome expressions as if shouting; some had a stubborn and furious appearance. As many as were about to die, with a thread-like detail rivaling nature, expressed the effect; and others were deceased, with unseen and manifold machines of war and death. This conflict and duel appeared so terrifying and horrible that you would say it was the bloodstained and powerful Mars himself at war with **Porphyrion and Alcyoneus** <note>leaders of the Giants in the Gigantomachia, the mythical battle against the Olympian gods</note>, and the flight that Pan <note>original: "heberon" — likely referring to the god Pan or Silenus, whose donkey's braying terrified the giants during the battle</note> caused with his donkey-like braying came back to memory. Here, then, were infinite giant bodies, final struggles, intense actions, breast-plated figures, and various deaths, with a victory hanging in the balance. Alas, my weary spirits and my intellect, confused by such constant variety, and my disordered senses, cannot properly endure, not only to narrate the whole, but even to express a part with the integrity of such polished stone-carving <note>term: "lithoglyphia" (the art of engraving or carving on stone)</note>.

And where, then, was born such great boasting, and such burning desire to pile up stones, joining them together into such a massive heap, pile, and summit? And with what vehicle? With what porters? ...fittingly composed, examining those excellent and choice stone statues of virginal workmanship, which suddenly moved me to sigh and sob warmly with emotion.

While my amorous and echoing sighs resounded in this solitary and deserted place, the heavy air reminded me of my **Divine** and immeasurably desired **Polia**. Oh, there was so little intermission where that amorous and celestial **Idea** <note>Poliphilo often refers to Polia as a "celestial Idea," blending his physical desire with Neoplatonic philosophy where the beloved is a reflection of divine perfection.</note> was not mirrored in my mind, serving as a constant companion on this, my so unknown journey. In her, my soul was firmly nested and rested contentedly, as if in a most safe fortress and a secure, unviolated **Asylum**. <note>original: "Asylo"; a place of refuge or sanctuary.</note> Having come to this place in such a manner, where my eyes were stolen and occupied by the sight of the copious and choice antiquarian work, I looked above all at a most beautiful door—so stupendous, of such incredible artifice, and of such elegant lineament as could ever be built or polished. Truly, I do not feel I possess enough knowledge to be able to describe it perfectly. This is chiefly because, in our age, the vernacular, proper, and ancestral terms peculiar to the art of building have been buried and extinguished along with the men of old. 

Oh, execrable and sacrilegious **barbarism**, <note>The author, Francesco Colonna, frequently laments the "barbarism" of the Middle Ages, which he believed destroyed the sophisticated Latin language and architectural secrets of Roman antiquity.</note> how you have invaded and plundered the most noble part of the precious Latin treasury and sanctuary! This ignorance, joined together with quivering, insatiable, and treacherous greed, has blinded that most high and excellent part of the world which **Rome** created as a sublime and far-reaching Empress.

In front of this egregious door (to speak of this first), in the open air, there was a **square plaza** <note>original: "platea Tetragona"</note> measuring thirty paces in diameter. It featured a remarkable pavement of marble squares, spaced one foot apart, interspersed with **tessellation** <note>Mosaic work made of small glass or stone cubes (tesserae).</note> in various intricate entwinings, bindings, and colors. In many parts, it was disrupted by the ruin of stones and overgrown with small bushes. At the far ends of this plaza, on the right and the left toward the mountains, there were two rows of colonnades arranged at a level, with the exquisite interval of the **Areostyle** <note term="Areostyle">An architectural term from Vitruvius describing a wide spacing between columns, specifically four diameters or more apart.</note> placed between them, according to the necessary requirement from one column to the next. Between one colonnade and the other, there was a space of fifteen paces. Some of these columns, indeed the greater part or number of them, could be seen intact. They featured **Doric** or **Pulvinated capitals**, <note term="Pulvinated">A "cushioned" or swelling architectural form. <meta>Continuing from the previous page, Poliphilo has entered the hollow, monumental statue of a human figure. After entering through its feet, he now explores the internal "anatomy" of the colossus, discovering it to be an intricate medical and philosophical diagram made manifest in three dimensions.</meta>

Having progressed from there into the stomach, and thence through hidden ducts <note>original: "latebroſi ducti"</note> to all the other parts of the internal organs, I arrived somewhat terrified. O wondrous conception! I gazed upon all the parts internally, just as they exist in a human body. And wherever I looked, the name of that part was inscribed in three languages <term>Chaldean, Greek, and Latin</term>—so that one could see the intestines, nerves, bones, veins, muscles, and flesh as they appear in any natural body. The inscriptions also explained which disease is generated in each part, its cause, cure, and remedy. Throughout all the coiled organs <note>original: "īglomate uiſcere"</note> there was a path and convenient access, with breathing holes <note>original: "reſpiracoli"</note> variously distributed through the body to illuminate the appropriate places. No part was less detailed than it is in nature.

And when I approached the heart, I saw by reading there how sighs are generated by love, and where love most heavily wounds. At this, entirely moved, from the depths of my own heart I drew a lowing sigh, calling upon **Polia** <note>Polia is the elusive beloved whom Poliphilo pursues throughout his dream-journey.</note>. At my cry, the whole bronze machine resounded with no small amount of terrifying sound. This was an art invented above all exquisite things, so that a man might become excellent in anatomy without even trying. O, illustrious geniuses of the past! O, truly golden age, when virtue competed with fortune! To this present age, you have left only ignorance and its rival, avarice, as our heritage.

I saw an exit in another part of the aforementioned thick structure: a forehead of a female head somewhat revealed among the ruins, with the rest buried by great ruptures. Because of this, assuming it was of similar workmanship but fearing the disordered and uneven ruins, I ceased my gazing and returned to the first location.

There, not far from the great horse, on a level plane, there appeared a massive **Elephant** made of a black stone, darker than obsidian <note>original: "Obſidio"</note>, sparked with gold and silver grains like scattered dust throughout the shining stone. The stubborn hardness of the stone was aptly shown by its clear luster, for it reflected every object placed before it perfectly, except where the metal had spread its green patina <note>original: "verdaceo erugine"</note>. And this was fitting, because on the summit of its very wide back, it had a marvelous bronze saddle <term>original: "Ephìppio Aeneo"</term>, with two tightening cinches wrapped around the monstrous body. Between these, held by large bindings with clasps made of the same stone, was a square base corresponding to the thickness of the **Obelisk** placed above it. For no weight should have air or a vacuum beneath it; because where there is a void, it is not solid nor durable.

This square part was beautifully polished on each of its four faces <note>The text says "three faces," but the context of a square base and obelisk usually implies four; I have stayed true to the narrative's focus on the visible sides.</note> with Egyptian characters <note>hieroglyphs</note>. This back-carrying monster was expressed with the most diligent wonder and precision, as perfectly as could be fashioned by rule and art. <meta>continuity: Poliphilo has just finished interpreting the hieroglyphic inscriptions on the base of the elephant statue and now turns his attention back to the surrounding ruins, specifically a horse, a colossus, and a magnificent gate.</meta>

Having left this most excellent, mysterious, and inconceivable structure, I returned again to gaze upon the marvelous **Horse**. It had a bony and lean head, proportionately small; it was an excellent representation, appearing restless and impatient of delay. One could almost see the quivering of its muscles <note>original: "pulpamenti," referring to the fleshy parts of the anatomy</note>, looking more alive than sculpted. It bore a Greek word carved into its forehead: **GENERATION** <note>original: "ΓΕΝΕA" (Genea), meaning origin, race, or birth</note>. Beyond it lay many other large shards and fragments of various outlines among massive heaps of jagged ruins. Of all these things, voracious and fleeting time had kindly spared only these four stupendous works: the **Gate**, the **Horse**, the **Colossus**, and the **Elephant**. O holy fathers, ancient craftsmen, what cruelty invaded your great virtue, that you carried the disinheritance of such great riches with you to the grave?

Having arrived then at this most ancient gate—a work most remarkable, constructed with exquisite regulation and art, and with noble ornaments of sculpture and various outlines—I was studious and inflamed with the pleasure of understanding the fertile intellect <note>original: "fetoso intellecto," a characteristic phrase of the author meaning an intellect pregnant with ideas</note> and the keen investigation of the perspective Architect. Thus, I subtly scrutinized its dimensions, its outline, and its practical execution.

I diligently measured a square placed beneath the columns, two per side. From this measurement, I easily understood the entire symmetry of the aforementioned gate, which I shall briefly explain. Imagine a four-sided figure <term>tetragona figura: a square or rectangle</term> marked **A. B. C. D.** divided by three vertical lines and three equidistant horizontal lines; these will create sixteen squares. By then adding to the figure an amount equal to half its size and dividing the addition with those same partitions, one finds twenty-four squares. This figure of "small cords" <note>original: "cordicelle," referring to the strings used by architects to lay out proportions</note> offers itself as a useful and opportune tool for recording segments in short form, or for use in fine craftsmanship <term>lepturgia: from the Greek for delicate or minute work</term> and in painting. By drawing two diagonal lines again in the first figure **A. B. C. D.**, and further marking it with two lines—one vertical and one horizontal—intersecting each other, four squares were made. Likewise, in that empty space above the equilateral sides <note>original: "isospleure," likely referring to the triangles formed by the grid</note>, four median points were made, and by drawing lines from one to another, a **Rhombus** is constituted.

Having drafted the predicted figures in such a way, I fitly considered what reason these blind moderns have for thinking so highly of themselves in the building art <term>ædificatoria: the science and art of architecture</term> when they do not even know what it is? They rule with such enormous errors in their false shrines <note>original: "ædicule"</note>, both sacred and profane, public and private, dishonoring the parts that proceed from the center and neglecting that which nature shows and teaches. It is a golden and heavenly saying and document that virtue consists in the "mean" <note>The "Golden Mean" or middle path</note> and happiness consists in it, as the poet sings; if this is deserted and neglected, it must necessarily result in disorder and everything being full of faults.

--- Page 39 ---
<meta>continuity: Having approached the Great Gate, Poliphilo begins to analyze its geometric and architectural principles, shifting from a description of its beauty to a technical explanation of its design.</meta>

c ii

Because it is unsightly for any part to be mismatched with its principal whole. Yet, if order and rules are removed, what thing can be offered that is fitting, or pleasing, or worthy of dignity? Therefore, the cause of such an unbecoming error arises from a lack of knowledge <note>original: "ignorantia negatiua," a philosophical term for the simple absence of knowledge</note> and has its origin in a lack of learning. Nevertheless, although the perfection of this most worthy art does not deviate from righteousness, the skillful and industrious **Architect**—in order to please the eye with the object—may licitly polish his work through addition and subtraction. Above all, he must preserve the solid whole, harmonized with the universe. 

This "solid" I call the entire body of the **Building** <term>fabrica: the physical structure or "fabric" of the edifice</term>, which is the primary intent, invention, foresight, and **Symmetry** <note>original: "Symmetria," referring to the classical concept of harmonious proportions between parts</note> of the Architect. When it is well-examined and executed without its accessories, it reveals (unless I am mistaken) the excellence of his genius, for ornamentation is thereafter an easy task. It is also of great importance how things are distributed: one should not place the **Corona** <term>the vertical "crown" or face of a cornice</term> at the feet, but at the head; and thus the **Ovolo** <term>ouolato: a rounded, convex molding, often carved with egg-and-dart patterns</term>, the **Dentil** <term>denticulato: small, block-like tooth moldings</term>, and the rest must be destined for their congruent places. 

Thus, the ordering and the principal invention are shared among the rare few, while for the many common or unlearned folk, the ornaments are provided as common labor. Therefore, the manual craftsmen are but the ministers of the Architect. The Architect himself must in no way succumb to cursed and treacherous avarice. Beyond his learning, he should be well-spoken, kind, benevolent, gentle, patient, witty, resourceful, a curious and universal investigator, and slow. I say "slow" so that he may not be hasty to make errors; of this, enough has been said.

Finally, by reducing the last three figures demonstrated into one, and adding the second made of the sixteen squares contained within it, this figure will be produced. From this, then remove the rhombus and the diagonals, leaving the three perpendiculars and the three straight lines, except for the middle one, which ends truncated between the perpendiculars. By this rule, two perfect squares are found, one upper and the other lower, each containing four squares within itself. 

In the lowest square, by drawing the diagonal and raising it perpendicularly toward the straight line A.B., one will easily find, through its offset, the thickness of the arch and the **Antae** <term>pilasters or piers formed by the thickening of the end of a wall</term>. Thus, the line A.B. will be the proper place for the extended or straight **Architrave** <term>trabe: the main beam resting on the columns</term>. The midpoint of the truncated line E.F. will be the point from which to curve the **Arched Architrave** <term>arcotrabe: a lintel that follows the curve of an arch</term> into a **Semicircle** <term>hemicyclo: a half-circle</term>. This should have as much addition at its inverted corners as the semi-diameter of its thickness. Otherwise, if there is such a defect, I do not call it perfect. But this was most beautifully and exquisitely and diligently observed by the excellent and skilled ancients in their arches, to give the arch elegance and suitable resistance, and to avoid the obstruction of the projections of the **Abaci** <term>abachi: the flat slabs forming the top of column capitals</term>.

<summary>This page outlines the theoretical and moral qualifications of an architect, emphasizing the importance of symmetry and the "solid" structure over mere ornament, followed by a technical geometric guide for constructing a perfectly proportioned arch and architrave.</summary>
<keywords>architectural theory, symmetry, building fabric, moldings, geometry, architrave, antae, abacus, architect's virtues</keywords>

<meta>continuity: Poliphilo continues his technical analysis of the Great Gate, moving from general architectural principles to the specific measurements and proportions of the base, the frieze, and the crowning pediment.</meta>

Now, beneath the paired columns on either side, the square base—whether you call it a **Small Altar** <term>arula: a small altar, here used to describe a pedestal base</term> or a **Podium** <term>podium: a continuous projecting base or pedestal</term>—began from a **Plinth** <term>plinth: the square block at the very bottom of a column base</term> raised one foot from the level of the stone-paved **Area** <note>original: "silicata Area," referring to a floor paved with flint or hard stone</note>. This plinth also served as the continuous border. From this, the recurved **Simas** <term>sima: a molding with a double curve, often used as a gutter or cap</term>, **Tori** <term>torus: a large, convex, cushion-like molding</term>, and **Small Channels** <term>canalioli: small decorative grooves or scotia moldings</term> with their **Astragals** <term>astragal: a small semi-circular molding, often shaped like a string of beads</term> harmoniously stepped up toward the Podium. With the proper and required binding, they formed the **Socles** <term>sochi: the lowest part of a base or pedestal</term> for the **Pilasters** <term>ante: the thickened ends of walls or square pillars flanking a doorway</term> or bases. Consequently, above the Podium, the **Cornice** was extended with the recurved Sima and the other intersecting lines.

Between the line A. B. and the final line of the master square M. N., I found that it was occupied by a third; that is, it was divided into four partitions. Three of these are attributed to the straight **Architrave** <term>trabe: the horizontal beam resting on the columns</term>, the **Frieze** <term>zophoro: a frieze, literally "bearing figures"</term>, and the Cornice. The Cornice claimed for itself one part more than the Architrave and the **Ornamented Frieze** <term>phrygio: an ornate frieze, named after Phrygian embroidery</term>. This means that if five portions are assigned to the Architrave, and just as many to the Frieze equally, the Cornice rightfully usurps six. And it exceeded this limited boundary by as much as the discreet and skilled architect had fashioned in a sloping drip-edge grazing over the margin determined for the Sima of the aforementioned Cornice—leaving it hollowed out by half a foot. This was not observed in vain, for it ensures that the bottom of the carved works placed above are not hidden by the projection or prominence of the Cornice. Nevertheless, the part following above the decorations can be made even more magnificent, just as it happens with the Frieze, which may exceed the assigned **Symmetry** <note>original: "Symmetria," referring to the harmonious proportion of parts</note> for this reason. Following thereafter, above this first crowning, came a perfect square with such a rule:

However much the Frieze projected over the plumb line of the columns, that square was extended by the same amount. This was divided into two partitions; however much one of these was found to be, that same thickness was attributed to the uppermost Cornice. These two squares having been established, one on each side, the remaining space between them—at the plumb line of the door opening—was divided into seven portions. The middle one was reserved for a leaf-pattern or a **Niche**, where a statue of a **Nymph** resided. Three portions were then left on the collateral sides, both here and there.

The extent of the projection of the upper Cornice is easily discovered: by making a **Square** <term>tetragono: a four-sided figure</term> from the line of its thickness and dividing it by the **Diagonal**, one finds the correct rule for its prominence.

Now, taking the entire figure of the twenty-four squares together, one finds it to be a **Sesquialter** <note>the sesquialter ratio is a 3:2 proportion, where one side is 1.5 times the length of the other</note>. This figure consists of O. P. Q. T. It is manifest that it contains within itself a square and a half. This half being equally divided into six portions by straight lines, there are five intersecting lines and six partitions. Above the fifth upper line, marked at its center, is found the regular height of the **Peak of the Pediment** <term>fastigio dil frontispicio: the triangular top of a classical building's facade</term>, with the lines sloping down from there over—

The carving of the lateral extension of the **Corona** <term>corona: the flat, vertical face of a cornice</term> appeared appropriately sloped. Its edges, or extremities, joined perfectly with the **Cyma** <term>cimacii: moldings with a wave-like profile</term> of the crowning projection.

Finally, the pediment, with exquisite correspondence, shared the lines of the elegant cornice; in its first order, it occupied the plane of the final square projection, followed by a portion of **Denticulated** <note>original: "coronice denticulata," a cornice featuring a row of small, tooth-like blocks</note> cornice, within which the angular flat surface continued.

The aforementioned door was most diligently crafted with a smooth, level finish of cut stone slabs, the wavy patterns of the stone matching perfectly across the joins of the slabs. It possessed a lovely harmony of inlaid work, and the material was bright and graceful. On one side and the other, separated from the door opening by two paces, there still stood two great and superb columns, buried up to their **Plinth** <term>crepidine: the base or pedestal of a structure</term> in the rough debris of the ruins. Removing the ruins as much as I was able, I laid bare the bronze bases, and the capitals were of the same material, excellently cast. For my own pleasure, I measured the thickness of one base; by doubling it, it gave the full diameter of the bottom thickness of the column. By this measurement, I found its height to be more than twenty-eight cubits <note>original: "dui detriginta cubiti," literally "two from thirty," a Latinism for twenty-eight</note>. The two columns closest to the door were of the finest **Porphyry** <term>Porphyrite: a hard purple igneous rock</term> and graceful **Ophite** <term>Ophites: a green mottled stone resembling snakeskin</term>; the other two were **Fluted** <note>original: "cariatice, ouero ſtriate, ouero canaliculate," referring to the vertical channels or grooves on a column shaft</note> and excellently finished. Beyond these, on the left and right sides, others stood in regular pairs with a modest **Entasis** <term>entheſi: the slight convex swelling in the shaft of a column</term>, made of the hardest **Laconian stone** <note>original: "petra duriffima Laconica," likely referring to *verde antico*, a green marble from Laconia, Greece</note>.

The radius of the bottom circumference of the column determined the height of the base, which consisted of **Tori** <term>thori: large, convex moldings</term>, an orbicule or **Scotia** <term>Scotia: a concave molding, also called a trochilus</term>, and a **Plinth**. That radius being divided into thirds, the Plinth took one part for itself; its width was one and a half diameters. Dividing the remaining two parts into four, one part was taken by the upper Torus. The remaining three parts were divided into two equal portions: one for the bottom Torus, and the other for the hollowed-out Scotia. With its edges taking a seventh part of it, I found such measurement to be elegantly observed by the skilled craftsmen. Above the regular capitals of the aforesaid columns, there extended a magnificent **Architrave** <term>trabe: the horizontal beam resting on the capitals</term> or epistyle, with its bottom **Fascia** <term>faſcia: a long, flat horizontal band</term> decorated with rounded whorls or beads, and the second fascia with a long sequence of truncated spindles, interspersed with two flattened spools in a line. The third fascia, with approved beauty, was covered with "eared" moldings and noble stalk-like foliage of the most excellent workmanship. Sitting above this was the **Frieze** <term>zophoro: a decorative band, literally "bearing life/figures"</term> of sinuous leaves; in its large spirals or whorls were various stalks and flowers with lovely tendrils deeply carved, in which many birds were nesting. Above this then followed a row of exquisite **Mutules** <term>mutuli: rectangular blocks projecting under a cornice</term>, with...

undulated insertion. Above these began the inverted progression of a copious cornice. Beyond this ruined crowning, the greater part appeared demolished and broken, with traces or imitations of large, paired windows, stripped of their ornaments, poorly indicating what the completed and perfect building might have been. Below the aforementioned beam <note>the entablature</note> descended the peak, or the gabled summit of the pediment of the preserved door. There, between its slope and the line of the beam, that space imitated a scalene figure, showing a triangle with unequal sides or ribs. Beneath the beam in the space between the columns, it was supported by wonderful **Mutules** <term>mutili: rectangular blocks positioned under the corona of a cornice</term>, with artful spacing. In this described figure, as much as the greater space could embrace, two roundels were hollowed out in imitation of a plate, bound around the edges with waves, **Guttae** <term>gullule: small drop-like ornaments</term>, and **Scotia** <term>scotie: concave moldings</term>, where at the highest level in the middle of the circumscribed lines, there swelled a **Torus** <term>thoro: a large convex molding</term>, nobly dressed in oak foliage, one leaf layered beneath the other in company, bound around by hollowed thongs with scattered fruits. The chest area was covered by a cloak <note>original: "palio," referring to the pallium or ancient mantle</note> with an ancient knot over the left shoulder, with shaggy beards and laureled brows, possessing a worthy and majestic character.

On the square projection of the **Frieze** <term>Zophoro: a frieze, often decorated with figures of animals or people</term> above the aforementioned columns in front, was such a carving: an **Eagle** with outspread wings, with its taloned claws resting upon a swollen bundle of leaves and fruit hanging in the middle. The slender ends of this bundle, here and there, were bound by spreading **Cymatia** <term>Cymoſe: wave-like moldings</term> and held suspended, with such precise carving they seemed almost hollowed through.

Therefore, the conspicuous Gate was set within the level surface of the intercolumniation, made of marble slabs joined together with the highest skill. Now that the required demonstration of the principal members of the said magnificent gate has been somewhat provided, it seems appropriate to explain its pleasing and most beautiful ornaments in what follows. For to a serious architect, *being* is more important than *well-being*. This is because it primarily belongs to him to optimally arrange the solid structure and to define in the mind (as I said above) the universal building, rather than its ornaments, which are accessories to the principal part. Thus, for the first, the fertile skill of one person alone is

# POLIPHILO, HAVING SUFFICIENTLY DEMONSTRATED THE SYMMETRY OF THE GREAT GATE, CONTINUES BY EXCELLENTLY DESCRIBING ITS POLISHED AND EXPERTLY CRAFTED ORNAMENTATION, AND HOW WONDERFULLY COMPOSED IT WAS.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring interlaced knotwork patterns.</image-desc>

To the noble crowd who assiduously devote their labor to pleasant Love: may it not be tiresome (I pray) that I have delayed somewhat in the narrative above. To those, perhaps, it is not in the least bit pleasing, being eager to understand that subject—which, however bitter it may be in itself—they nourish themselves by placing their festive hearts within it with a patient soul. Since human affection is naturally variable, let it not be held against them for this reason; bread is pleasing to an uninjured palate, even if sometimes it is displeasing to a corrupted one, but rather by the person whose tasting brings pleasure, let it be kindly received. Because in some part I have moved toward the proper goal of architectural design—which is the excellence of invention—to acquire the solid body of the building through modular measure. Then, once that invention is freely found, the Architect reduces it into minute divisions, no more and no less than a musician who, having discovered the intonation and the measured time in a single whole <note>original: "maxima," a musical note of the longest duration in medieval notation</note>, then proportions it into small, elegant chromatic notes <note>original: "Chromatice concinnamente," referring to the Greek chromatic scale used for ornamentation</note>, and harmoniously applies them over the solid foundation. By such a comparison, after the invention, the principal rule peculiar to the Architect is the squaring <note>original: "quadratura," the geometric process of determining proportions</note>. And by distributing this into the smallest parts, the harmony of the building and its proportional symmetry <term>commodulatione: the harmonious relationship between the parts and the whole</term> offer themselves, along with the appropriate corollaries to its principal part. For which reason, this gate being most beautiful by its admirable composition and invention, and having such remarkable elegance added to it, with such corrected distribution that no part, even in its lowest detail, was found lacking, I now consider it worthy to describe its perfect completion.

On the right, there first appears a **Stilypodio** <term>stilypodio: also called a stylobate or pedestal, the continuous base supporting a row of columns</term>, or column-footing, beneath the bases of the columns. From this, a small cornice <term>cornicetta: a decorative molding at the top of the pedestal</term> is measured out precisely above; and with its moderate joints at the bottom of the perfect square, it remains by rule wider than it is high—that is, rectangular. I am forced to use common expressions rather than the precise vernacular of the ancients, because we have degenerated and dwindled from such a treasure of knowledge that could explain it correctly.

...all the particulars of such a work. But for those who are unrefined in such matters, we shall reserve our reasoning.

So in this Altar <note>original: "Ara," a pedestal or sacrificial altar often used in classical architecture as a base for statues</note> (as I call it), deeply set with moldings <note>original: "gulature," referring to cyma-style architectural moldings</note> and covered in leaves, with modest stepping of fine incisions. Between these, made of transparent alabaster stone, the proportionate bands remained untouched, surrounding the extremity of the equal-sided, quadrangular front. With the greatest diligence, there was carved a man of an age exceeding virility, of a robust rusticity, with a thick beard of hair curled with hardness at the chin, emerging poorly from his tough skin.

He sat upon a stone, girded with a goatskin. Having been flayed, the skin was tied around his flanks by its hind parts. And the part of the neck, with the hair facing toward him, hung between his varicose shins. In front of him, in the middle of his swollen calves, was an *acmon* <note>original: "Acmone," from the Greek for anvil</note>, or anvil, fixed into a knotty piece of a truncated tree. Upon this he was intently fashioning a pair of glowing little wings, holding his mallet high and striking his craft. And there before him stood a most noble Matron <note>likely Venus</note>, to whose delicate shoulders were attached two wings of plumy feathers. She held a naked infant, her son <note>Cupid</note>, who sat with his little buttocks upon the fleshy thigh of his mother; the Mother Goddess held him slightly raised, with her bare foot placed upon a stone, which was joined to the seat of the hammering smith, fashioned as a small stony mound. There was a small furnace in a little cave in which burned a glowing coal fire. And the Matron had her tresses neatly brought back over her broad brow, adorning her full head, expressed so delicately that I do not know why the standing statues nearby, who also found themselves at the smith's work, were not moved to life by her beauty. Furthermore, there was an armed warrior of a ferocious countenance, dressed in an antique aegis-breastplate <note>original: "ægide," the mythological protective armor associated with Zeus or Athena, here likely worn by Mars</note>, with the terrifying head of Medusa on the chest, and with other noble and exquisite breastplate-pieces. With a transverse belt across his broad chest, he held a spear somewhat raised with his muscular arm. His head was protected by a crested helmet <note>original: "galea"</note>, while his other arm was not visible, being obstructed by the figures in front. There also appeared a youth, seen from the chest up, dressed in thin cloth, beyond the bowed head of the said smith.

The artist had diligently rendered the aforementioned story upon a flat surface of coral-colored stone, and set it within the wavy border of the Altar. This coloring shone through the translucent stone, the color being placed only behind the naked bodies and limbs, and in the surrounding spaces between the figures. They appeared like flesh-colored roses
