...rian. Every line of this pedestal base was seen equally in the other, differing only in the subject of the story.

Similarly, on the left pedestal base <note>original: "subcolumnio," the block or plinth forming the base for a column</note>, a naked man of mature years was carved. His face was kind, and he showed signs of great speed. He too sat upon a square seat, adorned with ancient carvings. He wore buskins <note>original: "coturni," high boots</note> on his feet, laced from the heel toward the calves. From there sprang two winged sandals <note>original: "petasi," usually referring to a traveler's hat, but here the text specifies "one for each foot," indicating the wings of Mercury</note>. There stood that same Matron <note>Venus</note>, depicted as a divine nude. Upon her narrow chest, two small breasts <note>original: "mamillule"</note> budded, firm in their hardness and roundness. With wide hips, she was so similar to the other one portrayed that they seemed to be struck from the same mold. She was offering her young son <note>Cupid</note> to this man to be tutored. The man leaned toward the winged boy, who stood on his little feet before him, and skillfully showed him three arrows. By his gesture, one could easily guess he was teaching him the art of how he should use them. The divine mother held the empty quiver and the unstrung bow. At the feet of this master lay a serpent-entwined caduceus <note>original: "uiperato caduceo," the staff of Mercury, messenger of the gods</note>. Also found there were a warrior and a helmeted woman <note>likely Minerva/Athena</note>, who bore a trophy <note>original: "Trophæo"</note> upon a spear, consisting of an ancient breastplate hanging there, and at the top a sphere with two wings. Between one wing and the other was inscribed: **NOTHING IS STABLE** <note>original Latin: "NIHIL FIRMUM"</note>. She was dressed in a fluttering draped garment <note>original: "fubula," likely a variant of fibula, a brooch, used here to describe the pinned garment</note> which revealed her chest.

The two prompt porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrice," a precious purple-red volcanic stone</note> Doric columns, seven diameters in height, pressed down upon each of these described squares. They were of a dark reddish-purple color with lighter spots scattered throughout, polished and shining. They were fluted <note>original: "canaliculate"</note> with twenty-four grooves each, separated by precise fillets or little cords. However, of the three parts, the lower one was rudented <note>original: "rudentata," a style where the lower third of the fluting is filled with a convex molding resembling rope</note>. I pondered the reason why they were carved thus, with the hollows and the rudented third, and I thought that this most excellent structure, or temple, must have been ritually dedicated to both sexes: that is, to a God and a Goddess, or to a mother and son, or a father and wife, or a father and son, and such. Therefore, the skilled ancient fathers attributed a greater portion of the hollow carving to the female sex and the rudenting to the male, because that slippery nature exceeds the virile in wantonness <note>original: "lasciuiuia"</note>.

The reason for all the fluting in a Goddess's temple was that the grooves signify the folds of a woman’s garment. Above these they placed the capital with hanging volutes <note>original: "Volute," the spiral scrolls of a capital</note>, as a sign of the curled hair and feminine ornament. Those caryatids <note>original: "cariatice," female figures used as columns</note> which have a curled <note>original: "Cincinata"</note> woman's head as a capital were first made for the temple of that rebellious people. Once they were brought back under the yoke, they were used as an exhibition of their inconstancy, just as women, in significance...

...of the columns thus built for perpetual memory.

These excellent and fine columns mentioned above were supported by bases made of bronze <note>original: "æramento"</note>, featuring torus moldings <note>convex, rounded moldings at the base of a column</note> or scotias <note>original: "cymbie," a concave molding</note> decorated with oak leaves and their fruits, tightly bound with a winding cord, resting upon the underlying plinth. The capitals placed on top were of the same material as the bases, crafted with all the harmony and requirement fitting for the work. Not even the skilled Callimachus <note>a 5th-century BCE Greek sculptor credited with inventing the Corinthian capital</note>, when he saw the acanthus sprouting from the basket <note>original: "calatho"</note> over the grave of the Corinthian maiden, created anything so beautiful to express its charming ornament. They were covered by curved abaci <note>the flat slab at the top of a capital</note>, or rather, inward-curving lids decorated with a lily in the center. The bell <note>original: "uaso," the core of the capital</note> of these was elegantly clothed in two rows of eight acanthus leaves, in the Roman and Corinthian manner. From these leaves emerged smaller spirals <note>original: "elices," the volutes of a capital</note> which met in the middle of the bell, producing the lily beautifully attached to the curve of the abacus. From there, the stalks <note>original: "cauliculi," the stems from which the acanthus leaves and volutes spring</note> curled under the overhang of the abacus. Such columns as Agrippa masterfully placed in the porch <note>original: "pronao"</note> of the wondrous Pantheon, assigned for their height a full diameter of the base of the column, with observable symmetry in every part and accessory.

Now speaking of the threshold of the door: it was made of a huge, leek-green stone <note>original: "petra praxina," likely prasin or a green porphyry</note>, mottled with a scattering of white, black, and yellow spots, and other various, irregular markings, and it was extremely hard. Above this stood the straight doorposts <note>original: "ante"</note>, clear and illustrious in their appearance within the opening; they were as wide as a single pace, matching the width of the threshold below. But their outward-facing surfaces were nobly carved. There was no sign of hinges in the threshold nor in the lintel above. Nor did there appear any trace of iron clamps or hooks <note>original: "harpiconi"</note> holding the stone capitals in place. From there, the architrave rose into an arch or semicircle <note>original: "hemicyclo"</note>, with the required lines and measured bands <note>original: "fascie"</note> of the entablature. These included beads <note>original: "piluli"</note> or berries, and joined spindles <note>original: "fusuli," referring to bead-and-reel molding</note>, as if sewn together in a single thread, and "dog's ears" <note>architectural extensions of the architrave</note>, with an undulating slope curved in the ancient fashion, or fringed with stalks. The keystone <note>original: "spina," "fibula," or "cuneo"</note> of this arch, worthy of admiration and of a subtle and daring invention, polished elegantly, presented itself as a most remarkable sight.

I gazed in astonishment, therefore, at an eagle carved into a hard, jet-black stone, appearing almost entirely detached from the solid rock, with its wings spread. It had lovingly snatched up a noble and most delicate boy <note>this refers to the myth of Ganymede</note> by his garments. The eagle was so careful that its sharp, hooked talons, though turned inward, did not harm his soft flesh. And so, by gripping him by the folds of his clothing and drawing its iron-strong feet toward its swollen and keeled bre—

...from the navel downward, the little infant was naked and hanging. His tender little buttocks rested between the feathered thighs of the Winged One <note>original: "Alite," referring here to a large bird, likely Jupiter's eagle in the myth of Ganymede</note>. This most beautiful little boy <note>original: "puerulo"</note>—worthy of the god who had snatched him for himself—showed in his little face a hint of fear of the fall. 

With both his little arms spread wide and his chubby little hands <note>original: "tuberule mane"</note> tightly gripping the wing-joint, he had committed himself to the spread wings—that is, to the wing-bone <note>original: "remigio," the primary structure of the wing</note>, which is the bone connected to the body that moves flexibly. Drawing up his plump little infant legs, he had his tiny feet crossed over the bird's widened tail, which most beautifully swept toward the underside of the arch’s ceiling. 

The little boy was carved with great artifice from the white vein of an Agate <note>original: "Achates"</note> or Onyx stone. The Winged One was made from the Sard <note>original: "Sardio," a reddish-brown stone</note>, which was the other vein joined within the same stone. Faced with such exquisite expression, I stood stunned, pondering how the elegant craftsman had so insightfully imagined applying that stone so perfectly to such a task and purpose. Indeed, I reasonably conjectured—from the ruffled feathers around the beak and the half-open beak with a playful tongue appearing—that the bird openly revealed itself to be entirely intent and dissolved in lust <note>The author suggests an erotic charge in the sculpture, common in Renaissance interpretations of the Ganymede or Leda myths</note>. The bird's back imitated the curve of the keystone <note>original: "clausula," the final stone at the top of an arch</note>, and it likewise carried the arched back of the little boy.

The rest of the arch-beam <note>original: "Arcotrabe"</note> was then arranged across the ceiling in square coffers <note>original: "cubiculi," recessed decorative panels</note> with excellent lines; from within these hung sharply carved rosettes, spanning the width of the pilasters <note>original: "Ante"</note> from the binding of the capitals. Above this binding, the structure extended beyond the pilasters, beneath the start of the curve of the wide vault, or rather, the opening of the gate.

In the triangles <note>the spandrels, the spaces between the curve of the arch and the rectangular frame</note> created by the arch, there was a shrine-bearer <note>original: "Pastophora," likely referring here to a winged Victory or Nymph</note> in most noble sculpture, of the craftsmanship the common people call a Cameo <note>original: "Chameo"</note>. With garments that fluttered to reveal the virginal little bodies, yielding in parts to show their beautiful calves, breasts, and arms, and with their hair loose and feet bare, they held out a victory trophy <note>original: "Trophæo"</note> toward the keystone. These figures perfectly occupied the entire triangular surface <note>original: "piano trigonale"</note> of the blackest stone, which served to highlight the reality of the metalwork and the milky-white, radiant Nymphs. Behind the colonnade, a bright white paneling of the finest marble was visible.

At each end of the bronze tablet were two supporting boys, or winged spirits, so perfectly formed that even the diligent sculptor of the famous carrying-boys on the **Ravenna Snail** <note>The "Ravenna Cochlea" or "Throne of Neptune," a famous classical relief known in the Renaissance for its exquisite carvings of putti.</note> never saw such a fine model. Their slightly swollen little hands reached out to the tablet, promptly holding it; they were naked and made of the same metal. This was aptly set upon a slab of **blue stone** <note>original: "petra Cyanea," likely lapis lazuli</note>, chosen more for its graceful color than for the kind that is ground into cakes to be made into perfect azure pigment, though it shone with a glassy luster.

On the front of the <term>frieze</term> <note>original: "Zophoro," the sculpted horizontal band between the architrave and the cornice</note> extending above the porphyry columns, there were spoils of war: breastplates, armor of interlaced rings, shields, helmets, bundles, axes, torches, quivers, javelins, and many other machines of war—no less of the air than of the sea and land, of most worthy craftsmanship. These trophies, even on the sides, undoubtedly indicated the victories, power, and triumphs that caused **High-Thundering Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> to be praised and caused mortals to perish in sweetness.

Following this in orderly fashion was the magnificent <term>cornice</term> <note>original: "Coronice," the topmost projecting part of the wall or entablature</note>, with lines that harmoniously joined such elegant work. For just as in the human body, when one quality disagrees with another, sickness follows because the parts do not exist in friendly agreement; and when the parts are not properly distributed in their rightful places, deformity ensues. In exactly the same way, a building is discordant and weak where one does not find the proper harmony and measured order. This is something modern **idiots** <note>Poliphilo frequently critiques contemporary architects who do not follow classical rules of proportion.</note> confuse, being ignorant of proper placement. Therefore, our most wise master likens a building to the human body—well-proportioned in its parts and decorously clothed.

Beyond this cornice, four square panels stood at different levels. Two stood above the order of the fluted <term>Caryatid columns</term> <note>columns carved in the shape of female figures</note>, and two were recessed. In the middle division between these two, there sat a Nymph, an excellent bronze relief <note>original: "anaglypho," a work carved in relief; "auricalcho," orichalcum or a golden-colored bronze</note>. She held two torches: one extinguished and turned toward the heavy earth, and one lit and held toward the Sun. The burning one was in her right hand, and the other in her left.

On the right side, then, in the square panel, I saw the jealous **Clymene** <note>Clymene was the mother of Phaethon by the Sun god Helios.</note> who...

It is evident that the rest of the aforementioned enclosure, on both sides, was a grand display of magnificent construction; this was clearly understood because some of the workmanship here and there remained preserved intact. In the lower sections, there were some short <term>dwarf columns<note>Original: "Nane columne." These are thick, stout columns designed to support massive weight.</note></term> designed to resist the unbearable weight. Others were of the **Corinthian** order with a masterful <term>entasis<note>Original: "Enthefi." The slight convex swelling in the shaft of a column, used to prevent the optical illusion of concavity.</note></term>, imbued with such moderate polish. Just as symmetry required, and as the demands of the heavy weight and ornamentation dictated, these proportions were modeled exactly after the human likeness, the rules of art having been skillfully acquired. Just as a man who must support a heavy weight needs to have large feet beneath robust legs, so in this measured building, the "dwarf" columns are assigned to the heavy load, and then the slender **Corinthian** and **Ionic** columns are added for decoration. According to the requirements of the building’s harmony, all parts consisted of a proven elegance. There was a fitting distribution of colored marbles and beautiful distinctions, offering a graceful sight: **Porphyry**, **Serpentine** <note>Original: "Ophite," a green stone with snake-like patterns.</note>, **Yellow Numidian**, **Alabaster**, **Red Granite** <note>Original: "Pyropecile," literally "fire-speckled."</note>, **Green Spartan**, and white marble with various undulating veins, and dark **Anthracite** stones mottled with the whitest spots. Others were of multiple colors confusedly mixed together. From the circumference, its height was determined by a different rule based on the diameter of the lower thickness.

I also found a rare form of cushioned <term>pulvinated<note>A "pulvinated" base or frieze has a convex, bulging profile, like a cushion.</note></term> bases. These, above the **Plinth**, had two <term>scotiae<note>Original: "trochili." The concave moldings at the base of a column.</note></term> separated by an interposition of necking and beads, along with the uppermost <term>torus<note>Original: "thoro." A large, convex semi-circular molding.</note></term>.

And in various parts, there was concealment by hanging and thick ivy, creeping up from the ground, that wood which separates Bacchus from Thetis <note>A poetic reference to ivy (associated with Bacchus) growing over stone or damp areas (Thetis, a sea nymph representing water/earth).</note> with its scattered clusters fertile with black berries and green down, occupying many places of the ancient building here and there, along with many other wall-growing shrubs. In the cracks grew the hardy **stonecrop**, and elsewhere hung the **navelwort** and the **Spring-born** flower <note>Original: "Erogenneto."</note>, which bears its own pleasing name, hanging down from the eaves. In other ruptures grew **pellitory-of-the-wall**, diuretic **chickweed**, **polypody** fern, **maidenhair** fern, and the fringed **spleenwort** with its rusty underside, and the jointed **lesser moonwort**, and other **houseleeks** that love ancient walls and stones, and **haircap moss**, and the green **spurge-olive** that dwells among ruins. Many worthy works of stone were clothed and covered by these and many other types of greenery.

And among the great and fluted columns, there was an inestimable collapse; they appeared not as columns, but as a confused heap of timber, broken upon the ground. Similarly, among the ruins were conspicuous remains of statues in multiple poses—many naked, some with wrinkled garments.

This was the true art, which reveals our confused ignorance, our detestable presumption, and our public and most harmful error. This is that clear light that sweetly invites us to its contemplation to illuminate our darkened eyes. For no one remains blind, except he who, resisting it, flees from it with open eyes. This art is she who accuses wicked greed—rapacious and the consumer of every virtue, a worm continually gnawing at the heart of whoever is its captive, a cursed obstacle and barrier to talented minds, and the mortal enemy of good architecture. It is the execrable idol of the present age, so unworthy and harmfully venerated. Oh, fatal poison, you know well how the wretched are harmed by you! How many magnificent works are ruined and partly forbidden because of it! 

For which reason, being seized and gripped by delight and unthinkable solace, and by holy and venerable antiquity with such grace and admiration, I found myself with wandering, unstable, and unsated gazes. WITHOUT FAIL, IT WOULD BE A GREAT AND LAUDABLE thing to be able to easily narrate and precisely describe the incredible workmanship and unbelievable composition of this vast structure, the magnitude of such a building, and the most remarkable gate, conveniently situated in a high and conspicuous place. Indeed, the delight of contemplating it exceeded my great admiration, because I judged that for the gods above, no work is difficult; yet I suspected that no artist or human knowledge could compose such vastness, express such grand concepts, devise such novelty, decorate with such elegance, or arrange with such singular <term>Symmetry<note>Original: "Symmetria," a Vitruvian term referring to the proportional relationship between the various parts of a building and the whole.</note></term>, and perfectly define—without need for addition or correction—the noble and inconceivable display of the aforementioned structure.

For this reason, I would not doubt for a moment that if the <term>natural historian<note>A reference to Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose "Natural History" served as the primary Roman encyclopedia for art and science.</note></term> had seen or understood this, he would have looked with disdain upon Egypt, even while admiring the industry and genius of its craftsmen. Such a fertile and delightful design was presented with outstanding carving, filled harmoniously with little aquatic monsters in simulated water and with modest sea-nymphs <note>Original: "plemmyruli," likely a diminutive of the Greek *plemmyra* (flood/tide), here referring to water spirits or beings of the waves.</note>, half-men and half-women, with breathing, fish-like tails. Some sat in strange chariots <note>Original: "Bige," a two-horse chariot.</note> drawn by swift dolphins, crowned with the cold flower of the water lily, their seats fashioned from their own leafy forms. Some carried multiple vessels filled with abundant fruit and packed riches. Others, with bundles of sweet flag <note>Original: "achori," a plant used in perfumes.</note> and flowers of wood-sage <note>Original: "barba Siluana," literally "sylvan beard," likely wood-sage or a similar wild herb.</note>, struck one another. Some were girded with thistles; on the other side, some wrestled while riding upon hippopotami. And there were various other unseen beasts protected by turtle-shells <note>Original: "protectione Chilonea," referring to the shell of a tortoise.</note>. Here one gave themselves to lust, and there to various games and festivities, with lively efforts and movements most excellently carved and expressed. These ornaments adorned both ends completely.

Within the curve of the vault, I saw most diligent vermiculated work <note>Original: "uermiculata," a type of mosaic where the tesserae are laid in curved lines to resemble the tracks of worms, often used to create detailed pictorial effects.</note> of exquisite glass tessellation, with a gilded surface and every most pleasing color. First, a frieze <note>Original: "phrygio," here meaning an ornamental border or band.</note> two feet wide presented itself. Circling around, it decorated the outer edges of the entire vaulted space from the aforementioned moldings upward, running along the length of the vaulted peak with social union and vibrant colors. They looked as if they had only just been composed, with natural foliage of emerald green, with crimson <note>Original: "Puniceo."</note> undersides, and flowers of blue <note>Original: "Cianei."</note> and purple <note>Original: "Phœnicei," likely referring to the deep Phoenician red or flame-color.</note> and blended hues, with graceful twists and knots. In the space contained within these, I marveled at such ancient history depicted there.

The young girl **Europa** swimming to Crete upon the deceptive bull <note>The god Zeus disguised himself as a bull to abduct the princess Europa.</note>. And the edict of **King Agenor** to his sons, **Cadmus**, **Phoenix**, and **Cilix**: that they must follow and find their violated sister. And if they did not find her, they were never to return. Having slain the scaly **Dragon** at the rising spring, and afterward having consulted **Apollo**, they were determined with their companions to build cities where the lowing heifer should stop. Thus that land preserves to this day the name of the **Bellowing** <note>Original: "Boato," referring to Boeotia, derived from the Greek *bous* (ox) and the sound it makes.</note> for all eternity. **Cadmus** then built Athens <note>Traditionally, Cadmus is the founder of Thebes; Poliphilo frequently alters or confuses classical myths.</note>. The other brother founded **Phoenicia**. The third, **Cilicia**. This mosaic painting was excellently arranged and executed with precise order, using natural colors as the fiction required for the actions, locations, and the appropriate expression of the story.

On the opposite side, in this same manner, I saw the lustful **Pasiphae**, inflamed by infamous love and hiding within the wooden machine <note>The wooden cow built by the inventor Daedalus to allow Pasiphae to mate with a bull, resulting in the birth of the Minotaur.</note>...

It happened that I, with lips parted, stared most intensely (my restless and ever-ready eyelids never moving), with my soul rapt, attending solely to the most beautiful, well-disposed, perfectly ordered, artfully depicted, and elegantly expressed histories. They remained inviolate by any rupture, for so tenacious was the powerful glue that the glass tesserae <note>Small square tiles used to create mosaics.</note>, pressed together like pages and perpetually bound, stood unharmed to this very hour, with not a single one moved from its place. For the outstanding artisan had gathered every possible diligence for this excellent work. I saw how the lines of the buildings drew toward the central point <note>original: "obiecto"</note>, and how some places almost vanished from the eyes, and how unfinished things were reduced little by little to perfection, and vice versa, his artistic judgment yielding to the eyes. All this was accompanied by exquisite details <note>original: "parergi," referring to the decorative background or accessory parts of a work of art.</note>: those fountains, mountains, hills, groves, and animals, their coloring softened by distance and by the opposing light, with graceful reflections in the folds of the garments and other features, with no small emulation of skillful nature. I was so full of wonder and so absorbed that I was almost no longer present in myself.

By this way, I reached the end of the passage where these gracious histories terminated, because beyond that point there was a most dense darkness that I did not dare to enter. But as I turned back from there—behold! Without any pause, I heard through the jagged ruins something like a crashing of bones and crackling branches. I stood still, trembling, my sweet solace interrupted and cut away. The noise came ever closer and louder toward the door, and then I heard a massive hissing of an enormous serpent. I was struck senseless. My voice failed me, my hair stood on end, and I did not have the courage to flee or to rush into that pitch-black darkness.

...Indeed, I firmly believed that I had arrived within the inextricable structure of the wise Daedalus <note>The mythical architect who designed the Labyrinth of Crete for King Minos.</note>, or perhaps that of Porsena <note>Lars Porsena, an Etruscan king whose legendary tomb was said to be a labyrinth so complex that no one could find their way out.</note>, containing so many inexplicable twists and turns with frequent doors that promised an exit, only to lead one back to those same errors. **Architrave, Frieze, and Cornice** <note>original: "Trabetta, Zophoro & Coronice"</note>. Above these was also added a fourth part of the square, dedicated to the pediment. This most beautiful Nymph lay sleeping comfortably upon a spread-out cloth. Under her head, the cloth was beautifully padded and folded into a cushion-like mound. These mixed waters then flowed out through a water channel or little stream. By the one being tempered by the other, they made all green things sprout. The hot water rose so high that it did not harmfully interfere with the other for anyone who placed their lips to the right breast to suck and drink as they passed by.

**R**eceived affably and greatly reassured by the compassionate nymphs, and entirely comforted by the charming maidens, my parched spirits were revived in no small measure. I reverently replied: "Most lovely Nymphs, if a thousand various tongues were found within me, I would not know how to properly render the well-deserved thanks and express gratitude for such domestic kindness; for you have most opportunely brought me back to life. What Propylaeum <term>Propylaeum</term><note>A monumental gateway leading into a temple or palace</note>, or indeed what vestibule or royal portico could compare? To this, Titus Caesar <note>Roman Emperor known for his lavish building projects</note> must justly yield, despite his Phoenician <note>deep crimson or purple-red</note> stones, so reflective and polished that any dull mind would find itself condemned in trying to describe them. Add further the dignity of the window-work and the conspicuous door, the most noble podium, and the outstanding expression of the builder’s art. No less excellent was the marvelous ceiling, most beautifully coffered <note>original: "lacunato"</note>, with small square and round recessed panels set within undulating patterns covered in foliage. These were decorated with exquisite outlines, gilded with pure gold and deep Cyanean <note>original: "Cyaneo"—a dark, lapis-lazuli blue</note> colors, and elegantly painted. Let every other marvelous building lose its fame here.

Having now reached the threshold of the spectacular door, behold, the way was closed by a pleasant and wonderful intervening curtain stretched across it. It was made entirely of gold thread and silk, woven and embroidered together, featuring two most worthy figures. One of them was surrounded by every tool fit for labor. The other, with a lifted virginal face, was gazing intently at the heavens. Their beauty was such that I could not wrongly say even the brush of the famous Apelles <note>The most celebrated painter of ancient Greece</note> could have equalled it.

Then my eloquent, most beautiful, and charming companions each kindly joined her right hand with mine, wishing to lead me in. Welcoming me, they said: "Poliphilo, this is the order to be observed by which one must enter into the venerable presence and sublime majesty of our Queen. This principal and primary curtain does not allow anyone to pass without being received by a simple and vigilant damsel who serves as gatekeeper, called Cinossia <note>original: "Cinosia"—derived from the Greek for "motion" or "activity"</note>." Hearing our arrival, she immediately presented herself and politely moved the curtain aside. And we entered. There was a space enclosed there, divided by another veil of the most noble craftsmanship and composition, varied with every kind of dye. In this were woven figures, shapes, plants, and animals of singular embroidery. In this place, upon our arrival, a similarly inquisitive lady immediately approached us, named Indalomene <note>original: "Indalomena"—derived from the Greek for "appearance" or "reflection"</note>. When she had gracefully drawn back her curtain <note>original: "Sipario"</note>, we were led further in. 

Again, there was an equal interval between the second and a third curtain, most excellently and rationally woven with wonderful patterns. It was decorated with infinite knots, restraints, and very ancient instruments for grappling and biting hold, painted in a <term>vermiculated</term><note>A pattern of wavy, worm-like lines</note> style...

HAVING ARRIVED AT THE FIRST DOORKEEPER, she beheld me with no small amazement. After I had greeted her with decency and paid her due reverence, she extended a domestic invitation to enter and offered kind hospitality. In the same manner, passing the subsequent guardians of the curtains, I saw a magnificent portico as long as the entire extent of the palace. The vaulted ceiling was golden, decorated with verdant foliage, distinct flowers, and intertwined branches with little birds in flight—all exquisitely embroidered <note>original: "imphrygiato" — referring to Phrygian embroidery, here used to describe the intricate detail of the mosaic</note> in mosaic work. The pavement was of the cleanest stone, like that of the enclosed courtyard outside. The walls were encrusted with sumptuous stones, artfully arranged in "vermiculated" patterns <note>original: "factura uermiculata" — a style of mosaic using tiny, wavy tiles resembling the tracks of worms</note>.

At the final curtain, the Matron Mnemosyne very affectionately urged me to have no doubts, but rather to submit myself as a strenuous follower and persevering executor of the Queen's royal persuasion and salutary counsel; for then, without fail, the outcome would prove most pleasant. Once private entry was granted, behold! My eyes were met with sights more divine than human. A most magnificent display appeared in a stupendous and spacious courtyard, contiguous with the palace and opposite the other court, forming a perfect square. The fourth wing <note>original: "alamento" — a side or section of the building's layout</note> formed the palace, with a distribution identical to those previously mentioned, with the exception of the door which occupied the central interval. By means of an intricate method and with a most beautiful gathering, they very skillfully covered this entire court with a most rich—indeed, inestimable—**ceiling** <note>original: "suffito"</note>. It was adorned with various foliage made of splendid **Scythian emerald** <note>Scythian emeralds were considered the finest and most vivid green gemstones in antiquity</note>, most pleasing to the eyes; such a gem was not even that which bore the engraved image of **Amymone** <note>original: "Amenone"; refers to the daughter of Danaus in Greek mythology, often depicted in ancient engraved gems</note>. All these excellent things, of incomparable, incredible, and almost unthinkable expense, shone most preciously everywhere, not only because of the most noble and wonderful material, but equally because of the grand and exquisite workmanship. 

For this reason, while diligently weighing this marvelous thing with a most subtle examination, I pondered the wandering extension of those most intricate branches, which were perfectly proportioned in their thickness. They were so ingenious that I wondered by what art, bold daring, and stubborn intent they were so aptly fashioned—whether by craftsman’s glue, or by **soldering** <term>ferruminatione: the process of joining or welding metals together</term>, or by **hammering** <term>malleatura: the art of shaping metal by beating it with a hammer</term>, or by the **art of casting** <note>original: "arte fusoria"</note>. Regarding these three methods of working and forging metal, it seemed impossible to me that a covering of such great width and complex connection could be so excellently manufactured.

Before such an imperial and sublime **presence** <note>original: "conspecto"</note>, feeling full of reverence and kneeling upon the earth, the ladies of the bedchamber and of the court all rose without delay from their quiet seats, provoked by such a novelty and spectacle, marvelling greatly that I had arrived in such a place. <meta>This page continues the narrative from the previous page, where Poliphilo stood in awe before the Queen and her court. Having been presented to her by his five companions (the Senses), he now receives her direct response and an invitation to join her banquet.</meta>

"...but flee and tell me, how did you enter here safe and sound? And how did you escape the mournful and horrible **dragon** <note>original: "dracone"</note>? And how did you find the exit from those hateful shadows and blind caverns? I have heard the whole story distinctly and in full. But I marvel at you not a little, for rare—indeed, most rare—are those who are able to venture here by such a path. Now, since your hairy **Fortune** <note>original: "capillosa fortuna"; a reference to the classical personification of Opportunity or Fortune, who had a long forelock of hair by which she could be seized, but was bald behind, meaning once she passes, she cannot be caught.</note> has destined you to arrive here unharmed, I judge it fitting that I should not for any reason deny you my kind grace, but rather host you with generous and most benevolent hospitality."

To this most liberal invitation, royal promise, and welcome, I replied with the best honorable and devout speech I knew, giving her immense thanks. Briefly and succinctly, I narrated to her point by point my flight from the formidable monster. Consequently, I described with what laborious difficulty I hurried until I reached this most acceptable place. At this, she marveled greatly, as did the venerable ladies. I also told how the five companions found me while I was terrified and wandering. Thus, I applied my mind to such distinguished magnificence with the highest pleasure. 

After this, she smiled pleasantly and said: "It is a worthy thing that a bad beginning sometimes strengthens a happy success and outcome. And before I command you to carry out anything else regarding your amorous and firm concept and burning desire, I want you—for the beneficial relief of your modest troubles—to recline with this distinguished company at a most bountiful **Philotesia** <term>Philotesia: A Greek term for a banquet or a ceremonial cup shared among friends to signify goodwill.</term>, since the favoring heavens have rightly shown you our munificent and pious hospitality and conducted you under our triumphant domicile. And therefore, my Poliphilo, sit yourself down here comfortably without any hesitation. For you shall most gratifiedly behold part of our most sumptuous arrangements: the copious diversity of my more-than-royal delights, the principal decoration of my elegant household staff, the domestic splendor, the inestimable preciousness of my vast wealth, and the broad effect of my beneficence."

Therefore, at this sincere and holy command, her eloquent and kind speech being finished, I humbly made myself a bowing servant. With a little boldness and a small amount of daring, appearing to obey immediately, I sat down upon those delightful benches on the right side. I sat there in my woolen toga, which still had the prickly burrs or seeds of the **Cleavers** <note>original: "Aperine"; the plant Galium aparine, famous for its seeds that "hitchhike" by sticking to fur or clothing.</note> clinging to it, placed between **Offresia** and **Achoe** <note>Offresia represents the sense of Smell (from the Greek *osphresis*), and Achoe represents Hearing (from the Greek *akoe*).</note>, following the Queen. Six other companions sat on the other side, spaced out from one another so that they occupied the length of the table in an orderly fashion. And the Queen, descending from her sublime throne, resided in a royal manner upon the step below it, with august dignity.

Maletus, the king of Etruria <note>original: "Maleto re di Etruria"; likely a reference to a legendary figure associated with the invention of the trumpet or pipes in central Italy</note>, and likewise the flute-players <term>flute-players; original: "Tibicinarie"</term> immediately began to play. Everything, therefore, came together mutually for dignity, grace, and delight without any defect.

At this primary and splendid table, all the tableware or instruments were of the finest gold, as was the round table itself before the Queen. A cordial confection <term>cordial confection; a restorative or medicinal sweet meant to strengthen the heart</term> was presented. Of this, two portions were given to each guest at a moderate interval, without any drink. This was a food meant to ward off any stubborn fever and to drive away any wretched weariness.

Once this was done, in an instant everything was lifted and removed; fragrant violets were scattered upon the ground and the table was stripped. After the joyful and most pleasing tasting of this wonderful confection, and after the flowers had been scattered on the ground with royal magnificence, there was brought without delay a large golden basin full of burning coals. Into this, the tablecloth and the napkins of asbestine linen were thrown. They left them in the fire for so long that everything became red-hot and caught fire, and then, being removed and cooled, they were seen to be unharmed, restored, and very clean, just as before. And this was yet another noble and unusual display. Finally, the tripods and the tables were quickly set down and then carried away.

The more I considered these things in my mind, the more ignorant and stupefied I became. But certainly, above all things, I took the greatest delight with intense admiration, seeing such grand, triumphant, and abundant sumptuosity of incredible expense and luxury, that I judge it better to remain silent than to say too little. Compared to this, the Sicilian feasts <note>original: "Sicule dape"; ancient Sicilian banquets were legendary for their decadence</note>, the Attalic ornaments <note>original: "ornamenti Attalici"; referring to the legendary wealth of the Kings of Pergamon</note>, the Corinthian vases, the Cypriot delights, and the Phalarid feasts <note>original: "faliare cene"; likely referring to the luxury of the tyrant Phalaris</note> would be considered of the least value. She possessed almost entirely the graceful face and sweet representative aspect of Polia, with exciting gestures and subtle, thieving glances. This added no small increase of sweetness to the supreme and principal delight of the satiating and rich seasonings and the most abundant refreshment. Yet, I properly and diligently withdrew my excited and enticed eyes from gazing at so many most precious gems, which everywhere shone with a flashing light. So great was the diversity of unseen beauties and conspicuous decorations that she had almost enslaved my eyes; with immoderate desire, I looked for the correspondence of that supreme beauty in her. **SUCH EXCESSIVE AND INCOMPARABLE** glory and triumphs, and unthinkable treasure, and refined delights, and supreme ceremonies, and a solemn feast, and a most lavish and sumptuous **Banquet** <note>original: "Symposio"</note> of this most happy and opulent Queen recounted—if I have not worthily expressed its principal dignity distinctly and perfectly, let the curious crowd <note>original: "curiosa turbula"</note> not wonder at this. Because anyone endowed with a sharp and ready wit, and decorated with a lavish and most fertile tongue, could not satisfy this task clearly or collectively.

This worthy order and manner was observed by everyone without defect, even though the rhythm of the learned and excellent music was played with a hurried brevity. This music incited all the bystanders to such movement no less than the dancers, for the suitability of the consonant harmony was in accord with the soul—and especially so here, being in the highest and most concordant consensus of the "Well-Feeling" <term>Eupathia: a Greek term for a state of harmonious physical and mental well-being</term> of their well-disposed bodies.

...time, and of the most subtle craftsmanship. This garden, in its perimeter and extent, was exactly as large as the area occupied by the majestic royal residence. Arranged all around it were garden planters <note>original: "capſule hortenſe"</note>, where instead of living greenery, every plant was made of the purest glass <note>original: "uitro"</note>. These were extraordinary—beyond anything one could imagine or believe—with topiary boxwood <term>topiati buxi: the art of clipping shrubs into ornamental shapes</term> and stems of gold. Between these, cypresses alternated; the cypresses did not exceed two paces in height, while the boxwoods were only one pace high. They were filled with a wonderful variety of diverse plants, mimicking the elegant patterns of nature, with the most delightful flowers of varied forms and distinct, pleasing colors. 

The flat upper edges of these square planters—or perhaps they were terraces—were crowned with gold and decorated with very fine, polished lines. The faces of these planters were made of glass plates, gilded on the inside and decorated with wondrous drawings of the most curious histories; they stood beautifully, enclosed in golden frames that gripped them tightly, with the base raised by a sixth part. 

The surrounding wall of this garden <note>original: "uiridario"</note> was set at a precise distance and featured swelling columns <note>original: "columne uentriculate"</note> made of the same material, covered with flowering climbing vines <note>original: "conuoluoli"</note> rendered in full relief. Here and there stood fluted golden squares, and from one to the next, arches were formed with the necessary beams, friezes <note>original: "Zophoro"</note>, and cornices, projecting properly above the glass capitals of the round columns. The solid base beneath these winding vines was made of jasper <term>diaſpro: an opaque, impure variety of silica, usually red, yellow, or brown</term> of many blending and brilliant colors. These vines were slightly raised and separated from the solid background. The openings of the arches were filled with the purest glass diamonds <note>original: "Rombi uitrini"</note>, each a third of a foot <note>original: "Triente"</note> in diameter, set into channels and surrounded by various encaustic paintings <term>enchauſtica: a technique using heated wax and pigments, here applied to glass</term> that were most pleasing to the senses.

The entire area was paved with small glass circles and other most appropriate shapes, achieving a supreme grace through their mutual harmony and firm cohesion. They possessed a remarkable gem-like brilliance, achieved without any deceptive foil backing. From the flowers wafted a singular fragrance, as they had been anointed and perfumed with a rose-scented ointment.

Here, the sweet-speaking Logistica <note>Reason</note> most skillfully gave a brief narration; speaking like a natural philosopher, she praised the excellent construction and the nobility of the material, the art, and the invention. She claimed such quality could not even be found in Murano <note>The famous center of Venetian glassmaking</note>, thus disparaging its common nature. She then said, "Poliphilo, let us ascend this most excellent observation tower <note>original: "ſpecula"</note> near the garden." 

While Thelemia <note>Will or Desire</note> remained below, we briskly climbed a spiral staircase <note>original: "cochleata ſcanſione"</note> to the flat upper part. There, with divine eloquence, she showed me a garden of vast circumference, laid out in the form of a complex, intricate labyrinth. Its circular paths were not meant to be walked upon, but...

This mysterious place was of itself a healthy land, pleasant and fertile in soil, filled with every abundance of sweet fruits, adorned with an overflow of fountains, delightful with every flowering greenery, filled with every comfort, and of the greatest delight. It devours those who have entered both at the entrance and as they progress, wherever it wishes by chance or design. And if it does not kill them between one watchtower and the next, they pass safely through the entire sevenfold circuit until the next watchtower."

Thus, those who enter here through that first Tower—look at the title written in Greek notation and consider it most carefully: <note>original: "ΔOZA KOΣMIKH ΩΣ POMΦOΛYΣ"</note> **Worldly Glory is like a Bubble**—they go with the little boat <term>nauicula: a small boat</term> following the current <note>original: "alueo ſecondo"</note>, and without any care or effort, fruits and flowers fall into the skiff <term>scaphidio: a small vessel or boat</term>, and with the greatest pleasure and play they pass through the seven revolutions until the second watchtower. And consider, Poliphilo, how much clarity of air there is in this beginning, increasing until the middle watchtower, and from there gradually toward the center it decreases, becoming dark, gloomy, and [yet] illuminated.

In that first tower, a most pious matron and benign giver dwells presiding eternally. Before her stands a very ancient, strong, and ready urn, adorned with seven Greek letters as you see here: <note>original: "ΘEΣPION"</note> **THESRION** <note>likely a vessel for divine lots or a treasury</note>, packed with the honeys of fate. To each of those entering, she most gracefully and munificently gives one of these <term>melli: honeys; symbolic portions of fate or character</term>, without regard for status, but according to the unfolding disposition of chance. Having received these and coming outside, they begin to sail in the labyrinth <term>labyrintho: a complex maze or symbolic path of life</term>, the channels being hedged with roses and fruit-bearing trees. Therefore, having completed the first long circuit of the seven revolutions—passing from the sign of Aries to the very end of the tail—and arriving at the second watchtower, they find countless maidens of various conditions. These maidens ask everyone to show their honeys, and they show it to them. These most expert maidens recognize the particular and destined honey; embracing the guest, they accept them and invite them to wander through the other seven circuits. According to their inclined readiness, they lead them indivisibly through various exercises until the third watchtower. In this place, whoever wishes to persevere with his companion, she never abandons or leaves him. Because here they find other, more voluptuous damsels, and many repudiate the [first ones]...

...the first ones, and they adhere to these. Then, departing from that second **watchtower** <term>specula: an observation point or tower</term>, and arriving at the third, they find the waters somewhat contrary, and it becomes a duty to **row** <note>remigare: often used as an allegory for the effort and labor required to navigate life</note>. Having reached the fifth watchtower, they find it worthy of contemplation, in which they observe how beautiful their own likeness is. ->**Blessed are those who have held the middle way.**<-
<note>original Latin: "Medium tenuere beati." A classical proverb advising moderation.</note>

This "middle" is not linear, nor local, but temporal, regarding this passage and limit; here, with sincere examination, the middle path is discerned, through which happiness—or the blessedness of intellect, or indeed of abundance—is joined. Those who do not have this with them find themselves almost less able to acquire it in the stages that follow.

Taking their leave from here, the waters begin to stretch somewhat through the circular windings, beginning their swift course toward the final center; with little or no rowing, they are led to the sixth tower. There they find elegant Matrons, with virginal and modest looks, intent on divine worship. By the divine sight of these women, the guests are captured by their love; condemning their former lives and turning them to disgust, they make a quiet commerce and a peaceful passage through the seven revolutions.

Once these have passed, through the following stages—with the air rising, and with many discomforts and a miserable journey—they weigh the crossing with great speed. For the more the revolution of the passages approaches the center of the figure, the shorter they become. And so much more does one slip down with ineffective speed and through slippery windings into the abyss of the central watchtower. This happens with the highest affliction of the soul due to the remembrance of the beautiful places and the society left behind. And it is all the more painful as they realize they cannot return by turning the prow of their bark, because the prows of other sailors are continually at their stern. 

Adding to this greater pain is the terrifying title above the entrance of the middle watchtower, expressed in such Attic Greek:

->**THE WOLF OF THE GODS IS RELENTLESS.**<-
<note>original Greek: "ΘΕΩΝ ΛΥΚΟΣ ΔΥΣ ΑΛΓΗΤΟΣ." This likely refers to Time or Fate which consumes all things.</note>

And here, considering the displeasing title, they are mournful, as if having entered such a labyrinthine orchard, which, though it comprises so many delights, yet is subject to such miserable and inevitable necessity. Then, smiling, Logistica, the messenger of the gods, added: "Poliphilo, in this devouring gap sits a severe spectator who holds the scales; she is the judge of those who enter, and with equal balance and a scale, she scrupulously weighs every action. By this, for better or for worse..."

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Logistica (Reason) as she explains the symbolic meaning of the monument’s base and the golden obelisk (referred to here as a "Pyra") to Poliphilo. The previous page established the physical components: the Sun, the Rudder, and the Fiery Vessel.</meta>

...brought forth, and on every side it is one, and of whatever figure it is the primary foundation, and in every base constant and enduring. The circular part placed above is free of beginning and of end. Within the encircled plane of this, those three lineaments are contained, facing each image according to its attributed property. The **Sun**, with its most joyful light, can do all things, and its nature is attributed to God. The second is the **Rudder**, which expresses the provident government of the universe with infinite wisdom. The third is the **fiery vessel**, by which I understand a participation in love. And although these three images are distinct, they are nonetheless one thing joined together, and singularly embraced and eternally connected as one, kindly communicating its good, as can be seen by the copies at the elbows of the existing figure. And continuing her consequent reasoned discourse <note>original: "factiloquia logistica," a Latinate phrasing for Logistica’s logical or eloquent speech</note>, she said:

To the image of the Sun, note this Greek word: **Α Δ Ι Η Γ Η Τ Ο Σ** <note>original: "adiēgētos," meaning "inexpressible" or "beyond description"</note>. To that of the Rudder, contemplate that Greek notation: **Α Δ Ι Α Χ Ω Ρ Ι Σ Τ Ο Σ** <note>original: "adiachōristos," meaning "inseparable"</note>. To that of the fire, there was inscribed: **Α Δ Ι Ε Ρ Ε Υ Ν Η Σ** <note>original: "adiereunēs" (usually "adiereunētos"), meaning "unsearchable" or "inscrutable"</note>. Therefore, by such effects, those three animals are placed beneath the golden Obelisk leaning above, which are of such figures according to three great and celebrated opinions. And just as the human face effectively excels over others, so too does this concept. In the Pyra <note>term: Pyra; here referring to the pyramid-shaped obelisk</note> there are three flat sides marked by three circles, each signifying a period of time: Past, Present, and Future. Understand that no other figure can contain those three circles except in that invariable one. And no mortal can perfectly discern or see two sides of the said figure at once, except for one entirely, which is the Present. And therefore, most wisely, those three characters were impressed: **Ω Ω Ν** <note>Greek: "ho on," meaning "The Being" or "The One Who Is," a name for God</note>.

Because of this, Poliphilo, do not accuse me of being wordy, for I am most ready to direct you in this narrative. Know that the first foundational figure is known only to itself, and to one it is human and transparent, but to us it is not totally clear. Then, he who is endowed with intellect ascends above, and diligently considers the coloring of the figure; searching further, they ascend to the third figure, which is obscure and hidden in its coloring within those three golden and surrounded images.

Finally, climbing further up, they consider a figure in its triune aspect; and from there, the more they rise toward the slender point <note>original: "pacuto gracilamento," referring to the apex of the obelisk</note> in contemplation, there, however well-instructed they may be, they have acquired nothing else except what is seen to be. But as to *what* it is, they remain ignorant, powerless, and weak.

Without hesitation, I perceived a greater delight than from any other marvelous work graciously beheld by my eyes. Consider the **Obelisk** of such great mystery, standing with ineffable balance, and for the sake of stability and perpetuity, remaining whole, solid, and eternal, persisting with an unbreakable and incorruptible equality of proportions. ->[An illustration of the god Jupiter seated upon a throne. He holds a vessel of fire in his left hand and a cornucopia in his right. Small winged figures, or putti, play at the base of his throne.]<-

And I, without delay, added: "Since our pleasant conversation has turned to this, most gracious companions—and because my burning desire to understand is not yet fully satisfied, and since I hope my boldness does not weary you—I pray you tell me this: before my horrible fright, I saw a stone monster of audacious size and craft, namely an **Elephant**. Entering then into its hollow belly, I found two tombs with inscriptions of ambiguous meaning regarding the finding of treasure; but they suggested that I should despise the body and take the head."

**Logistica** <note>Logistica represents Reason or Logic</note>, without further thought, cheerfully replied: "**Poliphilo**, I know fully what you inquire about. I wish you to know, however, that that massive machine was built with great admiration for human genius, with ardent study, and incredible diligence, meant to challenge the intellect to understand its divine concept. Notice that from its forehead hangs an ornament with that two-edged inscription which, in the common mother tongue, says: **Labor and Industry** <note>original: "Fatica & industria"</note>. For in this world, whoever wishes to possess treasure while living must leave behind rotting idleness—signified by the great body—and take the decorated head, which is that inscription; thus you shall have treasure by exerting yourself with industry."

No sooner had she finished her smooth and effective words than I, now perfectly instructed in everything, thanked her for her affable kindness. However, being still very eager to investigate all that I had previously understood only imperfectly, and having become familiar and comfortable with them, I made a third request: "Most wise Nymph, at my exit from the subterranean caverns, I found an ancient and elegant bridge. I saw that on its banks, made of **porphyry** <note>A hard, reddish-purple rock used in antiquity for royal monuments</note> stone on one side and **Ophite** <note>original: "Ophytico"; a green-spotted stone resembling a serpent's skin</note> on the other, certain **hieroglyphs** were carved. ...of **Fir** <note>original: "Abiete"</note>, and the other of **Larch** <note>original: "Larice"</note>. The nature of these woods is well-established: one does not easily consort with fire, and the other, when burdened by weight or shaped into a beam, does not bend. Therefore, that patience is commended which is not easily ignited by anger, nor bows under adversity. The **Porphyry** stone <note>A hard, purple-red volcanic rock prized by Roman emperors</note> stands out as a notable mystery expressed for such a person. For it is affirmed to be of such a nature that it not only does not cook in the furnace, but it even renders the other nearby stones incombustible. Such is true patience demonstrated: it does not so much ignite itself, but rather renders those already burning extinguished. The stone of **Ophite** <note>original: "Ophytes"; a green, serpentine-like stone</note> has its own very well-known property, suitable to that saying.

"Therefore, **Poliphilo**, I commend you in this regard, because you are greedy for such inquiry; for to examine, consider, and measure everything proves to be laudable." I then highly praised the wisdom of the most eloquent lady, giving innumerable thanks.

And so, with virtuous and most approved conversation, we most joyfully reached a most pleasant river. Upon its banks, I saw a charming **Plane-tree grove** <note>original: "Plataneto"</note>, alongside other very green shrubs and aquatic sprouts excellently arranged and situated, interspersed with **lotus trees** <note>original: "lothi"; likely referring to the Mediterranean hackberry or jujube</note>. Spanning this was a stone and magnificent bridge of three arches, with its ends fixed upon the banks over very firm foundations, with its piers carinated <note>shaped like the keel of a ship to part the water</note> on both faces to maintain the firmest structure, and with very noble parapets.

On these [parapets], in the middle rise above the supporting keystone of the arch, on this side and that, there rose a polished, peaked **porphyry** square, containing a **relief sculpture** <note>original: "cataglyphia"</note> of **hieroglyphs**. Nearby was a circle, the center of which was held by two **spirits** <note>original: "ſpiriti"; likely winged heads representing the breath of life or winds</note>, turning their backs to the circumference with their small chests.

Gazing presently upon the royal and intelligible object of so excellent a representation—of such a graceful presence and divine aspect, and of such an abundant heap and universal collection of unseen beauty and superhuman loveliness—I considered all previously seen, inestimable delights, riches, and lofty magnificence to be meager, trifling, and unequal compared to her great worth. ## POLIPHILO IN THIS ABOVE-DESCRIBED PLACE SEES THE FOUR TRIUMPHAL SIX-HORSE CHARIOTS ALL MADE OF VARIOUS STONES AND MOST PRECIOUS JEWELS. SURROUNDED BY A MIXED MULTITUDE OF BLESSED YOUTHS WHO ARE MOST REVERENT IN PRAISE OF SUPREME JOVE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'R' featuring classical foliate and floral motifs with winding vines and leaves within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

I reasonably consider it not even a little difficult for the high Gods to act; rather, any effect is easily made feasible according to their will, in every place and above every created thing. For this reason, they are rightly called omnipotent. Perhaps whoever hears the narration of such marvelous and stupendous—nay, divine—works might marvel supremely. For as much as emulative Art <note>original: "l’arte æmula"</note> strives to imitate natural things, the divine things, without doubt, cannot be aptly simulated or feigned by any created wit or intellect without their help and inspiration <note>original: "spiramine"</note>. Therefore, for such a reason, no one should allow themselves to be occupied by any doubt, but quietly paying attention, should hold in their mind that every workmanship unusual to us is possible for the gods above, just as I saw it.

### DESCRIPTION OF THE FIRST TRIUMPH.

The first of the four wondrous and divine triumphs had its four rapid wheels made of the finest stone of the greenest Scythian emerald <note>original: "smaragdo scythico"</note>, sparkling with copper-colored specks. I then gazed in astonishment at the rest of the chariot, which was made entirely of panels—not of Arabian or Cyprian stone—but of Indian diamond <term>adamante</term> <note>the hardest stone, often associated with diamonds in antiquity</note> with a ferrous shimmer, defying hard emery and steel. It was the victor over licking fire, contemptuous and defiant toward it, yet quiet and tamable by the warm blood of a goat <note>original: "cruore Hircino," reflecting the ancient belief that only goat blood could soften a diamond</note>, and pleasing to the magical arts. These panels, divinely fashioned with <term>cataglyphia</term> <note>sunken relief carving or intaglio</note> patterns, were carved and most wonderfully enclosed and framed in the purest gold.

Upon the right panel, I saw depicted a noble and royal Nymph with many companions of her own age in a meadow, crowning victorious bulls with multiple garlands <note>original: "strophii"</note> of flowers; and one of the bulls was close to her, having become remarkably tame.

This chariot frame was rectangular, formed of two perfect squares along its length of six feet; it was three feet high and of the same width, with a refined cornice <term>coronice: the decorative molding that crowns an architectural structure</term> above and a plinth <term>plintho: the heavy square base or slab supporting a pedestal or column</term> below. Above this, at a height of one and a half feet, was a flat surface two and a half feet wide and five and a half feet long, with a slope toward the cornice entirely covered in a scale-like pattern of most precious stones, arranged in a shifting sequence and order of colors. At the four corners were attached inverted cornucopias <note>original: "copie inverse." Literally 'horns of plenty' turned upside down.</note> with their openings facing upward, resting upon the projecting angles of the cornice. These were stuffed with many fruits and flowers made of thick, clustered gems budding among varied foliage of gold.

I saw these horns were decorated with an exquisite expression of horned poppy leaves, covered in twisted channels, with their slender ends winding toward the edge of the flat top. The ends broke into a jagged, antique-style leaf that flowed most beautifully over the back of the elegant cornucopia made of the aforementioned material. At each corner, from the plinth toward the cornice, a Harpy-style foot <note>original: "Harpyiatico pede." An ornamental support carved to resemble the clawed foot of a Harpy, a mythical winged creature.</note> was fixed to the projection with a moderate curve and an excellent turning of acanthus foliage here and there.

The wheels were enclosed within the chariot, with only half of them appearing. The plinth—that is, the outermost part of the machine—at the front, near the Harpy-style feet, rose up somewhat and thinned out elegantly, turning into a snail-like volute <term>limachale uoluto: a spiral, shell-like decorative scroll</term>. Within this were the loops or lashings <note>original: "laquei, o uero retinaculi"</note> appropriately placed for towing. Where the axle was fixed and attached to the plinth, there hung a pointed plate <note>original: "mucronato"</note> as wide at the joint of the plinth as twice the distance from the revolving center to the top. ## FRONT AND REAR PARTS.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration divided into two rectangular panels within a single black border. This triumphal chariot was pulled by six white **Elephants**, joined in pairs, such as could not be found in the **Aethiopian** <note>original: "Ageſinua patria"</note> homeland, nor among the **Gandari** <note>an ancient people of India</note>. Nor were such beasts ever subjugated for the African Triumph of **Pompey the Great**, nor were such used to draw the Triumph of **Father Liber** <term>Liber Pater: an ancient Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with Dionysus/Bacchus</term> when India was conquered. Armed with trunks and ivory, deadly tusks, they pulled the carriage fittingly with a sweet trumpeting. They were held with reins of the finest silk dyed in a deep **Cyan** <note>original: "Cyanea," a dark blue or sea-green</note> hue, most beautifully twisted with threads of gold and silver mixed together. These were tied in very tight, square-woven knots, resembling the ears of grain found on **Mount Gargano** <note>a mountain in Apulia, Italy, used here as a metaphor for intricate natural patterns</note>. They wore golden breastplates filled with a multitude of most brilliant and diverse gems, with golden armlets attached, through which the harnesses of all six elephants passed. 

Six very tender young girls also rode upon them in the same manner as the first ones, carrying other different instruments, all sharing perfectly in a single sound. And everything that the previous girls had done, these did the same. Two were dressed in **Crimson** <note>original: "Phœniceo"</note>, two in a shining **Yellow** <note>original: "luteo"</note>—the color found inside the **Buttercup** <term>Apio Ranino: likely the Ranunculus or 'frog-apium,' a bright yellow flower</term>—and two in violet purple. The elephants drawing the vehicle were covered in cloths of gold fringed with thick pearls and pompously decorated with other gems. Their necks were surrounded by round, thick jewels, and above their broad foreheads hung a dangling pommel of marvelous pearls, with a long tassel <note>original: "barbula," literally 'little beard'</note> of various silks and golden threads that swayed with every movement.

...and she wanted to pluck him apart, having already filled her hand with flying **little feathers** <note>original: "plumule"</note>, and while the child was crying, one sent with **winged sandals** <term>talaria: the winged sandals of Mercury, messenger of the gods</term> by the high Jove, who was seated upon a throne, freed him unhurt from the maternal shears. ### FRONT AND BACK PART

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration divided into three vertical panels. 
In the left panel, a group of figures stands near a small pedestal; one woman holds a staff and rests her hand on another woman's shoulder. 
The central panel shows a king seated on a high throne; a standing man presents a naked infant to him. Greek text is inscribed above: "YOU ARE SWEET BUT BITTER TO ME."
The right panel depicts a kneeling man in the foreground gesturing toward a woman and child; an angel with wings and a staff flies above them.</image-desc>

This chariot was pompously drawn by six fierce **unicorns** <note>original: "monoceri"</note>, with deer-like horned foreheads, showing reverence to the cold Diana. These were harnessed at their vigorous, horse-like chests in a golden ornament abundant with precious jewels, with twisted cords of silver thread and **yellow silk** <note>original: "lutea seta"</note>, which were artfully knotted to one another, forming highly polished knots with the excellent accessories described above. Six young maidens sat atop the chariot in the same manner and pomp as the others, wearing robes of gold interwoven with the finest **dark blue silk** <note>original: "cyanea"</note>, woven into various flowers and foliage; all six played ancient wind instruments in harmony, expressed with incredible spirit. 

Upon the flat top of the chariot, in the center, lay a precious seat of **green jasper** <note>Jasper was historically believed to assist in childbirth and protect the wearer's health</note>, mounted in silver, helpful for labor and a medicine for the chaste. Its base was hexagonal, rising gracefully into a platinum-coated shell. The lower part of this shell was laboriously grooved up to its middle, then curved smoothly up to the flaring lip. The hollow of the seat was shallow, carved with notable lines for the sitter’s comfort. Upon this sat a most ornate and beautiful **Nymph** in a golden dress interwoven with dark blue silk, in the subtle style of a young girl's refinement, adorned with many gems. She showed her affectionate delight by gazing into her lap at a bounty of **celestial gold** <note>A reference to Jove visiting Danaë in the form of a golden shower</note>. With the same solemn honors and joyful applause as the others, she sat with her breasts exposed and her hair poured out over her back, crowned with a golden diadem and multi-colored gemstones.

# TRIUMPH

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a triumphal procession. A woman sits atop an ornate four-wheeled chariot with a rounded canopy, which is drawn by two horses. A group of attendants on foot accompany the chariot, carrying various ritual and symbolic objects, including a standard topped with a pinecone, leafy branches, and banners. One banner features a flaming heart. The scene is set in a landscape with a single rolling hill in the background.</image-desc>

The **fourth triumphal chariot** <note>original: "EL QVARTO triumpho"</note> was supported by four wheels made of **asbestos** <term>asbestos: an "iron-like" mineral believed by ancient writers like Pliny to be fireproof; once set alight, it was thought to burn forever</term>. It was arched in such a way that, once it was set on fire, it resisted being extinguished. The rest of the rectangular paneling, along with the aforementioned base, was made of flashing **Troglodyte carbuncle** <term>carbuncle: a glowing red gemstone, typically a garnet; "Troglodyte" refers to the region along the Red Sea where the finest specimens were said to be found</term>. This stone did not fear the thickest darkness and was covered in the most polished carvings, which would take a long time to describe in detail. One can only wonder what kind of workman, in what place, and by which master artist they were fabricated.

The right side most excellently displayed the following story: A venerable **pregnant matron** <note>This is Semele, the daughter of Cadmus and mother of Bacchus</note>. The supreme Jupiter appeared to her divinely (just as he was accustomed to do with the Goddess Juno) with thunder and lightning, to such an extent that, caught in the blaze, she was burned to ashes. From her consumed body, they extracted a most noble and divine infant.

### FRONT AND REAR PARTS.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration framed by a black border, divided into two distinct scenes. In the left panel, a figure stands atop a decorated pedestal holding a long, flaming torch. This single line of verse <note>original: "monostichon"</note> was carved in our local characters <note>meaning Roman-style capital letters</note> upon a rectangular tablet in full view of the face of the venerable God. The rest was as described. This mysterious triumphal chariot was drawn with a steady motion by six spotted Hyrcanian tigresses <note>Hyrcania: a region near the Caspian Sea, legendary in antiquity for its fierce and exotic tigers</note>, their coats marked with shining tawny spots and extremely swift; they were harnessed most beautifully with flexible shoots of a fertile vine, full of tender leaves and winding tendrils <note>original: "capreoli"</note>, adorned with crimson clusters of berries.

Above this, in the middle of the flat top of the chariot, was situated a golden base, one foot in diameter at its lowest part and three palms high. One part at the bottom consisted of a rounded plinth <note>original: "latastro"</note>, a half-round molding, or rather a recumbent cyma <term>cyma: an S-shaped decorative molding used in classical architecture</term> and a small fillet. The rest of the base was composed of a pulley-like molding <note>original: "trochlea"</note> and an inverted molding with its accessory small rules and cords. The flat surface of this base was hollowed out circularly in the center. Into this excavation descended the tails of four eagles, which were seated upon the flattened surface of the base. These eagles were made of precious Persian purple aetite <term>aetite: also known as "eagle-stone," a hollow stone believed in folklore to be found in eagles' nests and to possess magical properties</term>. These stood back-to-back, with their golden talons fixed and treading upon the said base. Each had both wings raised and touching one another. Above these, supported at the "elbows" of the wings, was founded this marvelous vessel of brilliant Ethiopian jacinth <note>original: "hyacintho," referring to a reddish-orange gemstone</note>, which is an enemy of the cold and a gracious companion.

This vessel was encrusted with emerald <note>original: "smaragdo"</note> and many other veins of gems—an incredible thing. In height, it was two and a half feet, nearly round in shape. Its diameter (its thickness) measured one and a half feet, and its circumference was three times the diameter. ...a thickness of one palm <note>A "palmo" or palm is a traditional unit of measurement, roughly 3 to 4 inches.</note>. From this ornate frieze <term>phrygio</term> <note>original: "phrygio"; referring to a decorative border in high relief, named after the Phrygians who were famed for their embroidery.</note>, to the beginning of a narrow-necked pitcher <term>gutturnio</term> <note>original: "gutturnio"; a vessel designed for pouring liquids in small drops.</note> which was contained within this same palm-width, the total height reached one and a half feet. Above this dimension there arose the form of a vessel, raised one foot, and it began to widen until it reached one and a half palms. Half of this width was dedicated to the exquisite frieze of wound leaves and flowers, almost all of them appearing as if plucked from the hyacinth stone <term>hyacintho</term> <note>The author uses "hyacinth" to describe a precious gemstone, likely a blue or orange-red zircon or sapphire.</note> itself. The diameter was two and a half quarters [of a foot]. Under this small frieze, several modest relief-shingles <note>original: "scidule"; small overlapping decorative plates or scales.</note> projected in a circle, temperately ridged, somewhat thick at the top and tapering thin at the bottom. Then, it beautifully ascended two and a half quarters further toward the opening. This area was excellently hollowed with twisted little sunken panels <note>original: "lacunule"; small decorative recessed compartments, similar to those found in coffered ceilings.</note>. The opening was shaped like a shell with wide edges, its body having the texture of silk with an elegant curve <term>sima</term> <note>An architectural molding with a double-curve profile.</note>; and within the grasp of the vessel, there were turned little grooves, ripples, and rounded moldings. With such outlines, the friezes were enclosed both above and below.

At the lower frieze of the pitcher, within the said enclosure, were contained two mutilated knuckles <note>original: "conduli"; referring to joints or knots.</note>, or rather half-rings, set across from each other and following their own shape, with their curves facing one another. These were held in the biting jaws of two lizards, or rather small dragons <term>Draconculi</term>. These little dragons were perfectly fashioned from a vein of emerald <term>smaragdo</term>, while the rest of the encrusted surface remained [hyacinth]. They lay with four lizard-like feet <term>lacertacei</term> upon the top of the lower vessel; this summit, between the pitcher and the lower vessel, had an elevation of one quarter. And from its high, slender point, descending, it ended with a line of an inverted curve at the surrounding rim of the body, where the encompassing frieze was located. This sloped summit was most diligently carved with the scales of the hyacinth stone. Only the little dragons were left in the emerald vein, their serpent bellies resting upon the scaled surface, along with the four feet. These little dragons, one on each side at the carved end of the slope of said summit, above the carving of the small cornice, with their tails turning toward the spine, formed a circular and ready spiral. And then they made another similar one below. These coils served as the handles. The lower turn, where it joined the vessel, divided into two parts—one on this side and the other on that—merging into a marvelous foliage. And on the right and left sides, they entered half a foot into the frieze with elegant polish. These leaves appeared almost entirely in relief, and the bottom—that is, the solid flat base of the body <term>corpulétia</term>—was of hyacinth. The entire bulky circumference, or rather the encircling band of two feet, was occupied by these leaf-covered tails.

It remains to speak of the interval that stands one and a half feet on each side. The bulk of the vessel from the belt downwards I judged to be a stupendous work, and rather divine. I marveled at the said vessel, covered all over by an exact sculpture of a vine. Of which the stems, or rather the shoots adorned with vine-leaves <term>pampinulati</term>, with little tendrils and ringed curls, were of a vein suited to the design, made of topaz <term>Topacio</term>. Such as would not be found even on the island of Ophiade <note>Ophiade (or Topazos Island) in the Red Sea was the legendary source of the finest topaz in antiquity.</note>. 

The foliage was of the finest emerald, and the clusters of grapes were of amethyst. Oh, how much...
