To the sight it presented itself as most pleasant, and to the intellect as gracefully contemplative. The solid substance from which this work was carved and refined shone with the color of hyacinth <term>hyacintho</term> <note>original: "hyacintho"; in the Renaissance, this term often referred to a deep blue sapphire or a yellowish-red zircon.</note>, more polished and rounded than anything that could be produced on a lathe. Beneath the leaves, only a thin residue remained that held the foliage to the hyacinth base; the rest was so clean and separated from the background that it seemed almost distinct <note>original: "policario"; likely meaning the relief was so high it stood out like a thumb from the hand.</note>. The winding leaves, with all their finely polished secondary details, were made in a daring emulation of nature, no less than the little vine fruits and wandering shoots. To this miraculous workmanship, the small cups of the divine Alchimedon <note>A master wood-carver mentioned in Virgil's *Eclogues*.</note> do not equal, nor even the cup of Alcon <note>A legendary ancient engraver.</note>. This vessel was full of minute and elegant details.

Let us return to the surrounding band of this most precious vessel, or rather, the Phrygian border <term>phrygiale fascia</term> <note>original: "phrygiale fascia"; a decorative band in high relief, named after the Phrygian style of embroidery.</note>. In the empty space left between the ends of the foliage, I saw two historical scenes worthy of the greatest admiration in such sculpture. On the front face of this vessel, I marveled at an excellent engraving of the high-thundering Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note>. In his right hand he held a sharp golden sword made of a vein of glowing Ethiopian chrysolite. In the other, he held a flashing thunderbolt of a ruby-like vein. And he, with a menacing expression, was carved from a vein of galactite <term>gallatite</term> <note>original: "Gallatite"; a white stone, its name derived from the Greek word for milk.</note> and crowned with sparkling stars like lightning. He stood atop a sacred sapphire altar. Before his divine and awesome majesty, I watched a festive chorus of seven nymphs in white garments, religiously appearing to sing with venerable applause. These nymphs then transformed into green trees of emerald transparency, filled with glowing blue <term>cyanei</term> flowers. And they devoutly bowed to the supreme deity. Not all the nymphs were transformed into foliage at once; rather, the last one was entirely converted into a small tree with her feet turned into little roots, the next had only her feet transformed, the third was changed from the waist up including the start of her arms, and each of the others followed in succession. But at the top of each maidenly head, the sculpture indicated the metamorphosis that was to follow for them all.

...fragrant. The third corner was made of the finest Medea stone <note>A legendary gemstone mentioned by ancient naturalists, supposedly discovered by the sorceress Medea.</note>, of a dark golden color scattered throughout, possessing a nectar-like flavor. Around this divine triumph, with much solemn superstition and the greatest pomp and religious devotion, processed infinite Maenad nymphs with their hair loose and flowing. Some were naked, with small nymph-like cloaks <term>amiculi</term> flowing from their shoulders; others wore <term>nebrides</term>, which are garments made from the dappled skins of fawns. Without any men present, these women—cymbal-players and flute-players—performed the sacred Orgiastic rites, shouting with loud cries and ritual dances <term>thyasí</term>, such as those performed in the Trieteric festivals <note>Greek festivals held every three years in honor of Bacchus.</note>. Carrying <term>thyrsi</term> <note>Staffs topped with pinecones, a symbol of Bacchus.</note> made of coniferous branches and entwined with vine leaves, they ran about jumping, crowned and girded over their naked bodies. Following immediately after the chariot was a son of Silenus <note>Silenus was the foster father and tutor of Bacchus, often depicted as a jovial, drunk old man.</note> riding upon a little ass. Then, immediately behind this rider, they joyfully led a shaggy-haired goat <term>Hirco horricome</term> adorned for the sacrificial procession. And one member of this sect carried a wicker winnowing fan <term>vannus</term> <note>A basket used to separate grain from chaff, used symbolically in Dionysian initiation rites.</note>, with disorderly laughter and frantic gestures; with this ancient and sacred rite, they highly exalted this fourth triumph. And with the venerable cry of "Euibache!" <note>original: "Euibache"; a ritual shout of "Evoe Bacchus!"</note> shouted aloud, the followers—the Mimallones, Satyrs, Bacchae, Lenae, Thyades, Naiads, Tityri, and nymphs—followed in celebration, crying out in confusion.

No one, even with the most tireless eloquence, could ever adapt themselves so aptly as to copiously and fully emerge from the task of describing these divine mysteries. It is impossible to expressly narrate, or to sufficiently express in words, with what divine pomp, unending triumphs, perennial glory, festive joy, and happy dancing they surrounded these four unusual six-yoked teams <term>seiuge</term> <note>original: "seiuge," a chariot drawn by six animals; in this case, the illustration shows four, but the text emphasizes the grandeur of such large teams.</note> of memorable spectacle.

Beyond the illustrious youths and the crowded ranks of innumerable and delightful nymphs—who were more prudent, grave, and clever than their tender years suggested—there were most welcome lovers with youthful and beardless cheeks. ...and orderly, they proceeded together in a joyful and mysterious Triumph, with high jubilation resonating into the air. Some played trumpeting instruments, varied in form and character, such as ductile trumpets <term>tubæ ductiles</term> <note>Long trumpets made of beaten metal.</note>, both whole and resonant pipes <term>tibiæ</term>. Some sang with celestial notes like psalms, and with ineffable delight and eternal solace, exceeding all that human ingenuity could possibly imagine. Glorious, they circled the eternal triumphs, moving through the flowery and blessed land and happy homeland, and the vernal fields of a most holy place dedicated to the blessed. No rising shrub blocked or occupied the way. Instead, the entire flowery ground was a level meadow of fragrant herbs and flower-bearing plants of infinite colors and beautifully manifold forms, and of the sweetest scents, more than one could possibly describe. These did not fear the burning invasion of Phoebus <note>The sun god, Apollo.</note>, because in this most pleasant place, he does not race with his swiftest horses toward the furthest Hesperia <note>The West, where the sun sets.</note>. Rather, the air is always most pure and at every hour cleared of cloudy smoke; it is an eternally clear and unvariable day, and the earth is continuously herb-bearing, blooming with redolent flowers. Like a gracious and exquisite painting, they always remain uninjured in their dew-like freshness, and with color that knows no restriction of time.

Here were the four kinds of violets: cowslip <term>paralisis</term>, melilot, anemones, cornflowers <term>cyanei</term>, fennel-flower <term>gyth</term>, cyclamen, crowfoot <term>vatrachio</term>, columbine <term>aquilegia</term>, lily of the valley <term>lilium convallium</term>, and amaranth. Because of this, I was overcome with no less pleasure, delight, and wonder at these solemn rites and celebrated feasts than I had been by the admiration of the previous triumphs.

After we had both progressed a bit further from that spot, with unthinkable solace and proceeding even further, I gazed again at the clear and fresh springs of the gracious and grassy meadows and shady groves. There, I saw the dancing Cataract-Nymphs and Dell-Nymphs <note>original: "Cataryte Napee"</note>, the pleasant playing Naiads, and the singing marine Nereids. Some were dressed in the skins of the sea-calf <note>the Mediterranean monk seal, believed in antiquity to be the only animal never struck by lightning</note>, which is unharmed by the wrath of supreme Jove. They held large baskets <note>original: "Eſture"</note> made of bark in their hands, filled with fruits and flowers, having gathered from the pebbly shores and idly celebrating with diverse pastimes. Many carried in their hands green thyrsi <term>thyrsus: a ritual staff wreathed in ivy and topped with a pine cone, associated with the god Bacchus</term>. The tops of these were packed with orange blossoms and soft foliage, as well as yellow Egyptian and Persian roses, narcissus flowers, and handfuls of crimson flowers and fragrant abelmosk <note>original: "Amuleto"</note>. They were accompanied by the forest-dwelling Pan of Arcadia, the mountain-dwelling sylvan demigods, the Wood-Nymphs, and many others, including Zephyr with his beloved Chloris <note>the god of the west wind and his bride, the goddess of flowers</note>. To her, he had granted power over all beautiful flowers. Many active and singing shepherds, experts at competing in their songs and armed with their crooks, praised together with exultation and applause. With serious matters, games, and jests, and with very ancient instruments made of straw and reed, they glorified the amorous and omnipotent Jove. Amid the trumpeting of bark flutes shaped like a scytale <term>scytale: a cylindrical staff used in ancient Greece for cryptographic messages</term>, which produced a strange sound, they celebrated with holy wonder, most devoutly performing the floral festivals.

For which reason, how much voluptuous pleasure I felt, I leave to the judgment of whoever might know how to imagine it in their thoughts. Therefore, abundantly packed with incredible joy, wandering with my most pleasing companion, we continued our happy itinerary and amorous promenade. From her—at times moving my eyes somewhat from their sweet prison and bond, which felt almost like a voluntary exile—behold, looking out over the tender heads and greenest peaks of the playful trees, I saw an exceeding wing-like structure <term>pterygion: a wing-shaped architectural ornament</term> appearing above a round summit. I estimated it to be a short distance from the whispering shore, toward which she gracefully led me. It was there that the gliding and sloping streamlets that circled the valley ended; flowing from the feet of the most ornate hills and mounds—partly meadowy and partly wooded—they ran with very swift water in very clear channels with grassy and sandy beds, leaping down on each side. And then, beyond the said pinnacle, I saw a proud and eminent dome <note>original: "cupula"</note>, appearing to me to be covered in dark-blue lead. At its summit, it had an octagonal molding with columns, and above that, another dome. Then there were eight quadrangular pillars, covered by a peak, in the shape of a baluster. Above this projected a shaft with a most round triangle <note>original: "Trigono rotundiſſimo"; likely a sphere or a geometric paradox typical of the author's style</note> fixed to it, shining especially with a golden luster. <meta>The previous page described Poliphilo traveling through a lush landscape filled with nymphs, satyrs, and pastoral figures, eventually spotting a grand structure in the distance toward which he and his guide are now walking.</meta>

Moved by an ever-growing and burning desire, I longed to behold that structure more closely and perfectly, suspecting with good reason that a great and ancient building stood there. So much so that I almost wanted to beg my kind Guide to lead me to it, even as we continued toward that place. But, restraining and chastising such a desire within myself, I said: "Woe is me <note>original: "Heu me"</note>, I do not dare to ask for that thing which I am urged toward with a thorny sting and a constant, vehement impulse." This was especially true for a thing so warmly desired, which I firmly believed would make me more content than any other lover if I could only reach it. Therefore, suppressing, suffocating, and yearning over such an unadvised thought, and no longer asking for an end to such long torment—aided by the perpetual nourishment of sighs from my heart—I asked myself: "Why then should I ask for this, which is not so opportune for me? Woe is me, my active heart, shared and no longer entirely my own, how willingly it follows the predatory hawk <note>original: "Alieto," likely referring to a hobby or small falcon</note> of your existence!" Entangled in these lascivious snares and heavy thoughts, it stirred a continuous throbbing in my inflamed breast, much like the weeping pheasant <note>original: "Fasciano"</note> who, knocked from the foliage by the flight of the cruel falcon, feels its sad heart beat.

And thus, frequently agitated by these amorous consequences, and continuing further at our moderate pace while conversing eloquently with my **Venerable Nymph**—discussing clearly and with honey-sweet speech the marvelous things revealed by divine grace—we finally arrived a short distance from the rebounding shore, washed by the pleasant waves of the restless sea. In this most joyful spot, we found a most ornate, expertly crafted, and ancient temple of the builder's art, constructed with great expense in the antique style, and consecrated to **life-giving Venus** <note>original: "phyſizoa Venere," from the Greek for "life-giving"</note>.

This sacred **Temple**, then, was constructed in a circular shape according to architectural art, and skillfully fitted within a quadrangular figure on a level site. Its height was equal to its diameter. Within the circle contained in that area, a square was noted. From one side <note>original: "pleura"</note> of this square, extending along the diameter toward the circumference, the architect divided the space into five parts, while a sixth part extended toward the center. From this point, having drawn another circular figure with a compass, the learned **Architect** had raised this extraordinary structure and magnificent building. Regarding the principal parts, he had achieved perfect proportion <term>commodulatione: the symmetrical and harmonious relationship between the different parts of a building</term>, dimension, and total enclosure. He also determined the thickness of the walls and the external pillars, the space between one circuit and the next—that is, between the main wing and the colonnade <term>peristyle: a row of columns surrounding a building or an open courtyard</term>—and the open vaulted ceiling <note>original: "teſtudinato"</note>. Finally, from the center to the circumference, lines were drawn forming ten radii or divisions, where

<meta>This page continues the description of the magnificent structures Poliphilo encounters. Following the arrival at the shore mentioned on the previous page, the narrator now provides a technical architectural breakdown of a circular colonnade or "circus" they have reached.</meta>

As it cut through the circular space of the circus, it arranged ten arches resting upon **serpentine columns** <term>Ophytice; columns made of green-mottled "serpentine" stone</term>. Opposite the solid support, between one arch and the next, with a facial width of two feet from the inner circular wing, there stood readily a hewn and polished **Corinthian column**. Its height was equal to the Ionic order of nine diameters, excluding the capitals, and it was made of clear **Porphyry** <term>Porphyrite; a rare, hard purple volcanic rock prized in antiquity</term>. This column, with its bronze capital, supported the straight entablature <note>original: "trabe recta"</note>, which was wrapped with a frieze <term>Zophoro; a sculpted or decorated horizontal band</term> and a cornice. These were led above to the solid part of the pediment of the curved beam—or rather, the **Arch**.

These elements—the Phrygian beam and the cornice—projected outward from the "living" or firm line of the Corinthian order as much as the perpendicular line of the aforementioned Porphyry required. They featured bases and capitals made of fine metal, gilded by heat <note>original: "causticamente inaurato," likely referring to fire-gilding</note> and brilliant, with an elegant **entasis** <term>Enthesi; the subtle swelling or "corpulence" in the middle of a column's shaft to correct optical illusions</term>. This order of prominence was regularly observed for all the balanced and matched Porphyry columns. These were meant to stand upon the required low wall <note>original: "murulo"</note> of the colonnade. However, the illustrious Architect, in order to give the area a freer passage, made the space between the columns open and passable.

Wherefore the curved beams <note>the arches</note>, with their ends resting upon the **serpentine columns**—which were smooth, turned, and made lustrous by polishing—resided there. The appropriate slab or **plinth** had been placed above the capital to give it a solid footing and not one that appeared to hang in the air, due to the inserted lids of said capitals. Beneath the bases, a space was reserved for a "half-altar" <note>original: "semiarula"</note> which served as the low wall, upon which the bases of all the serpentine columns firmly rested.

The Corinthian columns stepped upon a sub-column, or rather a sub-base, in the shape of a half-cylinder <note>original: "semi Tubulo"</note>, neatly linked here and there with the half-altars. This base was derived exactly from two squares found from the diameter of the lowest thickness of the Corinthian column. A ratio of one-and-a-half <note>original: "sexquialtera"</note> remained for the rest of the moldings: the rounded **tori**, the **gululae** <term>small throat-shaped moldings</term>, the **astragals** <note>original: "nextruli"</note>, and the **simae** <term>the upturned edge of a cornice</term>, or similar decorative lines above and below. These were suitably distributed and decently joined with the free bases appointed above.

Each Arch stood elegantly decorated with its own **keystone**, featuring little boys <note>putti</note> and, alternately, small scrolls with floral foliage. And

<meta>This page continues the architectural description of the circular structure Poliphilo is observing. It moves from the description of the Porphyry columns to the pilasters and walls that form the inner and outer shell of the temple, detailing the decorative motifs and the placement of windows.</meta>

In the pillar of the Arches opposite the back of the Corinthian [column], a third whitewashed rectangular pillar projected. It rose from a base on the floor, facing another pillar fixed into the wing beneath the arch that divided the vaults, and was identical in every way. The interval between these, from one to the other, followed the radial lines <term>radii; lines drawn from the center of a circle to its edge</term> drawn to the circumference, which were fixed upon the line of the outer pillars. Above their semi-capitals ran a decorative wrapping <note>original: "circumligatione"</note> of graceful workmanship.

The semi-tubes and small half-altars <term>hemi Arule; small decorative altars or pedestals</term> were made of luminous **Alabaster**. They were adorned with curving swags—or rather, bunches of many leaves and the fruits of spurge <note>original: "Lacterii"</note>, of medlars <term>Mespili; a fruit similar to a small apple, popular in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</term>, and poppy stalks. These grew heavy in their middle descent, tied with spreading sprays, suspended and knotted into certain rings, and elegantly ornamented.

Below that wrapping described just above, between one fluted semi-square pillar and the other on the main wall, there was a rectangular window of one and a half squares in height, as is required in ancient temples. The opening—or rather, the lighting—of these windows was skillfully filled with a mirror-like or transparent pane of **Sogobrina stone** <term>petra Sogobrina; a type of translucent stone, likely selenite or "lapis specularis," used in antiquity for window panes before glass was common</term>, which does not fear the passage of time. In total, there were eight of these windows, because one part was occupied by the door of the temple itself, and directly opposite the **Pronaos** <term>the porch or entrance hall of a temple</term> at the front was another part of the door with the golden folding-doors of the rear chapel—or rather, of the sacred **Adyton** <term>the innermost, most sacred chamber of a temple, usually forbidden to the public</term>. The description of this sanctuary will be treated more appropriately in another place.

Opposite the aforementioned square columns fixed in the first circuit of the wall, the external pillars projected. They were drawn out from the wall with a thickness equal to that of the wall itself. Their width was determined by the radial lines of the division from the center to the circumference. Of this divided width, one portion was for the width of the pilaster. The other portion, further divided into two parts, with one assigned here and the other there from the adjacent pillar, was for an archway in the solid part of the wall—or rather, a vaulted recess—between one pilaster and the other. The projection <note>original: "proiectura," the distance a feature sticks out from the wall</note> of these pillars, divided by three, took its prominence from the archway carved into the plane of the wall. Two-thirds of the pillars projected from the solid wall of arches and pillars.

The elegant Architects praised this exquisite observation so as not to give the wall such a crude thickness that the windows would appear "blunt" <note>original: "obtuse," meaning the windows would look like deep, dark tunnels if the walls were too thick</note>. This was done with a clear respect for avoiding crude and superfluous bulk, and for exterior decoration. These arches turned in a circle, one perfectly joined to the other with the same thickness, and were bound as required by the pillars around the wall, all beautifully encircled. In no other way could the arches appropriately stand opposite one another.

<keywords>Renaissance architecture, Alabaster, Sogobrina stone, Adyton, pilasters, Corinthian order, sacred geometry, classical temples</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the detailed architectural survey of the temple, focusing on the windows of the outer wall, the small circular chapel (sacellum), and the transition from the columns to the great dome. It describes the elaborate astronomical and calendrical mosaics located in the upper reaches of the structure.</meta>

In this empty interval, between one pillar and the other, or rather between the openings of these aforementioned arches, the window was carved out above the remaining level of the wall. This arched window was as far from the pillar as it was circled under the first external cornice, which surrounded the first roof. There were ten pillars—the "bones" of the building—and just as many arches built solidly into the external wall, excluding the facade where the small chapel <term>facello; a small shrine or chapel, from the Latin 'sacellum'</term> was situated.

The aforementioned cornice, embracing the round chapel, linked it with the temple. Above this connection, its own roof rose, which was a "blind" cupola <note>a cupola without windows or openings at the top</note>, distinct and free from the larger one.

Let us now return to the interstitial binding above the circle of columns—or rather the peristyle—of the straight beam, the band, and the cornice, which extended perpendicularly above the **Porphyry columns**. From each extension of this binding rose fluted semi-columns of a square shape, made of excellent **Ophite** <term>Ophytes; a decorative green stone, often a type of green porphyry or serpentine, named for its snake-like patterns</term>. Above their semi-capitals, a cornice of conspicuous design encircled the space. From this cornice, the curve of the high cupola began its ascent.

Between one semi-square pillar and the next described above, I saw a well-proportioned window, seasonably placed, and made of a dull Bologna stone from Gaul <note>likely selenite or a similar translucent gypsum found near Bologna, used for windows</note>, set in a gilded field of artistic mosaic <note>original: "Muſeo," referring to opus musivum or mosaic work</note>. In these spaces, with balanced distribution and equal partitioning, I gazed upon most excellent depictions in "worm-like" tessellation <term>uermiculata teſſellatura; a style of mosaic using very tiny, curved pieces to create fine detail, resembling the paths of worms</term>. It showed the character of each month of the year with its specific activities, and above them the path of the Zodiac with the working Sun, and the phases <note>original: "Schematiſmi"</note> of the Moon. And there she was shown, appearing between the monthly new crescents, divided and full-bellied, and the circuit through which the months are enclosed. I saw the winding paths of the searching Sun, the winter solstices and the summer solstices, as it circles around; and the alternation of night and day, and the fourfold change of the seasons, and the nature of the fixed and wandering stars with their influences. I suspected that such art was arranged there by the most noble mathematician **Petosiris**, or perhaps by **Nechepso** <note>Petosiris and Nechepso were legendary Egyptian figures to whom many ancient astrological and mathematical texts were attributed</note>. The sight of these things would draw the observer, with excessive solace, into an extraordinary and wonderful contemplation. It was a remarkable spectacle, an elegant fiction, with a beautiful distribution of figures, and precise painting of colors and shadows. Through these, the proportions of the bodies and the necessary lighting were represented to perfection, with a most worthy expression of their effects, providing a praiseworthy and joyful feast for the senses of the mind. It was, without doubt, a work worthy of the deepest consideration, as much as one could ever contemplate. Within each division, the meaning of the aforementioned works was elegantly inscribed in ancient notes <note>original: "notule antiquarie"</note>. The spaces interposed between the semi-square pillars were surrounded by bands carved with beautiful ornamentation.

The massive dome <term>cupola; a rounded vault or dome</term> showed the greatest evidence of being a divine work rather than human ostentation. In open-air buildings <note>original: "subdiuo"</note>, stairs, drainage openings <term>compluvium; a square opening in the roof to collect rainwater</term>, or gutters should not be placed. First, because of the danger of slipping. Second, anyone who urinates near their feet ruins the masonry and soils their own footwear. Therefore, such inconveniences should be avoided. An uncovered gutter <term>imbricium; a curved roof tile or gutter system</term> carves out the ground below due to flooding water; the damage is even more enormous if no stone resistance is placed beneath, for the water splashes back up against the foundations and walls, which can hardly defend themselves against the constant spray.

Not without serious injury, damage, and loss—and through the force of the wind—the water pours over the walls, eventually making them rotten and crumbly; it wears away at the windows, exhausting and fading every decorative coating. Because of this moisture, plants grow in the joints: grassy weeds, navelwort or pennywort <note>original: "cotilidõe, o uero cimbalaria"</note>, maidenhair fern <note>original: "Adianto"</note>, stonecrop <note>original: "Digitello"</note>, pellitory <note>original: "Parietaria"</note>, and polypody fern <note>original: "Polypodio"</note>. The masonry is even prone to producing small shrubs and wild fig trees <note>original: "caprifici"</note>, which are the death of walls; their numerous and reviving fibers and roots render the walls unstable and full of rifts.

Let us return to the description. The wing <note>original: "alamento"</note> of the first wall derived its height from the level of the summit, matching the thickness of the curved beams or arches above the colonnade; those of the vaulted ceiling <term>testudinato; a structure shaped like a tortoise shell</term> rose from the wall opposite the Corinthian column. Into the aforementioned small channel carved into the flat of the cornice, the rainwater that flowed down the sloping roof poured into the receptacles of the pillars <note>original: "Pili"</note>. Finally, to complete the description of this wondrous temple structure, it remains to be said briefly that it was built of square blocks, partly of <term>Augustan stone</term> <note>original: "Augustea petra"; likely a high-quality travertine or limestone used in the monuments of Emperor Augustus</note> and partly of the aforementioned marble. The joints were so perfect that they required neither iron nor wooden supports, and the carvings were of such subtle investigation that in our own age one could neither execute nor even imagine them. No such structure did <note>original: "Api Deo"; referring to the Egyptian bull-god Apis</note> the Samnites or Egyptians ever build.

Beneath the bases of the small pilasters—or rather, the quadrangular pillars that formed the lowest and continuous binding of the first layer or wall—and similarly around the upper cornice with its encircling capitals, there ran along the perfectly level floor a border or band of the finest <term>Porphyry</term>, as wide as the projection of its square base; and joined to this, almost without a visible seam, was another band of <term>Ophite</term> <note>original: "Ophytes"; a green, mottled stone resembling snakeskin, often called serpentine</note>. Under the pedestal of the columns, a band of Porphyry was drawn around according to the column's thickness, with two flanking bands of the hardest serpentine, following the circular path of the <term>peristyle</term> <note>a porch or walkway defined by a row of columns</note>. A similar pattern was seen around the mouth of the cistern set into the floor: a band of Porphyry and another of Ophite.

The remainder of the magnificent floor between the well-opening and the peristyle was composed of marvelous <term>emblemata</term> <note>ornamental mosaic inlays</note> made of tiny pieces—a <term>tessellated</term> work of fine stones. These were elegantly arranged in a circle, enclosing ten round sections within the divided space, each one a foot in diameter. In color and type, each one matched the one opposite it. Two were of reddish jasper, most pleasingly dappled with various spots. Two were of <term>lytharmeno</term> <note>likely a reference to a stone containing mica or "glittering" particles</note>, smaller and scattered with tiny sparks of gold and glowing atoms. Two were of green jasper, variegated with chalcedony veins and red and yellow spots. Two were of agate, with "milky threads" in a confused, wavy pattern. Finally, two were of the clearest chalcedony. And as the lines narrowed toward the cistern, the circular figures decreased in size accordingly.

Under the vaulted ceiling, upon the floor itself, was a most solid <term>Asaroton</term> <note>original: "Asaroto"; from the Greek for "unswept floor," a style of mosaic depicting the remains of a banquet scattered on the ground</note> made of <term>vermiculated</term> work <note>original: "uermiculato"; a mosaic technique using tiny, undulating tiles that resemble the tracks of worms</note>: foliage, animals, and flowers formed of the smallest stone fragments, diligently inlaid and perfectly smoothed and polished. Such artistry was not found in the paving done by Zenodorus at Pergamon, nor was the <term>lithostratos</term> <note>a decorative stone or mosaic floor</note> at Praeneste in the temple of Fortune so fine.

Let us return to the <term>cyma</term> <note>original: "cimatio"; a molding or capstone</note>, or rather the pinnacle of the magnificent dome. It was made of the same metal, purely gilded, and sat above the "sky" <note>referring to the interior ceiling of the dome</note> of the...

A marvelous dome was supported by eight fluted and **hollow** <note>original: "somphe"; a rare term used by the author likely meaning porous or hollowed out for decorative effect</note> columns, which rose magnificently upon a noble pedestal. They were separated by a windowed gallery that circled the structure, with small arches spanning the space between one column and the next, positioned above the supporting pillars. Above these, following an exquisite <term>sesquialteral harmony</term> <note>original: "harmonia sexquialtera"; a mathematical ratio of 3:2, commonly used in Renaissance architecture to achieve pleasing proportions</note> in their height and design, were the **Architrave**, **Frieze**, and **Cornice**, with their projections aligned perfectly with the columns below. Above these rested a scale-patterned dome. Upon the flat projections above each column, I saw a statue of a **wind**, elegantly expressing its natural character; they were winged, with wings spread and stretching back to their shoulders. Each was fixed artistically upon an unstable **pivot** <note>original: "Perone"; a pin or axle that allows rotation</note> or spindle. Whichever way the wind blew, all eight of these winged figures <note>original: "Petasi"; literally "winged hats," here referring to the personified winds wearing them</note> would seek it out, turning and whirling so that their faces were always turned toward the breeze.

On the aforementioned summit of this dome, another eight small pilasters, twice as high as they were wide, rose straight upward. Atop these was a **pitcher-shaped vessel** <note>original: "uaso gutturnio"; a vessel used for pouring water</note> placed upside down with its opening facing upwards. The ascent of the whole structure was designed with such exquisite measurement and mathematical proportion for the viewer’s eye.

Around the base of this pitcher-shaped vessel (for so I interpreted it by its shape), it was beautifully covered in **melon-shaped shingles**. A shaft made of the same metal was set into it, beginning at the width of the base and rising with a moderate slenderness. When the shaft reached the midpoint of the vessel, it supported a massive, hollow **triangle**, cast together with the shaft with great skill.

At the very top of this triangle was a circular opening, and at its thickest part near the bottom, it was pierced in four places. I concluded, after careful observation, that this was a clever invention by the far-sighted builder so that water entering from rain or frost would not prevent it from functioning or weigh it down. Through the top opening of this pillar, the shaft or spindle passed freely, without touching the edges, ending in a sharpened point at the very top. The portion extending from the exit was equal in length to the distance from the bottom of the vessel to the pillar.

Fixed upon this pointed top was a **bronze moon**, in its eighth phase as its shape showed, with its horns pointing toward the heavens. Within the curve or lap of this moon sat a **falcon** <note>original: "Alieto"; likely a hobby or small eagle</note> with its wings spread. Below the moon, on the shaft, were four solid and firm **hooks**, which held four small chains made of the same metal, all cast together as a single piece of bronze to show the skill of the founder...

These small chains, descending equally over the middle bulge of the bronze **Ball** <note>original: "ænea Pila"; a large decorative sphere shown in the illustration.</note>, each held at its end, bound to it, a bronze **Bell** <term>Kodon</term> <note>original: "Chodono"; from the Greek 'kodon', meaning a bell.</note>. After we had all entered, I immediately stopped there without looking elsewhere, wanting to investigate whether these leaves had been drawn back so rhythmically and moderately by a counterweight, or by some other instrument. Whereupon I beheld a divine invention. Because in that part where the leaves met in a tongued closure, on the inner side, there was a plate of fine **steel** <term>calybe</term> <note>derived from the "Chalybes," an ancient people famous for their blacksmithing.</note> fastened over the highly polished metal.

There were also, marvelously, two small boards, a third of a foot wide, made of the best Indian **magnet** <note>lodestone; naturally magnetized mineral.</note>, which the **diamond** <term>Adamante</term> did not resist. It is the "lover of **Callisto**" <note>A poetic reference to the North Star/Great Bear constellation (Callisto); the magnet "loves" her because it always points toward her.</note>, superior to human eyes, though deadened by garlic <note>original: "ſcordeon"; refers to the ancient folk belief that the smell of garlic would strip a magnet of its power.</note>. Particularly useful to sailors, these magnets showed their proper cerulean color, smooth and bright, perfectly fixed into the thickness of the opening in the marble wall—that is, in the doorposts adjacent to the leaves of the ingenious door. Thus, in this way, by the violent attraction of the magnet, the steel plates were drawn, and consequently the door-leaves opened themselves with a tempered slowness. An excellent and most exact work, not only to look upon, but beyond measure subtle in its invention. What persistent effort of the craftsman in his investigation!

No sooner had I carried out this holy command, than she, taking the precious <term>hyacinth-colored vessel</term> <note>original: "lepista iacynthino"; a *lepista* was an ancient type of large drinking vessel or goblet.</note>, and using a cord of gold, crimson, and green silk designated for this office, lowered it into the cistern water, drew out the blessed water, and with religious ceremony offered it to the Nymph alone. **I** cannot in the least allow myself to be persuaded that such rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices were ever devised by Numa Pompilius <note>The second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious institutions</note>, nor at Caere in Tuscany <note>An ancient Etruscan city known for its religious traditions</note>, nor anywhere else in Etruria, nor even by the holy Jew <note>Likely a reference to Moses or the high priests of the Levant</note>. Nor was the goddess of Rhamnus <note>Nemesis, the goddess of retribution, who had a famous temple at Rhamnus</note> ever worshipped with such most religious veneration in the city of Rhamnus in Euboea. Nor was Jupiter Anxur <note>A representation of Jupiter as a youth or a bearded god worshipped at Anxur, modern Terracina</note> worshipped with such superstition. Nor those who, inspired by Feronia <note>An Italian goddess of fertility and abundance; her priests were said to walk on coals</note>, devised such rites, walking without harm over glowing coals. I rightly judged (beyond what I had already openly observed) that according to the things prepared and superstitiously arranged, a great event was about to follow. Because of this, the golden-haired <note>original: "isochrysia," from the Greek for "equal to gold"</note> nymph Polia, being worthy of such an office and initiated into the sacred mysteries, no sooner saw the nod of the temple’s monitress <note>a high-ranking priestess acting as an instructor or leader</note> than she most promptly and religiously rose from the spotless floor without a word, without a rustle of her garment, and without a sound—none of the others moving. Then, she was led by the sacred monitress to a marvelous little urn of hyacinth <note>A blue gemstone or precious glass</note> placed to one side in the chapel; an object of such craftsmanship that even Mentor <note>The most famous silversmith and engraver of ancient Greece</note> would never have known how to make it.

And I, most attentively watching her, observed her with a scrutinizing eye in all her actions. With exquisite and reverent diligence, as instructed, she set down the burning wax taper. After she had lit these aromatics, without further thought, she extinguished the taper and put it aside.

Then, intent and affectionately instructed, she cast the pair of white turtledoves into this fire. Singing in this mysterious manner to the sound of the pipes, they circled in an orbit with a most elegant dance while the sacrifice burned. As it was extinguishing, the little flame gave off smoke. I believe those scents were intended to stifle the smell of roasting flesh, which would have been contrary to the purpose. No sooner was it extinguished than they all suddenly and silently prostrated themselves on the floor (except for the High Priestess). Because of this, not much time passed before I clearly saw, emerging from the holy smoke, a most beautiful divine spirit <note>original: "spiritulo thesphato," from the Greek 'thesphatos,' meaning divinely decreed or heavenly</note>, in a form other than human—as beautiful as could be imagined by diligent thought and investigative fancy. Upon his divine shoulder blades, he had a pair of arched little wings <note>original: "alule"</note>, and he shone with an unusual and unprecedented light. Looking upon it, not without some injury to my eyes from the brilliance, I felt my heart truly and most greedily lost. With such a vehement rush, swifter than a lightning bolt...

Because of this, I was stupefied and totally alienated from my senses, becoming so fearful that not a single hair remained on my head that was not standing on end. Indeed, I shook as strongly as the flexible reeds vibrating in the impetuous and fierce winds. I was more tremulous than wooden shavings, and my mind was vibrating more than the slender reeds in the marshes when they are driven by forceful winds.

O long-desired and most pleasing companionship, so happy and prosperous an outcome of past sorrows! Now my heart, breathed upon by internal sweetness and drenched in celestial dew, no longer wavers regarding the harmful fire; but firmly and evidently, this is my so greatly desired Polia. My tutelary goddess. The genius of my heart. To whom I owe well-deserved and due celebration for her great service to the divine mother, and for such a display of love in this most pleasant company. While I was saying these and similar words most humbly, Polia, having at that moment noticed my low-voiced speech, looked at me with two festive eyes kindled with love. They were brighter than the clearest stars shimmering in a serene sky without the horned moon <note>original: "cynthia" — a poetic epithet for the moon goddess Diana</note>; just as the glowing steel <note>original: "Calybe" — referring to the Chalybes, an ancient people of Asia Minor famous for their blacksmithing</note> sparks when hammered upon the anvil, so did those frequent sparks fly into my struck breast. And in her charming speech with angelic accents, with her crimson mouth—the hiding place of every fragrance, the storehouse of oriental pearls, the most fertile nursery of choice and sweet little words—she seasonably smoothed away all my mental disquiet with sweetness. Her speech was, without doubt, capable of making the terrifying aspect of Medusa <note>the Gorgon whose gaze turned men to stone</note> pleasing, and of mitigating the horrid atrocity of inflamed Mars <note>the god of war</note> and stripping him of his bloody armor. It could steal the most beautiful Ganymede from the hooked talons of the supreme bird <note>referring to the eagle of Jupiter that abducted the youth Ganymede</note>. And by its tenderness, it was capable of uncoupling and splitting into the smallest crumbs the hardest marbles, whetstones, reefs, and the harshest and most abrupt rocks of Persia and of the pathless and cloud-bearing Mount Atlas in the region of the Ocean. And by its soothing, it was capable of taming or domesticating the most savage beasts of Libya, and of bringing back to life every dusty and ashen corpse; thus she spoke:

...monies <note>completing the word "ceremonie" from the previous page</note>. All those who, indulging in affable love, devoted their efforts to it, both men and women alike, did the same. In this place, for the celebrated funerary and solemn assemblies, mourners from diverse regions, neighboring provinces, and remote places came together, beseeching and propitiating the three-bodied divinity of Pluto <note>The god of the underworld, often depicted with three heads or bodies to represent his dominion</note>. They prayed that they might not stumble into such great impiety as to be conscious of their own untimely death. For this reason they sacrificed dark victims, or rather black sheep that had not yet known the male, upon a burning bronze altar—the males to the god and the females to the goddess—and performed the three-night rituals of the sacred couches <term>lectisternii: an ancient Roman ritual where images of gods were placed on couches and offered a banquet</term>. 

That flame and fire they afterwards extinguished by scattering a multitude of roses and with ritual water <note>original: "arferia", a term for a vessel or water used in sacrifices</note>, just as in this place you can still clearly see a large rose garden of every kind remaining. To gather them then was a wicked thing, but the priests would exchange them once the burnt sacrifice was finished. The high priest, adorned with sacred bands <note>original: "isulato", likely "infulato," referring to the 'infula,' a wooled headband worn by Roman priests</note> and with his breast decorated by a marvelous and mysterious golden brooch set with a precious Synochitide stone <note>A mythical stone said to have the power to summon ghosts</note>, then gave a portion of the holy ash to everyone using a small golden ladle <term>simpuleto: a small Roman ritual vessel used for pouring libations</term>, doing so with great devotion. 

Having received the ash, they left the temple in crowds with solemn veneration toward the rush-covered shores of the nearby sea, as you see. And having placed the sacred ash in a reed, they blew it out into the sea with religious superstition, with loud voices and dissonant cries, mixed with the confused wailing of women, saying: "Thus may he perish who shall be the cause of his lover’s death and an accomplice to it." 

After they had scattered the ash in the sea in this manner, they broke the reed and spat three times into the sea, saying three times: "Phui! Phui! Phui!" <note>original: "fu. fu. fu.", representing the sound of ritual spitting to ward off evil</note>. Lastly, each with their fellow countrymen, they placed tables and feasts and whatever food they had brought upon the floor in a circle, sharing it together with the priestly banquets. And here, with holy rite, they held the funeral feast <term>filicernio: a traditional meal eaten at a grave site</term>; the leftovers they then left for the spirits of the dead <term>mani: the Manes, or spirits of the ancestors</term> summoned to the sepulchral altars. Beyond this anniversary, the secular games <term>ludi seculari: a religious celebration involving sacrifices and theatrical performances</term> were held.

Having feasted, they left the temple, and each certainly provided himself with a crown of all fruits <term>pancarpia: a garland or offering made of various fruits and flowers</term>. Having placed it on his head, and with branches of mournful cypress in hand, they followed the leaping priests <term>Salii: Roman priests known for their ritual dances</term>, the sacrificing seers, the leaders carrying the sacred vessels, and the dancers mixed with women. With tumultuous applause and shouts of joy, and with various and multiple instruments—both wind and string—they circled the temple three times in a dance to appease the three fatal Fates: Nona, Decima, and Morta <note>The Roman personifications of the Fates: Nona (who spins the thread of life), Decima (who measures it), and Morta (who cuts it)</note>. Held in the balance of high-thundering Jove, they circled around briskly in a half-frenzied state. They returned into the sacred temple, where each [offered] the cypress branch they carried... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence</note>.

In this place, therefore, upon the fresh and flower-bearing little herbs, we joyfully settled ourselves to sit. Standing thus, with insatiable and wandering eyes <note>original: "vultispici," a word coined by the author meaning "face-watching" or "searching with the gaze"</note>, I gazed in vain upon a single, perfect, and undefiled little body <note>referring to Polia</note>, such harmony and accumulation of beauty—an object that surely forbade my eyes from seeking anything more graceful or of greater contentment. It was a most healthy field with pleasant grass, filled with many trees and echoing with the song of little birds. And sitting there together among the spring-like and fragrant flowers and roses, I kept my gaping eyes fixedly occupied with such delight upon this celestial figure. Devoted and applied with all my senses to such a beautiful and rare creation and divine image, the heated internal assaults resulted more pleasantly within me; in these, my soul being liquefied by sweetness, I remained frantic and entirely anxious, my breast full of curiosity to consider it with wonder. I marveled at what manner and reason that purple liquid <note>the blood beneath her skin</note>, upon the touch of the precious flesh of her smooth hand, remained as purest milk for a short time and did not return to its place <note>He is describing the way her skin turns white when pressed, then slowly flushes pink again</note>. Therefore, wishing to put an end to this incentive and frequent goading through this path, behold, my scarred heart felt itself begin to burn anew with other, even more savage fires. Alas, Poliphilo, how will you fare here? Think for a moment on the violence done to Deianira <note>The wife of Hercules, who was abducted by the centaur Nessus</note>, and to the chaste Roman woman <note>Lucretia, whose rape led to the fall of the Roman monarchy</note>, which turned out poorly and unhappily, and many others. Consider that even the omnipotent gods have faced resistance in earthly loves, let alone a torn and most abject man.

Recall to your memory that over a long period of time, success comes to those who can wait; even fierce lions are tamed by the passing of days, as is every other wild and cruel animal. Even the grain-bearing ant, through constant travel—tiny as it is—imprints its path in the hard flint. How much more should a divine form hiding in a most human little body take within itself a trace of fervent love? And so, turning these thoughts over and rejecting them, I refuted such harmful and vexing passion, subduing it in the hope of achieving the amorous fruits, the desired effects, and the triumphant <term>agonisma</term> <note>original: "agoniſma"; a Greek term for a prize-winning struggle or contest</note>. 

I scrutinized in my memory the holy prayers, the sacrifices, the libations, and the extinguishing of the torch—those divine offices in which she [Polia] had involved herself and her Poliphilo, especially commemorating him with commendatory prayers. Therefore, I thought that by suffering I would obtain a more effective reward and a better return than by trying to ease my bitter languors with dangerous impropriety, only to lose all hope thereafter.

The nymph Polia, having noticed the changing colors of my face—shifting more than the renowned <term>tripolion</term> <note>original: "Tripoliõ"; a plant mentioned by ancient naturalists like Pliny that was said to change its flower color three times a day</note>, or the germander—and seeing me altered and agitated by many hot and sharp sighs from my innermost love, piteously looked upon me with her flattering glances. She opportunely hoped for and soothed my impetuous movements and rushing agitation. And so, no differently than the Arabian phoenix <note>A mythical bird that burns itself on a funeral pyre and is reborn from the ashes</note> which, ignited upon aromatic twigs in the sight of the burning sun, hopes to be renewed from the dry ashes, my soul, burning in these continuous flames and terrible harshness, was urged by love to hope patiently.

<image-desc>A large, square decorative initial letter 'S' featuring a complex, interlaced knotwork pattern in a style reminiscent of Celtic or basket-weave ornamentation.</image-desc>ABOVE ALL THE DEVISED AND EXQUISITE torments of love, I found myself no moderately besieged; and being near to the long-desired, healing, and immediate remedy, my chief-guider <note>original: "architratrice"; a word coined by the author to describe Polia as the primary director or architect of his fate</note> being close by, I wondered with amazement that, against all natural order, she was the one who most softly afflicted me. And yet, every one of her excellent acts, her ornate speech, and her biting glance offered such timely health. Finding myself so near, my senses were forsaking me, whence there multiplied ever more a demanding persuasion within me: that I should not show myself ungrateful or faint-hearted toward this provoking opportunity (a welcome little gift for those who seize it). Growling like a furious and snarling dog once the pursued beast is caught in the mountain leaps; just so I, no more nor less a furious craver, having here reached my own desired prey, sought to satisfy myself entirely. Having become accustomed by now to an assiduous and familiar death of love, I did not consider her cruelty a passion, even if death should follow from it. And I persuaded myself that every improper act, however harmful, was permissible. Wherefore my witty <term>eutrapela</term> <note>original: "eutrapela"; from Greek, meaning witty, pleasant, or versatile</note> Polia, skillful in the ways of blind love <note>original: "cœcutiente amore"</note>, and having noticed how to mortify such an importunate fire and somewhat shorten its beat, and as my singular preserver succoring me, she thus kindly spoke to me: "Poliphilo, my most beloved of all, I am never unaware that ancient works <note>original: "antiquarie ope"</note> please you exceedingly to behold. Therefore, you may conveniently in this interval, while we await the Lord Cupid, go freely to admire for your solace these deserted temples, collapsed by gluttonous and obsolete antiquity, or consumed by fire, or indeed shaken by age, and speculate upon the noble fragments remaining, most worthy of veneration. <meta>Poliphilo continues his descent into the subterranean realm, having just described the terrifying guardians and the entrance to a place of dual torments—fire and ice.</meta>

It appeared to me that the souls who were damned to the burning fire longed to migrate into the ice, and those who were judged to the most numbing lake—far colder than the **Stygian marsh** <note>original: "styge palude," the swampy river of the underworld in Greek mythology</note>—exceedingly desired to enter the cursed and heat-bearing, fresh-burning flames.
But as they struggled to climb the deceptive crossing, the glowing path, by fatal disposition, divided itself in such a way that the souls prescribed to the inextinguishable fire fell back again into their eternally ordained place.
By the same token, those who attempted to escape the unavoidable cold as fugitives were plunged back by the bridge into the freezing depths. Afterwards, by virtue of divine justice, the passage returned to its former state.
Without interval, other sorrowful souls successively attempted this same thing, with vain and powerless desire, and in no way were they able to achieve the desired effect.
Therefore, those most wretched souls who hurried to flee without rest, agitated by furious horror and rage, could not leave the incendiary flames to find relief and refresh themselves in the ice.
And likewise, those who gave constant effort to flee the harshest cold and enter the burning flames were frustrated in their greatest desire and could not succeed. And this was for them an inescapable and unending punishment, always becoming more desirous as they lost all hope.
This ardent greed increased all the more because, while on the bridge, both groups felt the opposite: those from the heat felt the reflection of the cold, and those from the ice felt the heat, the one meeting the other at their boundary. And this sensation was the greatest intensification of pain and torment.
For which reason, with such persistent skill in coloring and simulated gestures and expressive efforts, I saw such a **painting** <note>original: "pictura"; the narrator realizes that this hellscape is actually an incredibly realistic work of art or a relief</note> masterfully made and exquisitely perfected, as much as could ever be made or shown.
And the indicating title was inscribed: **That in the burning flames were condemned the souls who, through too much fire of love, killed themselves. And in the horrid frost were submerged those who, rigid and chilly, had obstinately shown themselves reluctant to Love.**
Finally, with such an arrangement, I marveled at this hateful, terrifying, and avoidable **Abyss** <note>original: "Barathro," a Latin term for a pit or the underworld</note>, where the lakes met—that is, the freezing one with the most burning one. By their opposition, they were made to produce a terrible thundering in eternal controversy, because afterwards, meeting each other, they both plunged into a steep precipice, poured out into a dark, vast, and most deep passage and immense abyss.
Where the depth was so skillfully fashioned by the craftsman that, through the coloring, those appearances falsely claimed to be real, showing a most absorbing vortex with marvelous imitation of colors. And with linear symmetry of perspective, and the elegance of the figures, and copious invention, and skillful design, and with incredible wit, such that **Parrhasius of Ephesus** <note>original: "Parrhasio Ephesio," a famous ancient Greek painter known for his realistic "trompe l'oeil" style</note>, the illustrious painter, could never boast of having first conceived anything different.

These shadows could not appear unless the air were made concrete and condensed into that likeness <note>This reflects a Renaissance belief that spirits or "shadows" became visible by condensing the surrounding air into a physical shape</note>, through which the effect is understood. And therefore many souls were blocking their ears, while others did not dare to look—having covered their eyes with their palms—into the terrifying and swirling abyss, full of frightening, terrible, and various monsters. Others were pale to express the numbing cold, pressing their arms tightly to their chests; some, to demonstrate the burning heat, exhaled a smoky spirit; others, to indicate grieving sadness and painful punishment, wept with their fingers interlaced <note>original: "impectine giuncti," literally "joined like a comb," a classical gesture of extreme distress or prayer</note>. 

Whereupon, on the narrow bridge in its diagonal structure, meeting each other in crowds, one group collided with the other, and they were unable to proceed because of the trampling of those following behind. Then the bridge, by eternal fatal order, having separated itself and throwing them back, returned them to their own proper place; and once it was restored and joined again, others tried without ceasing, one after another, to cross that...

<summary>Poliphilo describes a vivid artistic representation of souls suffering in the underworld, noting how their physical gestures—covering eyes, shivering, or exhaling smoke—depict their specific torments. He details the mechanical failure of the bridge, which periodically separates to plunge the crowds of souls back into their respective pits of fire or ice.</summary>

ALAS, WAYFARER, PAUSE A MOMENT. BY THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD <note>original: "MANIBVS ADIVRAT," a solemn oath invoking the Manes, the souls of deceased loved ones</note>, HE SWEARS. HAVING COME FORWARD AND READING THESE GRIEVOUS WORDS <note>original: "POLYSTONOS," from the Greek for 'much-sighing' or 'full of grief'</note>, GIVE LITTLE KISSES TO THE METAL, ADDING: "AH, CRUEL MONSTER OF FORTUNE, THEY OUGHT TO HAVE LIVED!" LEONTIA, A MAIDEN, AND LOLLIUS, A NOBLE YOUTH, WHEN URGED BY AN IMMODERATE INTENSITY OF LOVE, FLED FROM THE TORTURES INFLICTED BY HER FATHER. LOLLIUS FOLLOWED. BUT WHILE EMBRACING, THEY WERE CAPTURED BY PIRATES AND SOLD TO A CERTAIN MERCHANT. BOTH CAPTIVES BOARDED A SHIP. WHEN, DURING THE NIGHT, LEONTIA SUSPECTED THAT LOLLIUS WAS BEING TAKEN AWAY FROM HER, SHE SEIZED A SWORD AND SLEW ALL THE SAILORS. A RAGING STORM AROSE AT SEA. THE SHIP SANK NEAR THE ROCKS OF A LANDING-HILL. ASCENDING THE ROCKS, DRIVEN BY THE IMPULSE OF HUNGER, I <note>The voice shifts here to Lollius, the male protagonist</note> PLACED LEONTIA UPON MY SHOULDERS TO CARRY HER. "BE FAVORABLE AND PRESENT WHILE HE KNOTS <note>original: "NEDT," likely 'nectit'</note>, O FATHER," I SAID, "I COMMIT US AND OUR FORTUNE TO THEE." THEN, WITH A DOLPHIN-LIKE STRIVING <note>original: "DELPHINEO NIXV"</note>, I CUT THE WAVES WITH MY ARMS, WHILE LEONTIA SPOKE TO ME AS WE SWAM: "MY LIFE, AM I A BURDEN TO YOU?" SHE COMFORTED ME, ENCOURAGED ME, AND ANIMATED ME AS I DIVED. I REJOICED; AT LAST WE REACHED THE SHORE SAFELY. UNEXPECTEDLY, A ROARING LION ATTACKED. WE BOTH ROWED, SINGING ALTERNATELY. THEY WANDERED FOR A DAY AND A THIRD NIGHT. NOTHING BUT THE SKY OPENED UP EVERYWHERE. WE WERE TORMENTED BY A LETHAL HUNGER, AND AS WE WASTED AWAY FROM LONG STARVATION, WE FELL INTO EACH OTHER'S EMBRACE. LEONTIA SAID, "MY LOVE, ARE YOU PERISHING OF HUNGER?" "IT IS ENOUGH TO BE WITH YOU, LOLLIUS, I AM FED," SHE SAID. BUT SIGHING, SHE ASKED, "MY LOLLIUS, ARE YOU FAINTING?" "NOT IN LOVE," I SAID, "BUT IN BODY." Not very far from this, still moved to soft sighs by the unhappy story I had just read, I found another remarkable and most worthy monument. It featured two fluted columns—one on each side—carved in a semicircle from solid rock of the whitest marble, complete with small bases and capitals, a small architrave, a frieze <term>zophorulo</term> <note>original: "zophorulo," a decorative frieze, often featuring animal or human figures.</note>, small cornices, and a little triangular pediment. Within this pediment, two white turtledoves <note>original: "turturule." These birds are traditional symbols of devoted love and mourning.</note> were drinking together from a small vessel.

In the space between the fluted columns was a carved arched ceiling, divided into equal square coffers <note>original: "quadriculi lacunulati," the recessed panels often seen in classical ceilings like that of the Pantheon.</note>. Each of these was occupied by a five-leaved plant <term>pentaphila</term> <note>A decorative floral motif with five leaves.</note> rendered in perspective, the lines and contents diminishing as they receded. 

Beneath this, an artfully crafted chest <term>arca</term> <note>Here used both as a stone sarcophagus and a symbolic "ark" or vessel.</note> projected slightly, fitted with two small doors. Through one of these, naked figures were entering; through the other, naked boys were exiting. Based on the inscriptions placed between them, I reasonably conjectured that this indicated the world is like a chest with two doors: those who enter it are dying, and those who exit it are being born, and both alike are weeping. 

The chest rested upon two harpy-like feet <term>harpyiatici</term> <note>Feet shaped like those of Harpies, mythological creatures with the bodies of birds and faces of women, often used in funerary art to represent the snatching away of life.</note> that turned into leafy foliage, with a third foot in the center of simple design. Underneath the curve of the vault, I beheld the following epitaph concerning a piteous and desperate event.

**TO DIS AND SACRED TO PROSERPINA**

A vow was made.
To Trebia Q., daughter of L. S. Trebius A.
A monument of love and a magnificent display of piety.
Fibustius, her husband, with whom, with the greatest
desire, he lived delightfully for 1 month, 3 days.

This my wife, who was most loving to me,
left behind most unhappy tears and eternal sorrows.
Disturbed by extreme jealousy,
when she suspected another woman had
lain with me, her love, having been turned
into a most sweet frenzy, she herself with iron
through the middle of her breast
stabbed herself to death. Alas, wife, why this?
Oh dear wife, neither such a deed, but even a suspicion,
you should have removed from your lover. Farewell,
my dear. But I, uncertain, unhappy, and
with my trembling life dissolved,
I rest.

Having departed from there with the most joyful solace, and with a burning desire to behold new things, I hurried toward a half-ruined vaulted gallery. There, I gazed upon some exquisite remains of <term>mosaic painting</term><note>original: "pictura muscea"</note>, crafted in the <term>vermiculated style</term><note>A fine mosaic technique using tiny, curved tiles to mimic brushstrokes.</note>. In this place, I found no tomb; instead, in that glassy painting, one could still clearly see Proserpina with Cyane and the Sirens, gathering flowers near the burning Mount Etna. There, Pluto—emerging from the <note>original: "pyriurizo"</note> fire-breathing crater of the mountain—was rapturously snatching her away for his love, while Cyane piteously wept, unable to help her. Here I found massive stones of the decaying wall gaping open, turning green through the cracks with Starwort and Pellitory. The wall was further tangled and destroyed by the wedged-in root of an ancient wild fig tree, which, creeping everywhere with its encroaching roots, had destroyed the <term>tessellation</term><note>The patterns formed by mosaic tiles.</note>; the bond of the joints being ruined, they left great gaps in the masonry.

Of this work, I could only see part of a small stream that seemed to be the remains of a human form transformed into it <note>This depicts the nymph Cyane dissolving into a fountain out of grief for Proserpina.</note>, fashioned with incredible art and wonderfully expressed. It was similar to the painting of the same abduction seen in the shrine of Minerva on the Capitoline, painted by Nicomachus. While my mind was intent upon this pleasing sight, I suddenly heard the falling of some mosaic tiles behind my back. Finding myself alone in this deserted and silent place, I was suddenly quite terrified; turning around to look, I saw a gecko—or wall-lizard—which had been the cause of that ruin.

Nevertheless, no small displeasure overcame me because I could not view the entire work in its integrity, as the greater part was demolished, broken, and damaged by exposure to the open sky. Considering then the violent manner in which Proserpina was suddenly snatched away, a sudden and sad thought struck my loving heart, saying:

> "Oh, wretched, shameless, and unhappy me! Oh, troublesome investigation and unbridled curiosity for things of the past and for searching through worn stones, to what have I fallen? What if, by my ill fortune, my most beautiful Polia were snatched from me, and through my neglect of such a precious present thing—more pleasing than all the treasures in the world—she were struck down?"

And in a moment, a more bitter blow pierced my sad heart with a vehement and rapid pulse, as there presented itself to my confused mind that piteous and lamentable case of the fugitive from his burning homeland <note>Aeneas, fleeing Troy.</note> who carelessly lost his beloved Creusa. This memory disturbed me even more excessively, invading me with such a terrifying thought: that upon these sandy and solitary shores, my most beloved Polia sat alone, distracted from my presence—

My eyes, because of the disproportion <note>The "disproportion" refers to the human eye's inability to process the overwhelming intensity of a divine sight.</note>, could not endure gazing firmly into the celestial form (unless my eyelids were closed); such a glowing splendor emanated from that boyish and divine appearance, which reasonably persuaded me that I was no longer among mortals. Falling into a state of maximum wonder, my spirit said within me: "Behold that which I ardently desired."

I wanted most willingly, with reverent and proper observation, and with every possible effort, to gaze upon the **Divine Navigator** <term>Nauclero</term> <note>The pilot or captain of the ship, here referring to Cupid.</note>; yet my weak vision could not properly endure such a disproportionate object. But by squinting my eyes, I was able in this way to somewhat comprehend the divine child in his many forms. At one moment he appeared to me with a double aspect; at another, triple; and yet again he showed himself with infinite images. He, along with **Polia**, made our itinerary happy, blessed, and glorious. And along this path the amorous pilot **Cupid**, fluttering his sacred feathers and eternal wings—in which **Canens** <note>The text reads "Tanes," likely a corruption of Canens, a nymph famous for her song who loved King Picus.</note>, the lover of **Picus**, would have found solace—shone more brightly than **refined gold** <term>obrizo</term> <note>Gold of the highest purity, refined by fire.</note> in various and joyful colors as he circled above the small waves. He appeared more beautiful and more pleasing to the eyes than **Euclid’s crystalline triangular column** <note>A reference to a prism, which refracts light into a spectrum of colors.</note> held close to the sight.

Now the nautical nymphs began to sing with the sweetest notes and with a celestial intonation, totally different from the human voice, and beyond belief with **musical logic** <term>ragiõe catiõica</term> <note>Likely referring to "canonic" or mathematical principles of harmony.</note>. They sang a most sweet harmony with a matching voice and a trilling melody. I truly feared I would burst from excessive sweetness, for I felt my heart, struck by the sound, leaping from its place; and it seemed to me that my heart might reasonably flee through my lips for the sake of that sweetness. And the nymphs, following the melody with vibrating tongues, broke the notes in their echoing throats, curling, doubling, and tripling the tiny **chromatic notes** <term>cromaticule</term> <note>Small, rapid notes that create a "colorful" or chromatic effect in music.</note> or "tailed" notes <note>original: "accodate notule"; refers to the stems on musical notes.</note>. First they sang two by two, then three by three, then by fours, and finally all six together. Opening their trembling, rosy little lips moderately and joining them gracefully, they breathed out the modulating spirits with **music-filled proportion** <term>emuficata proportione</term>, with honeyed voices syncopated in my warm heart and through the wearying expressions of love. Their voices sighed through those spaces, trilling most sweetly from their throats, making one forget and neglect all natural needs. With stringed instruments they sang of the sweetness and the qualities of love: the clever thefts of supreme **Jupiter** <note>A reference to the many disguises Jupiter used to pursue his lovers.</note>; the comforting warmth of the most holy **Erothea** <note>A name for the goddess of love or a personification of erotic desire.</note>; the lusts of festive **Bacchus**; the fruitfulness of the nourished and golden **Ceres**; and the flavorful fruits of **Hymen** <note>The god of marriage.</note>, expressing these in verse and reciting them rhythmically in **metrical song** <term>melos emmetron</term> <note>Greek for a song following a specific poetic meter.</note>.

Because of this, I held most firmly in my mind that the sweet sound that drew **Eurydice** into the flying shadows of the underworld <note>original: "adlinfere," referring to the Inferno or Hades.</note> was not like this...

...from the darkest seats, liberated from the eternal flames. Neither with such a sound did **Hermes** <note>Mercury, the messenger god.</note> ever lull the **many-eyed shepherd** <note>Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant who guarded Io.</note> to sleep. This voice seemed to breathe through the purest air, spreading out from her precious and coral-red lips. And through her white throat, one could see the vocal spirits being cast forth, diffusing with a modulated sweetness. For that was celestial flesh, a divine and transparent composition, like the coldest crystal or refined camphor tinted with **crimson** <term>chermeo</term> <note>From 'kermes,' a red dye derived from insects, used for high-status textiles.</note>.

Because of this sound, **Phoebus** <note>The Sun god, Apollo.</note> would have stopped himself from coming to dew the dawn with his shining rays; he would have forgotten to paint and give colors to the flowers, or to offer himself graciously to mortals. And because of this, without a doubt, the bow-bearing **Diana** would have forgotten her curved bows, her flying arrows, her diligent hunts, and the dense forests; she would have stayed in the chilly fountain and would not have despised the presence of the incautious hunter <note>Actaeon, who saw Diana bathing.</note>, nor would she have transformed him into a **horned stag** to be torn apart by biting dogs. And the all-wandering **Selene** <note>The Moon.</note> would have withdrawn from illuminating the high heavens and the shadowed earth with her splendor. Even the terrifying **Proserpina** <note>Queen of the Underworld.</note> in her mournful kingdom would not have tormented her grieving subjects if such a tone had reached her ears. And joyful **Bacchus** would have resisted slippery lust and neglected the ancient **Ogygian** hills, and **Elis, Nysa, Chios, and Mount Massicus, and Mareotis**, and he would have made little of the musty delights of the wine-harvesting Autumn. And bountiful **Ceres** would have kept the ears of corn forever green, setting aside the abundant kingdoms of **Ausonia** <note>An ancient name for Italy.</note>, nor would she have traded the thick, four-grained ears for those of **Chaonia** <note>Chaonia was famous for its acorns, the food of primitive man before Ceres introduced grain.</note>. And the **bird that thunders in the clouds** <note>The Eagle of Jove (Jupiter).</note> would not have felt the abducted **Phrygian cup-bearer** <note>Ganymede, whom Jove snatched away in the form of an eagle.</note> fleeing from his curved talons—so most sweetly did the nymphs sing and play in concord, each of them singing along with my **Polia**, dispensing celestial melodies to our open ears.

By these songs, the dark, multi-formed, and night-watching **Cerberus** <note>The three-headed hound of Hades.</note> would have been lulled to sleep, and he would not have guarded the metallic gates of **Taenarus** <note>A legendary entrance to the Underworld.</note> with his many eyes. Then the furious **Tisiphone** <note>One of the Furies.</note>, with her monstrous sisters, would have appeared most peaceful and kind to the miserable souls. Never were **Parthenope** and her sisters, **Leucosia and Ligeia**—the daughters of **Achelous and Calliope** <note>The Sirens, whose song famously lured sailors to their doom.</note>—heard to sing with such harmony near the islands of the goats by **Pelorus**, whether with voice, melody, **Lyre**, or the **hollow flute** <term>forabile tibie</term>. Wherefore my soul, set on fire and moved from its place by the blissful songs, the sounds, the beautiful faces, the company, and the majesty, was unable to redeem itself or call itself its own. Instead, tightly bound, it commended its state into her delicate arms and pledged itself as a perpetual hostage and surrendered prisoner within **Polia’s** white breast. Later, reflecting on this, it reached secret delights through delectable paths and voluptuous channels. And from there, with all my faculties aroused and drawn back into myself, I could resume nothing but a comforting and glorious imagination.
