Because of this, I fed my soul anxiously with tireless contemplation <note>original: "inubere pensiculatione"</note> and restored it with curious glances and eager appetites. I gazed most greedily upon the manifest and perfect beauties—a sight of such rarity—of **Polia**, refusing to look at any other thing worth seeing. But especially then, her shimmering breast was most pleasing to me, wonderfully painted with crimson roses and milky lilies at their first opening in the tearful dawn <note>The "tearful dawn" refers to the dew of early morning.</note>. It was a most placid spectacle, openly granted to my eyes without any obstacle or middle-ground, yet sufficiently colored for that most excellent object: her face. Her face was so enticing, so wonderfully beautiful, graceful, and clear—more so than any decorated star <note>original: "hippe"; a Greek-derived neologism used by the author to denote a celestial body or jewel.</note> appearing in the pure sky—with curling ringlets above it, and her rosy forehead and smooth temples slightly trembling. These flowed with great decorum over her snowy neck and whitening shoulders, while the wanton and truth-bearing breeze blew through them exquisitely. Even the high **Jupiter** could not imagine such a thing within the power of Nature to produce or manufacture; nor could **Apelles** <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, known for his realism.</note> ever have painted its equal, and much less **Aristides** <note>A Greek painter famous for depicting human emotions and the expressions of the soul.</note>, who used his brush to represent the human spirit. I could not satisfy myself with this sight, any more than the humming bees are ever satisfied with fragrant **Thyme** and **Amellus** <note>A purple flower mentioned by Virgil in his poetry.</note>, or the eager goats with the flowering **Cytisus** <note>A clover-like shrub used for fodder.</note> and its tender leaves.

And with a willing spirit and incredible pleasure, I would have unlocked my most loving heart—judging it no burden—and displayed it like a mosaic <note>original: "tessellato"</note>, so that she might have evidence of what qualities one endures while loving. Just as **Antipater** showed his scars <note>Likely referring to Antipater of Sidon, or a general showing wounds to prove his service.</note>, she would see how my soul was immediately seduced by her sweet face and noble figure, reduced to a state of servant-like surrender. I would have made my breast a visible, windowed wound, not unlike the most pious **Egyptian Pelican** dwelling in the solitude of the turbulent and headless **Nile** <note>The Nile was called "headless" because its source remained a mystery to the ancient world.</note>. This bird, with its sharp and cruel beak, cuts and tears itself open for its chicks shivering with hunger, pulling out its own merciful maternal heart. My heart is dedicated perpetually and excitably not to **Dionysus** <note>The god of wine and frenzy.</note>, but to her alone. Mad and Lernaean <note>A reference to the poisonous blood of the Lernaean Hydra, implying a love that consumes like venom.</note> loves and fiery desires poured into me, and she fashioned inciting thoughts in my consenting heart, creating a burning and scorching flame that consumed me entirely. With a greater miracle, she balanced the lethal and death-dealing arrow, which had pierced me harmlessly <note>The arrow is "harmless" because it has not yet caused physical death, though its spiritual effect is "lethal."</note>, in my wounded heart—more so than the lethal hanging weapon in **Ephesus**, which hangs without a cord in the **Temple of Diana** <note>A reference to a legend of a magnetically suspended object in the temple.</note>. Because of this, my forbidden soul was unable to fully bring me back to life.

Therefore, because of these events, I was mortified beyond measure by my burning passion, had her delightful glances not refreshed and recreated me, and her loving nods comforted...

With these amorous triumphs <note>original: "triũphi"; referring to ceremonial processions or displays of victory</note> and the euphonic voices <note>original: "euphonice uoce"</note> of the nautical maidens, and with the presence of marine deities, the serene air was filled, and the azure sea <note>original: "ceruleo pelago"</note> echoed with a confusion of shouts and a multitude of sounds resulting from the waves. With festivities, and dances, and exceptional gestures and festive joy, and with devout veneration as we glided toward that most pleasant place, we arrived. It was so benign and most pleasing, so delightful and beautiful, offering to the senses a singular arboreal ornament, as excellent and voluptuous a thing as the eyes could ever behold. For any fertile tongue would find itself lacking in charity and too sparse to describe it. By such a likeness, the gardens of the ancients would be judged quite unsuitable and an abusive comparison to this one. For it was beyond estimation how very solacing it was: a garden of delights, entirely planted and adorned with vegetables, herbs, a fertile orchard <note>original: "pomario"</note>, a pleasant grove <note>original: "uiridario"</note>, a gracious collection of trees, and a most joyful plantation of shrubs. It was a place not of pathless and rugged mountains <note>original: "mōtideuii"; from the Latin for 'straying from the path'</note>, for every roughness had been smoothed away. Instead, it was leveled and even, right up to the circling steps toward the marvelous, exclusive theater <note>original: "theatro"; Poliphilo is describing the island of Cythera, which is shaped like an amphitheater</note>. The trees possessed a most sweet scent, were most fecund in their harvest, and wide-reaching in the expansion of their branches. It was an incomparable garden of flowing delights, of the widest abundance, most joyful and filled with flowers, free of impediments and snares, entirely adorned with flowing fountains and fresh streams.

The sky was not harsh, but tempered, vast, clear, and bright; not full of the horrific shadows of the underworld, but immune to the variable and inconstant weather that might offend with the snares of biting winds or with troublesome winter frosts. There was no burning from an importunate sun, nor was it a dry or parched place of summer heat, nor shriveled by horrid freezing. Instead, it was entirely vernal and healthy, such as the air is not even for the Egyptians looking toward Libya; it was a place of long health and wholesomeness, destined for eternity. The place was planted with greenery, with a remarkable density of leafy trees, a most grateful display with a most beautiful presentation of verdure. Throughout the liquid air, there was an incredible breath of floral fragrance, with the whole area turning green with herbs and soaked with fresh dew, and with flowering meadows. Beyond this was the abundance of every fertile pleasure and natural good, with colorful fruits among the perennial green foliage, held together with stable cohesion and harmony, with paths defined among the plants and covered by arches of manifold roses. Let the well-watered and wooded plain of Thermiscyra <note>original: "thermiscyra campo"; a legendary fertile plain home to the Amazons</note> yield to this place.

For which reason, I judge it more than arduous and a difficult task—even with a sharp wit—to wish to narrate it. But as much as my rapacious, retaining, and dry memory, placed within this hall of praise, shall support me, I will adapt myself to write it down briefly.

This holy place, dedicated to that nature which is witty and elegant <note>original: "faceta"</note> (though to mortals it is a place of misery <note>original: "miserabūda"</note>), a foster-child of the gods and a station and dwelling for the blessed spirits, had a circumference (as I could rightly estimate) of three miles, and from every side it was intersected by flowing salt

...of most limpid waters. This was not composed of tufa crags <note>original: "tophei ſcopuli"; tufa is a porous limestone</note> eroded by the stubbornness of protruding and foaming waves, nor full of ledges like crashing reefs. Nor was it made of shallow shores, broken and eaten away by the injury of the waves or by biting salt. Nor was it even composed of the proud, stony Niobe <note>A reference to the mythological figure Niobe, who was turned into a weeping stone by grief; here it signifies that the rocks were not jagged or "sorrowful" in appearance</note>, nor do her sharp and hardest children appear here. But it was entirely mineral, made of the brightest substance, not brittle nor crumbly, nor turning to mud, but translucent, whole, and unsullied, like a clear and skillfully worked crystal.

Where, with careful diligence, I explored the pebbly shores, washed clean by a benign flood, strewn with gems of various forms and shimmering colors. There also appeared a great abundance of the fragrant secretion of monstrous whales <note>original: "fragrante coito dille monſtroſe Balene"; this refers to ambergris, a highly prized aromatic substance found on beaches, which was historically—and incorrectly—associated with whale mating</note>, brought back by the productive tides. But first, upon the bare shores of the adjacent coast, I saw the ancient <note>original: "æqueui"; equal in age or long-lived</note> and lofty cypresses, with their astringent and cracked cones, persistent and durable for heavy roofs. Their beams are not tasty to gnawing woodworms <note>original: "teredini"; larvae that bore into and destroy timber</note>, and they were spaced at intervals of three paces, one separated from the other. This regular order, drawn around in a rotating circle, was observed throughout the entire compass-measured <note>original: "circinao"</note> edge of the island. Afterward, a most delightful and flowery myrtle-grove <note>original: "myrteto"</note> encircled it. Myrtle loves the talkative shores; it is consecrated and dedicated to the divine mother of amorous fires <note>The goddess Venus, to whom the myrtle was sacred</note>. It was compact and brought together so densely and shaped in the manner of a wall-like fence <note>original: "murale ſepto"</note>, about a pace and a half high, enclosing within itself the trunks and stems of the very straight cypresses, with the start of their foliage rising two feet above the level top, or flat surface, of the myrtle-grove. Thus, this greenery so constructed walled in the coastal banks, with appropriate paths left and distributed in suitable places. This hedge showed very little wood, being protected by the delightful and flowery foliage, so that one tip or leaf did not exceed another, but with exquisite evenness of pruning, it maintained its top and its circular form.

Inside this walled-in myrtle and green hedge (which could have been about one-sixth of a mile <note>original: "ſemitertio di miliario"</note> from the shore toward the center of the island), I saw, by lines drawn from the center to the coastal circumference, twenty equal divisions, each measuring one stadium <note>An ancient unit of length, approximately 600 feet</note> and an additional fifth part. These imitated the outer enclosure of the myrtle. In each division was a small grove of various meadows with different herbs, and similarly of trees. It was specifically distributed according to the required aspect of the benign sky. Here was a Dodonian forest <note>original: "dodona ſilua"; a reference to the sacred oak grove of Dodona in Greece, famous for its oracles</note>. These divisions, in the decagonal <note>ten-sided</note> figure, by appropriately placing a line in each interval, multiplied into twenty. These twenty divisions were made of most noble enclosures <note>original: "septi"; barriers or partitions</note>, variously latticed with appropriate and convenient gaps in the stonework, two inches thick, with measured placement of small, exquisitely crafted pillars made of white marble, and the rest of a most brilliant reddish color, dressed in various delightful climbing plants, each excluded and separated from the other. In the middle of the enclosure, a door opened level in each one, seven feet wide and nine high up to the top of its convex arch. Neither did the laurel-bearing land of Brutus produce such as these, which were most pleasing to Tiberius; nor did Drusilla see such as these brought by the white hen <note>A reference to a legend where a white hen dropped a laurel branch into the lap of Drusilla, Livia's daughter, which was then planted to provide wreaths for Caesar's triumphs</note>. Apollo was accustomed to decorating both his lyre and his quiver with her leaves. Let the towering Sicilian mountains yield here, both in terms of their sweet springs and their pleasantness. However much the most beautiful son of Mercury <note>Hermaphroditus</note> delighted in those places with Diana, they were not protected from the wrath of highest Jove as these were, offering themselves so gracefully to cover the bald head of Caesar, mixed with many strawberry trees <note>original: "Comari"</note> in the most pleasant soil.

In another enclosure followed, in equal order, another most delightful grove of fragrant wild cypresses, *gilibano* <note>original: "gilibano"; a resinous shrub</note>, and juniper <note>original: "romidascalo, ouero iunipi"</note>, shaped by the art of topiary <note>original: "topiariamente"</note> into many expressive figures. These had minute and prickly foliage, and were the favorite of the husband of the divine mother <note>note: Possibly a reference to Vulcan or the durability of the wood in divine architecture</note>, well-preserved. There were also very tall cedars of manifold utility, dripping with cedar oil, with foliage resembling the cypress; it was from this wood that the statue of Diana in Ephesus was made, highly prized in the most noble temples for its eternal durability, as it resists ancient rot and gnawing moths. This tree is fertile in great Crete, beautiful in Africa, and fragrant in Assyria. It was gracefully interspersed with *urate* <note>original: "urate"; likely a variety of juniper</note> or savine, of perennial greenness but harmful to Lucina <note>note: Savine was traditionally used as an abortifacient, thus "harmful" to Lucina, the goddess of childbirth</note>, shaped into various and changing forms.

Furthermore, in another enclosure, there stood a most abundant boxwood grove <note>original: "buxeto"</note>. The plants were set in round and square marble basins among fragrant herbs and flowers, the likes of which would not be found even on the Macedonian Mount Cytherus. They were very dense, of a beautiful dark green, tapering into points with just measure and degree, rising with a charming ascent—not without the companionship of many other most excellent shapes, beautifully rendered. But one marvelous work exceeded all these: for among this species of shrub, I saw all the labors of the tall Hercules, industriously composed with antique shaping, along with many other representations of diverse animals, ever-green with non-falling leaves, regularly placed and distributed through the grassy and flowery meadow with proportionate and fitting intervals.

Similarly, there was another enclosure of manifold trees harmoniously planted. These little trees were distributed in a most elegant and skillful order. The landscape did not lack for the favor of the heavens, for everything stood perfectly situated without any resistance from nature. Here, ingenious nature clearly confessed to all the delights that she had skillfully produced and scattered throughout the universe. One could surmise that everything had been created here collectively and with particular care. The soil was also grassy and flowery, moistened by rising and shaded springs of crystal-clear water <note>original: "uitreo latice perlucidi"</note>, wetter with most sweet waters than the Fountain of Salmacis <note>note: A legendary fountain in Caria (modern Turkey) known for its clear, still waters</note>.

And here they did not suffer the frost-bearing North wind <note>original: "rigifero arcto"; literally the 'cold-bearing Bear,' referring to the northern constellation</note>, nor the cloud-bringing South wind <note>original: "nubigeno noto"</note>, but the air was most healthy and purified, exceedingly pure and by far the most lucid, freely visible to the eyes, most light, even, and unchanging. This was accompanied by the great pleasantness and moderate sunniness of the place and the sky, which never suffers turbulent alteration; instead, every cloud is dispelled and driven away, and the liquid sky shows itself. The bold winds <note>original: "procaci uēti"</note> are excluded, as are the crashing East winds, the whistling North wind <note>original: "Aquilo"</note>, and the malice and harshness of the raging storm with its great roar. Indeed, any inclemency of the seasons is absent, not subject to the tumultuous changes of the rainy seasons <note>original: "aq̄ne"</note> or the cold sign of Libra <note>note: The scales of Libra mark the autumn equinox</note>.

Rather, one can look upon everything with bright clarity and desirable light, joyful and budding in the station of the woolly Aries <note>note: The constellation of the Ram, marking the beginning of Spring</note> drying his fleece in the luminous and Herculean Sun <note>original: "heracleo Phœbo"</note>. All things exist with a perpetual, rather than fading, vigor <note>original: "uirore"</note>, celebrated by the manifold song of birds; the crested lark <note>original: "galericola"</note> flying through the air together with the singing nightingale <note>original: "Luscinia"</note> made the air ring with their song.

At the outer boundary of this sixth of a mile <note>original: "semitertio di milliario"</note>, all distributed in small groves toward the center—since the circumference of a circular figure is as large as its three diameters, plus an additional amount where, if a diameter is divided into eleven parts, two of those portions are added <note>note: Colonna is providing a Renaissance approximation of Pi (π) as 3 and 2/11, or 3.18, used to calculate the relationship between the island's diameter and circumference</note>. Thus, the diameter of this voluptuous island was one mile and two-elevenths.

An extraordinary enclosure surrounded it, eight paces high and a foot thick, so densely leafy that not the smallest trunk appeared. It was pierced with paired windows and, arranged in suitable places for passage, it formed arched open gates. This hedge was made and compactly fashioned of orange trees <note>original: "meli rancii"</note>, lemons, and citrons, adorned with brilliant greenery in the mature leaves and new shoots, and scattered with early and ripe fruits and most fragrant flowers. It was so pleasing and remarkable to the sight, especially since it is very rarely granted to human eyes to see such equivalent workmanship.

In this delightful and pleasing enclosure, between the greenest myrtle grove and this flowering orange-tree hedge surrounding it, countless and various animals, enclosed within, wandered about charmingly. Even though their natures were dissimilar, they were harmless and gentle. They wandered here in mutual friendship. First, the goat-born satyrs <note>original: "caprigeni satyri"</note> with their hanging and twisted spiraling horns. Then the two-horned fauns with those of the other sex. Then the half-wild stags and rock-climbing goats, the fearful does, the spotted fawns, and the leaping roe deer. There were long-eared hares and timid rabbits. There were polecats <note>original: "fele pulluarie"; literally "chicken-cats," referring to weasel-like predators</note>, white and yellow weasels, and the deceptive ermine <note>original: "mendace gallante"</note>. There were restless squirrels and sleepy dormice. There were fierce unicorns <note>original: "Alicorni"</note>, goat-stags <note>original: "tragope & Tragelaphi"; mythical hybrids of goats and deer</note>, and every species of lion, without any ferocity but rather full of play. There were colossal giraffes, swift gulls <note>original: "gauielle"; likely referring to the Mediterranean gull</note>, and infinite other animals, intent on the comforts of nature.

Further beyond this enclosure toward the center, I found the magnificence of an extraordinary orchard <note>original: "pomerio"</note>, or rather a delightful pleasure garden <note>original: "uiridario"</note>. Never could humans not only arrange such a thing, but I am persuaded they could not even imagine it. It is easy, then, for the secondary creator <note>meaning Nature</note> to make the work of the first creator <note>meaning the Divine Mind</note> fertile. And I also agree that no genius is so fertile as to be uniquely capable of worthily describing even a little of so many excellent works of this sacred place. Let the hanging gardens built by the Syrian king <note>A reference to the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, attributed to Nebuchadnezzar or Semiramis</note> yield to this place. For this reason, I rightly judged that this most exquisite design was produced for the contemplation of the soul of the Goddess of Nature in such order and effect by no other than a divine artisan.

This most remarkable garden, extending toward the center, was 166 and a half paces across, divided into meadows. This division consisted of paths going straight to the center and others crossing them circularly. These paths were five paces wide. The primary meadows in the first line of their square-like section toward the enclosure, along with the sides, were 50 paces. But the fourth line toward the center decreased in size, and from this line the first line of the second meadow took its dimension; the third meadow was squared in the same way. This was because the force of the lines tending toward the center caused a skew <note>original: "scambro"; a technical term describing how a rectangular plot becomes trapezoidal when drawn within a circle</note>. Because of this, the squareness was altered by the narrowing of these meadows and paths, though the transverse paths remained whole.

These paths were covered with pergolas, and at each junction <note>original: "grummia"</note> there was a vaulted mound supported upon four Ionic columns. The shaft or height of these columns was nine times the diameter of their base thickness. And on either side of the paths or ways, there were terraces <note>original: "altane"</note> encased in the finest marbles with most fitting outlines. And for every four diameters of distance, there stood one of the aforementioned columns. This arrangement of columns and the spacing between them <note>term: <term>intercolumniation</term> — the architectural practice of maintaining consistent gaps between pillars</note> was observed throughout.

Outside the planters <note>original: "capsule"</note>, or rather the terraces beneath the solid columns, rose bushes sprouted, their height not exceeding one pace. The height of this pergola <note>original: "pergula"</note>, including the planters, columns, and the straight beam, stood five paces high. From this height, the small domes <note>original: "cupule"</note> began to round out and swell into the shape of bubbles. These domes were covered only in yellow roses. The long pergolas were covered in all species of white roses, while the cross-sections were covered in crimson roses of every kind, with eternal foliage and blooms in great abundance and fragrant scent. Outside the planters, every kind of flower and aromatic herb germinated.

The first circular pergola joined the enclosure of the orange grove <note>original: "aranceto"</note>. It had a window where the curve ended, leading toward the center of the pergola, open one pace from the ground, equal to the space between the columns.

Each meadow had four gates in the middle of the columned hedge. The planters were left open for passage. These gates across all the meadows were perfectly aligned with one another.

In the middle of the olive and flower-bearing meadows, I saw an elegant structure of extraordinary design and particular refinement. First, in the primary meadows, I marveled at a most celebrated construction of a flowing fountain, situated beneath a lookout <note>original: "specula"</note> of green boxwood, skillfully shaped. This was found uniformly throughout the first order of meadows and around the circuit in this manner:

In the center of each, with equal distribution, three circular steps were built. On the top level, the diameter was two and a half paces, with a colonnade <note>original: "peristylio"</note> of eight small columns (previously mentioned) with their bases arranged in a circle on the upper step, along with their capitals. Their height was seven times their diameter (following the Doric style <note>original: "doricamēte"</note> based on the thickness at the bottom), and they featured arches swelling from one to the next. Above the arches ran the beam, the band, and the cornice. Exactly above each supporting column was placed an antique-style vase. The diameter of its wide body was three feet, with a rounded, pointed base that gradually widened toward the middle, where it was decorated with an exquisite little belt <note>original: "zonula"</note>. From there, the rim sloped gently up to the mouth, with highly polished lips around the opening. From the mouth to the belt was one and a half feet, and the rest down to the foot...

Above the vessels, everything was composed of the tight and cohesive greenery of the boxwood <note>original: "buxi"</note>, which had been skillfully planted and packed into the vessels, grown with great density, and perfectly trimmed <note>original: "decimato tonsile"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the architectural tour of the island garden. After describing the boxwood structures, Poliphilo focuses on a central jasper fountain featuring golden hydras and tiered garden beds planted with aromatic herbs in the corners of the meadow.</meta>

In the central space of the level and very solid mosaic floor <note>original: "emblematura solistima"</note> of the peristyle <note>a porch or walkway lined with columns</note>, there was a fountain set within a circular depression, somewhat hollowed out like a shell. From its center rose an inverted pedestal <note>original: "balusto"</note> two feet high. Upon this sat a flat plate, the opening of which had a diameter of four feet. In its very center, the three spreading tails of three golden hydras <note>mythical water serpents</note> rose from the bottom in a strange, three-fold manner. These then twisted tightly into a beautiful knot, their bellies separating in the shape of a snail shell <note>original: "collea"</note> with outward-curving variation. Their throats were knotted like snakes, and their three heads poured out scented water into the shell-basin. They equally supported an upright, two-foot-high vessel of an oval shape. From the top of this vessel were fixed eight small golden pipes <note>original: "fistulete"</note>, from which a very thin stream of water flowed. Through the gaps or intervals between the boxwood columns, the water sprayed out, moistening the entire meadow as if with dew <note>original: "roscidamente"</note>. The space within this viewing-point was clear and passable. All the stonework was made of the finest red and shining jasper <note>original: "diaspro"</note>, speckled with infinite spots of various colors, featuring elegant and exquisite carving <note>original: "caelatura"</note> in all the appropriate places.

Now, in each corner of the square meadow, at a proportionate distance from the planting boxes, there was a tiered terrace <note>original: "altana"</note> of four steps in a square shape. The first step, which was very solid, appeared to be two feet high at the front. On the flat top, or mouth, it was one and a half feet wide <note>original: "selquipedale"</note>, and these were hollowed out as planting beds. Then followed the next step above in tiered order, as high as the open width of the first, and so on for the third and the fourth. In the first step, fragrant herbs sprouted, and likewise in the following ones. Here, then, were curly and very tiny basil <note>original: "ocimi"</note>, lemon-balm <note>original: "citroei"</note>, and chervil <note>original: "cheropholii"</note>. These did not grow past the middle of the step's front, their foliage being kept perfectly level; this uniform appearance was maintained throughout. Another tier had fragrant and tiny thyme, pleasing to the honey-making bees. In the third was the small and bitter "sweet-cone" <note>original: "gliciacono," perhaps a type of aromatic cumin or nectar-plant</note>, or southernwood <note>original: "abrotano"</note>, such as does not even grow in Sicily. In the highest tier grew Celtic spikenard <note>original: "spica celtica"</note> with a delightful scent.

This arrangement was distributed among all four tiered terraces <note>original: "altane"</note> placed at the corners of this first meadow, each completely covered with flowering ground-laurel <note>original: "camædaphne"</note>. <meta>This page continues the description of the garden's elaborate geometry, moving from the boxwood topiary structures of the first meadow to the tiered garden beds and fruit trees of the second meadow. In the corners of this second meadow, toward the center, just as they were established in the first, there were tiered boxes <note>original: "capse"</note> of four levels. These followed the same arrangement, dimensions, and placement as the other raised beds <note>original: "altane"</note> of the first meadow. However, they differed in their material. These were made not of common stone, but of the blackest jet-amber <note>original: "nigerrimo succino, oueramente ambrum"</note>.

Never did the sisters of Phaethon <note>the Heliades, who in Greek myth were transformed into poplar trees and wept tears of amber following the death of their brother Phaethon</note> by the river Po <note>original: "Eridano"</note> pour out such resin; nor could such be found in the Amber Islands <note>the Electrides</note>, nor does the temple of Ammon produce anything like it. It possessed a mirror-like polish, and when rubbed, it would attract a straw <note>an observation of the static electrical properties of amber, which the Greeks called "elektron"</note>. These boxes were fashioned in circular shapes.

In the lowest level germinated the fragrant cassia <note>an aromatic bark related to cinnamon</note>; in the next grew the scent-bearing nard <note>a plant used since antiquity to produce a heavy, spicy perfume oil</note>. In the third was the nymph Mint <note>original: "Mente Nympha"</note>, representing the fierce hatred of Proserpina <note>in mythology, Proserpina transformed the nymph Mint into a lowly plant out of jealousy over her husband Pluto</note>. In the fourth grew the ill-fated royal marjoram <note>original: "amaracon"</note>, perishing amidst its own scent; even Cyprus does not produce its equal.

In the upper middle of these beds, an orchard was similarly planted. However, these were different in their fruit and in their <term>topiary</term> <note>the art of shearing and training plants into ornamental shapes</note> form from the previous ones. Next in order follows the description of the third meadow toward the center. In its midpoint, it featured a circular box <note>original: "capsa," a raised enclosure or planter</note> three feet high and two paces in diameter, including all its decorative features. Above these were small crowns, and below were appropriate gathered decorations, all trimmed with perfect precision. The height, not counting the decorative lines, was three feet. Upon the flat surface of each sat an **ancient water jar** <note>original: "hydria"</note>, four feet high and decorated on four sides. <meta>This page continues the description of the garden's flora, moving from the structure of the branches to the perpetual nature of the fruits and flowers, then detailing the various species of roses and the architectural enclosure of the meadow.</meta>

These overflowed with fruits and flowers with leaves that never fell, offering the highest delight to the senses of the spectators. Furthermore, they did not struggle with crooked, wayward, or tangled branches, but were neatly intertwined into various shapes. They were not subject to seasonal changes, nor to the fading power of **Phoebus** <note>original: "Phœbo," referring to the sun god whose heat or absence usually changes the seasons</note>, but were always subject to a tender and succulent greenery, unchangingly and in the same state, remaining durable and producing a fertile yield.

And by this same condition, the flowers and the fragrant shrubs similarly endured. From them, an unfamiliar fragrance, most welcome, spread extensively everywhere. The rose gardens then presented themselves with even greater grace, as they were of many diverse and, to me, unusual types. Here flourished abundantly the **Damascene**, **Praenestine**, **Pentaphylle** <note>five-leaved</note>, **Campanian**, **Milesian**, **Red**, **Paestum**, **Trachinian**, and **Alabandian** roses <note>These names refer to famous rose varieties and growing regions described in classical antiquity, such as those mentioned by Pliny the Elder</note>, and every noble and most praised species. These persisted among the green foliage with their sweetest scent, very pleasant color, and most graceful bloom, remaining eternally preserved. No sooner did one fall than another succeeded it.

The planters <note>original: "capse," literally boxes or chests</note> were fashioned with the most skillful art. Their polishing was so mirror-like that they reflected the air, the leaves, the flowers, and the bountiful foliage within themselves.

Beneath the **topiary** <term>topiarie: the ancient art of clipping and training shrubs or trees into ornamental shapes</term> works and pergolas, the paved paths were of a stonework more excellent in its making than could ever be conceived or devised by human intellect.

Beyond the aforementioned and equally tripartite meadows, a most magnificent boundary—consisting of an extraordinary and remarkable **peristyle** <term>peristyle: a continuous porch formed by a row of columns surrounding a courtyard or garden</term>, **eustyle** <term>eustyle: an architectural arrangement where columns are spaced at a distance of two and a quarter diameters, considered the most ideal proportion</term> and **ventriculated** <note>referring to 'entasis,' the slight swelling in the middle of a column to create an optical illusion of straightness</note>—beautifully enclosed the area, surrounding it like a defensive wall. The low wall of this circular colonnade was constructed of noble and orderly **lattice-work** <note>original: "cancellatura"</note>, intricately fashioned in the style of Daedalus. ...the plinth and the molding, featuring corresponding wavy and throat-like <note>original: "gululato," referring to a *gula*, a type of S-shaped architectural molding</note> patterns. The **intercolumniation** <term>intercolumniation: the clear space between two adjacent columns</term> had spaces measuring two and a quarter column-widths. At the points where the paths led into the **peristyle** <note>a porch or walkway formed by a row of columns</note>, an opening was created as wide as the path itself, which broke the continuous line of the enclosure. Here, a most noble gate was crafted. Its slightly curved arch rested with its ends upon columns on either side, which matched the other columns in their shafts and placement. However, they differed in thickness, having been proportioned to support the structure above. 

Beyond the curved beam, the **pediment** <note>original: "fastigio" or "frontispicio," the triangular or decorative upper part of a gate</note> was situated, with all its decorative elements most exquisitely carved. Above the ring of columns, the **architrave**, **frieze**, and **cornice** <note>original: "epystylio, zophoro & coronice," the three parts of a classical entablature</note> extended in a continuous circle with marvelous precision and fitting lines. These were hollowed out with wonderful sculptural work and filled with earth. From these, all kinds of most excellent flowers germinated. 

Directly above the columns were planted topiary boxwoods and junipers. Thus, above the side columns, in a steady order without any visible trunk, was a perfectly round ball of boxwood; and above the next, alternating in this way, the juniper rose more than a foot above its trunk with four flattened spheres that decreased in size step-by-step, with flowers placed between them.

This marvelous peristyle had low walls and an upper structure made entirely of the most noble **translucent alabaster**, shining and bright, without needing to be rubbed with **Theban earth** <note>a fine volcanic powder used in antiquity for polishing</note> or pumice. ...of the greenest stone, the **sixty-colored stone** <note>original: *hexaconthalitho*, a legendary stone mentioned by Pliny as having sixty different colors</note>, which shone with varied hues. And so they alternated harmoniously <note>original: *emuficataméte*, a word coined by the author suggesting a musical or rhythmic arrangement</note>, with an incredible delight to the viewer. They featured **inlays** <term>enthefi: decorative inlaid work</term> crafted with such skill and were turned so exactly on a lathe that such art was never found in the workshops of the architects Theodorus and Tholos <note>Theodorus of Samos was a legendary Greek architect credited with inventing the lathe for turning columns</note>. The **Ionic columns** with their capitals featured **echinus** <term>echinus: the rounded, decorative molding sitting just below the top of a column capital</term> carvings set between dart-like patterns. Upon the flat surface of the low wall, in each interval between one column and the next, stood an ancient vase of workmanship matching the rest of the description. Their surfaces were so clean that they reflected every object, shaped and polished with such mastery that I thought the lines were not made by human hands. And innumerable other famous small plants, aromatic and of the most pleasant scent. And the white, blue, and purple **Hyacinths**, such as are not even produced in Gaul.

For a more evident demonstration, the circumference of this delightful and most pleasant island <note>original: *insula*</note> measured three miles <note>original: *milliarii*</note>. Its shape provided a diameter of one mile. This diameter was divided into three parts; one third contained 333 paces <note>The author uses the Roman "passus" or pace as a unit of measurement</note>, one foot, and two palms, and slightly more, extending from the outermost edge of the coastal shores to the **orange enclosure** <note>original: *claustro naranceo*; a hedge or boundary made of orange trees</note>.

The measurement of a half-third <note>original: *semitertio*; mathematically one-sixth of the total diameter</note>, consisting of 166 paces and 10 palms, was also occupied. From this boundary, the meadows began, tending toward the center <note>original: *meditulo*</note>, spanning another such half-third. Having thus appropriately distributed one full third, there remained one half-third to be allocated as far as the center, consisting of 166 paces and 10 palms. 

From the aforementioned **peristyle** <note>A continuous porch formed by a row of columns surrounding a courtyard or garden</note>, a certain amount of remaining space was granted due to the narrowing of the aforementioned meadows, in order to avoid the crowding of the squares <note>original: *quadrature*; likely referring to the geometric divisions of the garden plots</note>. These did not reach their boundary until the completion of the third part, and this occurred skillfully to somewhat proportion the final square through lines drawn toward the center point. This space, interspersed between the river <note>original: *flume*</note> and the peristyle, was all graciously—

<meta>The previous page established the geometric dimensions of the Island of Cythera, moving from the outer shores toward the center. ...completely covered with the most pleasing greenery, just as has been sufficiently described and narrated before.

The boundary of the area just described ended at the flower-strewn banks of a river of the utmost clarity, surpassing the **Argyrondes** <note>original: *Argyrondes*; a legendary river in Aetolia, Greece, noted for its silver-clear water</note> in **Aetolia**, and even the **Thessalian Peneus** <note>A river in Greece famous in mythology for its beauty</note>. The banks of this river were made of the most verdant **Spartan stone** <term>Spartan stone: also known as *Lapis Lacedaemonius* or *Verde Antico*, a prestigious green marble</term>, which were paneled in the Doric style like the **Tiberian** and **Augustan** stones <note>Refers to specific types of marble favored by Roman emperors</note>; the entire river was enclosed within these marble limits. These banks were not tangled or occupied by water-weeds, nor by willow thickets, nor by osiers, nor by common reeds. Instead, they were enclosed by the purest, silvery waters. The surface of these waters appeared most joyful and beautiful, covered with many celebrated flowers. This rising and flowing river gushed forth in an orderly fashion through subterranean channels and pipes in various designated places. Then, running swiftly through aqueducts of the finest stone, it equally irrigated this delightful and happy site everywhere with a pleasant murmur.

The water then poured headlong into the neighboring sea. In this way, the clear river—by exhausting its increase through the distributed drainage outlets <note>original: *emissarii voratori*; literally "devouring emissaries," referring to overflow drains</note>—did not overflow, but remained steady and content at a perennial level. The width of the river was twelve paces. Its rising veins exceeded any famous spring, even the **Cabille** of **Mesopotamia**, in excellence. Nor did the **Castalian Spring** <note>The sacred spring of the Muses at Delphi</note> produce such water as these banks did—sweet, smelling of musk, and pure, sixteen palms deep. The **Spring of Hercules** in **Gades** <note>Modern-day Cadiz, Spain; a site of ancient myth</note> did not flow so abundantly with such sweet water. The waters were so clear, purified, and subtle that they did not obstruct the space between the eye and the object, nor did they distort it <note>This reflects the Aristotelian theory of "the medium," suggesting the water is so clear it is invisible to the eye</note>. Rather, everything resting on the open bottom could be seen perfectly throughout. With the quality of a mirror, the waters fully reflected the things presented to them. The bottom was composed of golden sand, leveled and full of fine pebbles of many colors and brilliant luster.

The lush, leafy, and moist banks were most richly adorned with flowering **narcissus** and the **sea onion** <note>original: *bulbo uomico, ouero cepe marino*; likely the *Urginea maritima*</note> or squill. There was no lack of **hyacinth**, **lilies of the valley**, the **sword-lily** <note>original: *Xiphion segetale*</note>, and the **Illyrian iris**. Here, there was an abundance of **marsh marigolds** <note>original: *Caltha*</note>, and the **lion’s tail** <note>original: *Hippotesi, ouero cauda leonina*</note>, and the **lion's leaf**. There were infinite **Tusculan violets**, sea violets, Callatian violets, autumn violets, and **balsam** <note>original: *balsamita*; likely costmary or a fragrant mint</note>, or "cimiadeo," or "trachiotis," and other most noble plants that grow by the water. There were also innumerable water birds. Here was the **Halcyon** <note>The kingfisher, associated in myth with calm seas</note> with its blue-tinted feathers, and other small, fleeting river birds. Here also were the gluttonous and swimming **swans**, graceful in their appearance, singing their final song by the waters of the **Meander** <note>A winding river in Asia Minor, famous for the legend that swans sang there before dying</note>.

Above the aforementioned most spectacular banks, on one side and the other, orange, citron, and lemon trees were distributed with marvelous artifice. The space from trunk to stem was three paces. These trees began to spread their branches one pace above the ground, meeting one another and perfectly intertwining to form an arch, curved three paces from the ground to the summit.
   The remaining branches then reached from one bank to the other over the river, meeting those from the opposite side in a skillful marriage and a social embrace, curving and entangling themselves. They cast a pleasant shade in a work of most excellent **pergularia** <term>pergularia: an ornamental trellis or arbor-work made of living plants</term>.
   The curvature of this arbor was elegantly packed with dense foliage, displaying an even shearing—or rather, a pruning—where one leaf did not exceed another except with the greatest grace and beauty. It provided a most peaceful shade, and through the sweet breath of **Favonius** <note>original: *Phauonio*; the Roman name for the West Wind, associated with springtime and gentle breezes</note>, the leaves were trembling and fluttering. They were full of nourishment, which made them illustrious in their greenery, appearing as they do at their first budding, with white little flowers and hanging fruits. These provided suitable hiding places for the plaintive **Philomela** <note>Philomela is the poetic name for the nightingale</note>, who sang her ever-sweet and mournful song, perfectly without **Echo** <note>In mythology, Echo was a nymph who could only repeat the words of others; here, it suggests the song is clear and direct</note>, sounding clean and most purely refined by the daughter of the **bright-eyed** <note>original: *Glaucopi*; an epithet for the goddess Athena/Minerva</note> [Minerva] of high and thunderous Jove. This vaulted work of greenery stood seven paces above the water from its highest convex point. Oh, how easily this attracted wandering eyes to its contemplation with such allure and sweetest suggestion!
   For upon this river there traveled several **lintri** and **scaphidii** <note>types of small, light boats or skiffs used in antiquity</note> fashioned of gold, delightfully covered. Within them were many girls with long, flowing hair—**Euplocame** <note>Greek-derived name meaning "fair-tressed"</note> and **Alphesibean** <note>original: *Alphesiue*; likely referring to Alphesiboea, a figure of pastoral beauty</note> beauties—wandering and rowing here and there, crowned with wreaths of various fragrant flowers. They were dressed in clear, shimmering, and saffron-colored <note>original: *crocotuli*; saffron-colored garments were a mark of luxury and refinement in the ancient world</note> shifts or under-tunics, hemmed everywhere with gold. These were worn over their naked bodies <note>original: *nympheo nudo*</note> with playful ornament, and girded in such a way that they did not prevent the sight of their voluptuous, rosy flesh. Indeed, as they were sensuously pushed and pressed against the women by the spring breezes, their delightful forms and every other part were excellently revealed according to their movement. Their very white and apple-like breasts were exposed to the greatest and most voluptuous grace down to the rounding of their nipples, elegantly encircled by golden, gem-studded **Phrygian work** <term>phrysii: ornate embroidery, often featuring gold thread and jewels, for which Phrygia was famous</term>.
   With them were many youths from every warlike nation, gesturing, quarreling, and running among themselves in play. In a laughing naval battle, they competed stubbornly against those attackers; intent on the spoils, they overturned their boats and carried them off. The girls remained despoiled and stripped in the waters without favor, nor did they resist their misfortune, but instead let themselves go festively. Leaving these behind, the youths then mocked each other and started new battles among themselves, submerging the captured little boats, and in such a way they worked to recover the submerged prows <note>original: *embole*; the "embolos" was the bronze ram or beak of an ancient ship</note> in the water...

<meta>This page continues the description of the architectural features of the Island of Cythera, picking up from the previous page's description of the dimensions and materials of the terraces near the river. The catchword "tudine" completes the word "latitudine" (width).</meta>

[lati]tude just as much, of marble-work, one of reddish-striped <term>trigla-stone</term> <note>original: *trigle rubente strisso*; likely a mottled red marble resembling the scales of the red mullet fish</note>, and one of a blackish stone darker than the <term>Celtis</term> <note>original: *petra nigella obstante al celte*; likely comparing the stone's darkness to the bark or wood of the hackberry tree</note>, and of a greater natural hardness than the most illustrious Paduan stone <note>original: *patauia*; likely trachyte from the Euganean Hills near Padua</note>, without the smoothing of a cylinder, or the use of dust and dross; excluding the rule of a thickness of two-twelfths or nine-twelfths of a foot <note>original: *sextante... dodrante*; Roman units of measurement</note>, nor with a retraction of a foot and a half or two feet, but as reviewed above, and with such measurement all the others.

Above the topmost step of the blackest stone, a surrounding and elegant <term>pycnostyle</term> <note>original: *picnostylo*; an architectural term for columns spaced very close together</note> colonnade stood out, its continuity interrupted or spaced according to the rule of the width of the bridges, following that of the streets. These excellent bridges were duly covered by the unblemished pergola above the river, and although the streets tended directly toward the center, the steps were not for this reason intersected in their full circular path. Then, as was recently said, above the ascent of the steps there was as much spacing of the small columns as the width of the pathways provided. But the royal road, leading directly to the gate of the wondrous circus, stood out, appropriately exempt from the narrowing of the lines toward the center; it remained alone, equal and uniform in its width, and its ascent over the steps rose most conveniently as a ramp. And therefore, in this place, the steps were necessarily found to be discontinuous.

This pycnostyle featured double columns whose <term>plinths</term> <note>the square bases of the columns</note> and <term>spires</term> <note>the molded bases above the plinths</note> were arranged in an unusual distribution, making mutual contact with one another at the corners along a diagonal line, and joined in successive pairs along the straight sides <note>original: *pleure recte*; using the Greek word for "ribs" to describe the sides of the structure</note>. Between every two columns was one of alternating coloration made of excellent, most shining <term>jasper</term>, and among every seven columns resided a square one of reddish hue, crowned with a translucent gilded bronze ball; the others were bound and encircled in the same way with a small beam, a <term>zophorulo</term> <note>original: *zophorulo*; a small frieze, usually decorated with figures</note>, and a small cornice of the same material and coloring as the square column, with most graceful lines. These rested upon the capitals of the small columns, the spaces between which consisted of <term>chalcedony</term> <note>a translucent variety of quartz</note>; these numbered six, with one of green jasper, spotted with many tiny specks, placed between every two, at a proper and companionable distance.

Above this most pleasant pycnostyle, I saw countless peacocks playfully running and resting—some white, some red, and some wheeling their natural colors, while others had their most remarkable feathers lowered; here and there all the species of <term>parrots</term> <note>original: *psitaci*</note> were intermixed, providing no small ornament and a delightful sight to the aforementioned workmanship.

The fronts of the steps were seen to be wonderfully carved with a noble and <term>Assyrian knotwork</term> <note>original: *assyriana innodatura*; complex interlacing patterns or guilloche designs</note>, and for greater visual effect, the depths of the carving were beautifully and fully packed with a reddish-azure material, while the black steps were filled with a white substance.

From this most spectacular colonnade as far as the following steps, the ground was leveled into a marble-paved street circling around, six feet in width. Where immediately another seven steps began to rise, with the aforementioned workmanship, measurement, material, and coloring; and all this was preserved entirely in the tiers that followed.

Above the uppermost step was a box-like excavation <note>original: *capsea excauatura*; a stone trough or planter</note>, four feet in width. The depth of which was sufficient, and it was the same in the following tiers. In this excavation there grew a boxwood hedge <term>septo buxeo</term> <note>a hedge made of boxwood (*Buxus sempervirens*), a staple of Renaissance topiary</note>, most pleasingly green with a glassy brilliance. And level with the bridges and streets, I saw a tower made of that same greenery, raised nine feet high and five wide, with an open doorway three feet wide and six high, and so it was for the following ones.

This first hedge was three feet thick and six high, and so were the following ones; it appeared with very dense foliage and was thus arranged by the clipping <note>original: *pinnatura*; the art of trimming or "feathering" topiary</note> of the trees themselves. Between one tower and another, I saw excellently fashioned a "triumph" with horses drawing a chariot <term>rheda</term> <note>a four-wheeled Roman carriage</note>, and preceding the one celebrating the ovation were several sword-bearing soldiers <term>macherophori</term> <note>from the Greek *makhaira* (sword) and *phoros* (bearing)</note> with triumphal spears, artfully shaped by varying the greenery most beautifully. In another space between towers <note>original: *interturrio*</note> there projected a naval scene of war <term>enyo</term> <note>original: *navale enyo*; Enyo was the Greek goddess of war</note>. Between two other towers, a standard land battle. Between two others, hunts and ancient fables of love. All were expressed with the most diligent detail and exquisite form. Such an order continued all around, varying the subsequent scenes.

Inside this primary enclosure, after a surrounding street—which was like the lower one between the small columns and the steps—there appeared a wonderful mosaic <term>tessellatura</term> of great admiration and excessively delightful artifice, which undoubtedly would exhaust all human intuition and sense. At first sight, I easily judged them to be Cairene carpets <note>original: *tapeti charaini*; prestigious carpets imported from Cairo, known for their intricate geometric patterns</note> arranged and spread across the flat surface. It featured all kinds of colors that were worthily expressed in such a display, conducted in the manner of a graceful painting in most varied and multiple knots, figures, and signs, with the appropriate diversity of colors of the little plants <note>original: *holuscule*; likely referring to the tiny colored stones or perhaps literal low-growing herbs used to create the mosaic effect</note> to provide the required distinction of the artificial work. Some were full of color, others with dark coloration; some moderate, others more clear and yellowish-green <note>original: *festichine*</note>; some leek-green <note>original: *prasine*</note>, others of a pale greenness, some less so, and of a reddish color, all in a most pleasant harmony. The main figures contained multiple designs within themselves: there was a circle between two rhombuses, and a rhombus between two circles, alternating continuously in a circuit, except for those parts where the paths were providently left to intersperse. Which streets always passed between two uniform figures.

These patterns were arranged in seven circular lines, imitating (as I have said) the shape of an island. First, they were surrounded by the ambient path next to the boxwood enclosure, connected in a mosaic-like fashion <note>original: *emusicataméte*; implying a harmony or precision akin to music or fine mosaic work</note> with the lines tending toward the center. These paths were paved; the middle part, consisting of seven divisions, took up three for itself, made of very black, hard, and reflective stone, such that a touchstone <term>coticula</term> <note>a small stone used to test the purity of precious metals</note> of such deep blackness would not even be found in the River Ochos <note>the Oxus river, famed in antiquity for its stones</note>. ## THE SECOND 

kitchen-garden enclosure <note>original: *clauſtro olitorio*; a garden space dedicated to herbs and vegetables, though here it is highly ornamental</note> follows immediately after the previously described work. At the edge of this enclosure, the other seven steps began in an orderly fashion toward the center. Above the last step was fixed a varied enclosure of arboreal coloring, most spectacular to behold, with towers or lookouts excellently fashioned from **Orange trees**. Flanking the gate in an orderly fashion were two planted trunks—that is, between the wall of the tower and the wings of the gate—which rose above the summit of the tower, joining together into one at a height of three feet above the tower’s top. Then, the leafy growth began to take the shape of a moderate **cypress**. And so it continued in a circuit throughout, each two paces in height. The fence between the towers varied in color and in its planting; between two towers it was woven of **juniper**. Between two others, of **mastic**. Then of **strawberry trees**, and of **privet**. Of **rosemary** <note>original: *Dendro Liuano*, from the Greek for "incense tree"</note>, and of **dog-rose** <note>original: *Cynocanthe*</note>. Of **olive**. Of **laurel**. It was fashioned in such a way that it always remained in its fresh, leafy vigor. After the last, the first would repeat successively, forming most beautiful works of <term>topiary</term> <note>the art of clipping shrubs into ornamental shapes</note>, free from any unsightly display of woody stems, clothed in everlasting foliage.

Between two towers, above the level ground, a marvelous feathered peak rose up in the middle. For at intervals along the wall-fence, plants of <term>boxwood</term> <note>original: *buxo*; a dense evergreen shrub favored for carving into shapes</note> grew out, shaped with exquisite skill into the symmetry of crescent moons. These filled the space between the towers with their width, or upward-turned opening, shaped with singular diligence. In the center between the two horns of the moon rose a juniper, shaped into a series of tiered, feathered layers, tapering toward the top as if they had been turned on a lathe, with the prickly little leaves made perfectly even. The thickest part was placed in the middle of the opening. Between the horns, a straight stem rose up, transcending them by a foot and a half, bearing a round ball of boxwood, most perfectly proportioned.

Within this enclosure, between the boundaries of the paths, were square vegetable plots <note>original: *holuſcularii*</note> of marvelous workmanship, varying in their herbaceous designs, which alternately filled the entirety of this spectacular circuit.

The first square, separated from the next by the paths (which resulted in irregular squares), was a knot-work <note>original: *inodatura*</note> of square lines formed by small bundles, finished with the greatest refinement, three palms wide. The first band was curved into a circle in the middle, and from the two corners the bands met the circular line, one over the other. In the middle square, a porphyry <note>A hard, purple-red volcanic stone highly prized in antiquity for imperial monuments.</note> altar resided. At its corners, near the small crown molding, four horned ram's heads projected, carved with fluid and refined skill. Upon this altar sat an antique amphora-style vase with four equidistant handles, made of the finest sardonyx <note>A variety of onyx with reddish-brown and white bands.</note> beautifully joined with its sister stone, agate, expressed with marvelous artistry. Out of this vase grew a perfectly trimmed boxwood tree, shaped into a globe or sphere one pace in diameter. At its summit were four equally spaced foot-tall stems, each supporting a well-proportioned ball; upon each of these sat a peacock with its tail lowered. Their heads pointed toward a small platform on a central stem that rose higher than the four balls. From this platform ascended another stem with four branches, each supporting a ball. In the center, the raised stem held yet another ball. From the top of this, an oval ring emerged, spreading two branches per side, each with a ball, and another at its very peak. This arrangement was consistently observed in every vase, uniform in location, boxwood, altar, vase, and design.

The bands, the circles, and the rounded intersections were densely packed. The **Eagle** was fashioned from creeping thyme <note>original: *serpilo*</note>; the area outside the circular borders was filled with mountain germander <note>original: *polio montano*, a silvery-green herb</note>. One circle was filled with blooming violets <note>original: *Ianthine*</note>, another with yellow-flowered herbs <note>original: *luteole*</note>. The third had white flowers in great abundance; these were never falling <note>The author uses "nunque cadivi" to imply they are evergreen or everlasting.</note> but were perpetually in bloom. And these small garden plants were kept at a uniform, evergreen height, forbidden from growing beyond the design intended by their "second nature" <note>This refers to topiary or the art of shaping nature through human skill.</note>. In each of the triangular spaces formed by the rounding and the corners of the inner bands, there was a circle of grassy green color, filled with spurge-laurel <note>original: *Myrfinites*</note>. In the center of these were planted four spherical balls of very densely packed and perfectly trimmed myrtle <note>original: *myrto*</note>, each on a two-foot stem, just like the others.

In the other square—with bands and a circle like the one just described—two birds were depicted within the circular border. In the centers of the circles between the triangles was a pillar—two of fragrant southernwood <note>original: *aurotano*</note>, and two of lavender <note>original: *lauendula*</note>—raised one and a half feet above its stem. In the remaining ones alternately stood a pillar of savin juniper <note>original: *sauina*</note> and one of common juniper <note>original: *iunipero*</note>, three feet high. All the herbs had the most beautiful foliage, the freshest vigor, and a most pleasant appearance. It was a marvelous work of exquisite beauty and delight, irrigated by very narrow little pipes orderly distributed, pouring out a very fine and droplet-like spray.

### SUBSEQUENTLY, keeping to the established rule, they ascended another seven steps, atop the highest of which a most remarkable railing surrounded everything, made of red and most brilliant jasper <note>original: *diaspide*</note>, with elegant carving harmoniously meeting in most pleasing patterns, two inches <note>original: *sextante*, literally a sixth of a foot</note> thick. This railed enclosure and the one following it had no opening at all but were continuous; here ended the straight paths tending toward the center of the island, being passable only at the triumphal path, and likewise for the next level.

In this voluptuous enclosure, I admired a grove of conspicuously shady density, composed of the most celebrated trees. Here were the two female terebinth trees <note>original: *terebinthi*, sources of resin</note>, persistent in their great age, of extraordinary and blackish brilliance and pleasant scent; bdellium <note>original: *bedellio*, a semi-transparent oleo-gum resin</note> with oak-like foliage; and the Median citron tree <note>original: *malo, ouero medica phēne*, known as the "Median Apple"</note> laden with fruit. Here was the white costus <note>original: *costo*</note>, which even the island of Patala <note>original: *Patale*, an ancient port in India</note> does not produce. ...the frankincense <note>original: *thurea*</note> and myrtle trees, of a kind that does not even grow in Sheba <note>original: *Sabea*, an ancient kingdom in the Arabian Peninsula famous for perfumes</note>, and countless other small trees and aromatic shrubs. The ground was perfectly level, covered everywhere with asarabacca <note>original: *assaro*</note>—more lush than any found in Pontus, Phrygia, or Illyria—which rivaled the scent of spikenard <note>original: *nardo*</note>.

This most delightful place was the station and gathering point for the rarest and most beautiful little birds ever seen or known by human eyes. Intent on the works of love, they flitted about with a most pleasing warbling amidst the modest density of the branches, which were filled with a vibrant, evergreen foliage that never falls. Within this blessed, happy, pleasant, and leafy grove, gushing waters flowed with a sleepy murmur through small channels and running rivulets from clear, liquid, and sacred springs. 

And there, beneath the cool and thick shade, and in the sweet reflection among the young leaves, countless illustrious nymphs were hiding with the other sex, enjoying a discreet pleasure apart from the others. They sang with ancient instruments, fleeing from sweet Cupid <note>original: *Cupidine*</note> and intent on the deep shadows and rural tasks. They were dressed elegantly in silken garments, fine and pleated, of a pale saffron dye; the larger crowd wore swan-white, marigold-yellow, and greenish-yellow <note>original: *galbani*</note>, while some wore a deep violet <note>original: *colossino*</note>, with small sandals and nymph-like footwear.

Now, all the inhabitants <note>original: *inquiline*</note> of these voluptuous places, hearing the triumphant arrival of the lord of arrows <note>original: *sagittate signore*, referring to Cupid</note>, immediately came forward without delay in a festive and venerable greeting, except for the very newest arrivals. Afterward, they returned to their own particular solace and continuous delight.

Lastly, beyond the aforementioned little grove, without any interval, there followed the final gradation of seven steps. Following the established rule, above the highest step was a most remarkable enclosure of a small colonnade, similar in craftsmanship and material to the first one encountered after the previously mentioned river. And here, a spacious, unobstructed, and leveled area was enclosed, featuring a wonderful invention of emblematic mosaic <note>original: *tessellato emblematico*</note> with intertwinings of small circles, triangles <note>original: *triquetri*</note>, squares, cone-like figures, almond-shapes <note>original: *almoide*</note>, semi-circles, rhomboids, and scalenes, all most beautifully formed in multiple converging designs, with a mirror-like shine and distinguished by various and exquisite colors.

Finally, the middle third of the mile, from the river to the center, was distributed in such a musical proportion. This half-third, therefore, consisted of 166 and a half steps <note>original: *passi .clxvi. & semisso*</note>, as was said before. Of these, 12 steps are given to the river; 10 to the meadow beyond the river. All the steps together occupied 8 steps and 2 feet in length, and just as much in total height. The small path was 6 feet <note>original: *pedi*</note>. The first garden was 33 steps. The second, 27. The third, 23. The woods, 25. The area surrounding the theater, 16. The theater itself, measured to the center, was 16 continuous steps. Enough has been said of the measurements of the island.

Sweetly, with a mild breeze—the West Wind <note>original: *zephyro*</note> breathing—the decorative and golden wings of the divine boy <note>Cupid</note> vibrated softly. With such provocation that a man voluntarily and willingly offers himself even to a harsh death. O contagious artifice! O seductive ministry! O battling siege-engines! <note>Poliphilo uses military metaphors—siege engines and "propugnante machine"—to describe how beauty assaults the human senses.</note> Which easily infect any healthy heart—no matter how safe, strong, quiet, free, and resistant—suddenly subverting and laying it waste, prostrating it without delay, disturbing it without hesitation, totally subjugating it and dragging it along without resistance. It utterly casts down all moderate, incredible, and stubborn self-restraint. These are those true and infallible satellites of laborious Love, with an increasing number of most cruel executioners; they lie in wait for immune, remote, and detached thoughts. Those who are excluded from such inclining subjection are unable to prevail in any way, even with a daring spirit, against the unavoidable and drawing sweetness, ensnared with such skillful and diligent study. By a subtle genius, such an exquisite work was invented—a most beautiful and shapely masterpiece—created by fertile Nature herself as a device found for destruction, and an extraordinary addition and accessory for torture. 

Alas! This should reasonably be fashioned and used for marble statues, and not for human and fragile hearts. For even that noble and divine sex <note>Referring to women.</note>, when stripped and laid bare, is most greatly tormented and infected by peril. Not that they are investigated with this voluptuous addition of pernicious snares, but this only happens: that they do not think it enough to perish naturally from love, without adding so many increased and devised ways to lead miserable and tender lovers more easily to the death of heartache <note>original: *cordolio*</note>, and continually excite sparks that are extremely fiery, to nourish the loving and burning little flames until they are consumed; divine objects to fill and confound the warm breast with boiling little sighs, and to ferment the heart with love. 

Now I would not know how to duly express in what way such a foundation of stable and sincere love, firmly placed in Polia, felt itself somewhat shaken by these inevitable and ready traps and impetuous violences. Alas, then I repeated silently to myself: O my beloved Polia, my little beauty <note>original: *prophilea Pollia bellatula mia*</note>, guard your hard-won prey! For the passage through so many piratical deceits, manifest assassins, and thieving ambushers is of great danger. These, against all sincere righteousness, are commended and laudably approved for their loving offense; and by those who are sadly offended, they are all the more desired, and reverently sought after, and more sweetly loved.

The small, slanting channels, like moderate rivulets flowing in their carved beds, ended above in a small knob—a moderate swelling discovered by a clever hand—with a smooth pedestal packed with many beautiful flowers, which were scattered there. Like a butting, greedy beggar, she displayed the most obscene insolence of a *Tribaba* <note>a term implying lewdness or friction</note>, with the rolling of her inconstant, bluish-gray eyes and with prurient gestures, like a bold girl from Cadiz <note>original: "procace gaditana"; girls from Gades (Cadiz) were famous in Roman times for their erotic dances</note>, gesturing crudely with excessive lasciviousness. By these divine things, I am firmly persuaded that every fertile and eloquent tongue would prove useless in trying to express even a small part of the most sweet sounds, the sweetest songs, and the solemn and joyful dances and festivities of the divine nymphs and distinguished maidens—of their singular and incomparable beauties, and of their excellent, illustrious, and most elegant adornment. The bases and the capitals of the columns were perfectly fashioned. The architrave <term>trabe: the horizontal beam resting on columns</term>, the frieze <term>zophoro: a decorative band, often featuring animals or figures</term>, the cornice, the pediment, the threshold, the fronts, and every other ornament of the previously mentioned material were visible. The hard and stubborn steel <term>chalybe: a term for high-quality steel or iron, named after the Chalybes people</term> would have been defeated by the task, and the anciently-varied relief work <term>toreumata: intricate work in relief, often in metal or stone</term> appeared insignificant by comparison. It was expressed with such grace, elegance, and remarkable beauty, forming a structure magnificent beyond measure. 

I believe it could not have been built by mortals <note>original: "terriculi"; literally "little earth-dwellers," used here to suggest humans are small compared to such grand architecture</note>, even with the highest expense, patience, and heavy, long-lasting labor. It was completed with no small amount of genius, care, industry, and diligence, standing as a masterful display. The entire arch was enclosed in serpentine stone <term>ophitea: a green-mottled stone resembling snakeskin</term>, and the side columns were both of porphyry <term>pphyrica: a hard, purple-toned volcanic rock prized in antiquity</term>. Beyond these, the others varied, one being serpentine and the next porphyry. The middle columns standing above the porphyry ones were both serpentine, and the square ones above those in the middle were of porphyry. By alternating one against the other in this contrary arrangement, the capitals, bases, and small pedestals <term>arule: literally "small altars," used here as decorative bases</term> followed the same pattern of variation.

Beyond this primary entablature <note>original: "illigamēto"</note> followed, ascending in order, a similar tier of columns, matching the first in every way and differing in no part. And although the art of building <term>ædificamētaria: the science and practice of architecture</term> requires that the columns placed above should be one-fourth shorter than those beneath—where the vertical line of the upper column should fall precisely over the center of the one below—and the third tier a fifth shorter; nevertheless, in this elegant and symmetrical building, this rule was not observed. Instead, the upper columns were of the same height <note>original: "p̄ceritate"</note> as the lower ones. The third tier of quadrangular columns in the third order followed this same rule. These upper-seated columns also featured the same encircling entablature as those below. Beyond this joint, fluted pilasters <term>pilastrelli sulcati: small, rectangular columns with vertical grooves</term> rose up. Between one and the other, recessed from the solid stone by a third of its depth, a window gaped in the equalized space. These were not quadrangular in the style of a temple, but were slanted or arched, as is required in secular buildings <note>original: "p̄fane ædificature"</note>.

Highest of all, encircling the structure above the square columns, the royal cornice, without any carvings but with every required ornament and lineament, and with its proper overhanging eaves <term>suggrundio: the projecting part of a roof or cornice; a soffit</term>, bound the whole together with every harmonic proportion. Beyond the said cornice, raised up, a bright and unobstructed parapet <note>original: "alamēto"</note> one and a half paces high circled the top.

All of this celebrated, illustrious, proud, and most highly praised building was constructed of the finest Indian alabaster <term>alabastryte: a fine-grained, translucent form of gypsum or calcite</term>. It was built with a glassy brilliance, artistically decorated, and excellently finished without any smearing of lime paste or cement <note>original: "calice pulte. ouero cēmēto"</note>, but rather with stable cohesion and perfect, tight-fitting joints. This shining material was not marred by staining smoke, nor did it show any greasiness from oil, nor was it yellowed by the infusion of vermilion-like dyes; but in every part it was pure and without any infection, preserved in its proud and brilliant clarity <note>original: "nitella"</note>.

The paved floor was an excellent example of inlaid stonework <term>secticio: a technique of mosaic using larger pieces of stone or marble, also known as opus sectile</term>, of wonderful invention and striking artistry.
