Remaining there, devoutly kneeling, my mind wavered, marveling beyond measure and excessively. I was unable to gaze fixedly upon the divine presence breathing everywhere. And pondering the reason no less thoughtfully—considering by what sweetness of fate and faith, by what manner and merit, it was granted to me to clearly discern such mysteries with my eyes so ill-suited to such an object—I judged it to be only the free will of the immortal Gods and the benign consent of Polia and her faithful prayer. But above all things, it seemed displeasing to me that among so many celestial and divine persons, I alone stood there, contemptible and foreign, with my devout garments worn and tattered, and in every other way dissimilar, most abject and poor. And then it would have been most welcome to find a way to cover my deformity, just as **Erichthonius** <note>A legendary king of Athens born from the earth with serpent-like legs, which he concealed from view</note> sought to hide his viper-like feet. Nevertheless, stunned by incredible wonder, I praised the divine benevolence within my soul, which had allowed an earth-born man to openly contemplate divine works and the treasure of generative nature.

For which reason, those noble nymphs who were joyfully celebrating under the pergolas with their applause, songs, and sweet harmony because of the conquered prey—which the winged and bold **Cupid** <note>The god of love, here called "pinnato & temerario Cupidine"</note> was to attain in triumph; he who was more sharp-sighted than **Lynceus** <note>An Argonaut famous for his keen sight</note> or hundred-eyed **Argus** <note>The giant from Greek myth whose eyes were moved to the peacock's tail</note>, and was vigorously ready with his weapons—after a short time had passed, the Mother Goddess, amidst the celestial sounds and songs, having allowed a brief interval of silence for us both, with divine eloquence and soothing charm, produced from her most holy mouth such sweet-spoken, witty words. They were words surely capable of lulling to sleep and putting to rest the vigilant guard of the fatal treasure of **Colchis** <note>The dragon guarding the Golden Fleece</note>, and of restoring to a benign form **Aglauros** <note>A princess of Athens turned to stone by Mercury</note>, daughter of **Cecrops**, and of restoring **Daphnis of Ida** <note>A mythological shepherd associated with pastoral song</note> to the pleasing herd in human form, and of calling back **Cadmus and Harmonia** <note>A husband and wife who were famously transformed into serpents at the end of their lives</note> from their hissing voices and scaly bodies. Thus she spoke to Polia:

Through the favor of your religious service <note>original: "religiosi ministerii"; refers to the sacred rites they have just performed</note>, you have been made worthy of our most sweet and fruitful graces. Because of your sincere supplications, your pure sacrifices <note>original: "illibate litatione"; a "litatio" is a sacrifice that yields favorable omens</note>, and the solemn ceremonies commended for my pacification, I wish to incline myself toward you with a devoted heart and through your observable apprenticeship <note>original: "tirocinio"; the initial stage of training for a soldier or initiate</note> as a beneficent, favoring, and munificently rewarding protector. And I grant that your inseparable companion Poliphilo, standing here glowing with your love, shall likewise be numbered among the true and happy lovers. May he be cleansed here of plebeian and vulgar dross, and—if perhaps his chastity has been stained by any foul impurity—may he be purified by being sprinkled with my dew, and may he be unceasingly most devoted to you. May he be ready and diligent for your placid desires, and may he never refuse any wish of yours. And both of you, equally loving one another, shall serve my amorous fires voluntarily and with the most complete consent, flourishing ever more. Which these divine nymphs and we devoutly revered; a marvelous tomb <note>original: "sepulchro"</note> full of mystery was set there, five feet in length, and in width ten-twelfths <note>original: "dextante"</note>, and raised just as high, excluding the base, with a little cornice that was five-twelfths <note>original: "quincuncio"</note> high. This tomb, the Nymphs said, belonged to the hunter Adonis, killed in that place by the tusked Boar. And in this place also, similarly, Holy Venus <note>original: "Sancta Venere"</note>, emerging naked from this fountain, wounded her divine calf <note>original: "Sura"</note> in those rosebushes while running to aid him, who was being beaten by jealous Mars with a grim and indignant face, and with anguish of soul.

This little story could be seen perfectly carved on one long side of the tomb. And her son Cupid was then shown gathering the deep-purple blood in an oyster shell. They added that the divine gore <note>original: "cruore"</note> was placed in that tomb with the ashes, situated with every holy rite. On the front of our entrance to the tomb, a circular hole was hollowed out through the center of the square; it was then sealed with a precious Hyacinth stone of a transparent vermillion color, with a great flashing of flame-like splendor. Because of the light positioned opposite, it burned unsteadily, so that I was hardly able to fix my eyes upon it because of the flickering.

On the other side along the length of the tomb, I similarly saw Adonis carved with some shepherd hunters among several small trees, with dogs and the dead Boar, and he himself killed by it. And Venus, sorrowfully weeping, was falling into the compassionate embraces of three half-fainting Nymphs; dressed in very fine cloth, they wept together with the goddess. And her son, with a bundle of roses, was wiping his mother's eyes, which were weeping with flowing tears.

# POLIPHILO BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK OF HIS HYPNEROTOMACHIA <note>The title is a Greek compound meaning "The Strife of Love in a Dream."</note>. IN WHICH POLIA AND HE, WANDERING FORLORN, NARRATE ALTERNATELY THE MANNER AND VARIOUS CIRCUMSTANCES OF THEIR FALLING IN LOVE.

## HERE THE DIVINE POLIA NARRATES HER NOBLE AND ANCIENT ORIGIN; AND HOW TREVISO WAS BUILT BY HER ANCESTORS; AND OF THAT LINEAGE DESCENDED FROM LELIA; AND IN WHAT MANNER HER BELOVED POLIPHILO, UNNOTICED AND UNKNOWN, DISORDERLY FELL IN LOVE WITH HER.

MY WEAK VOICE, O gracious and divine Nymphs, will reach your kindly hearing as discordant and inharmonious as the terrifying hoarseness of the diving Aesacus <note>In mythology, Aesacus was a son of Priam transformed into a diving bird; his voice is traditionally described as harsh.</note> compared to the sweet song of the mournful Philomela <note>The nightingale.</note>. Nevertheless, wishing with all the meager efforts of my intellect and my tiny sufficiency to satisfy your pleasant petitions, I shall not hold back my power. These requests of yours—setting aside any hesitation that might more fittingly come from elsewhere—rightly deserve a more fertile river of eloquence, with a much more rounded elegance and a more adorned polish of speech than can be found in me by any means to achieve their gracious intent. But to you, Heavenly Nymphs, and to me in some small measure, though I am confused and sobbing unbecomingly, I will have given enough gratification. For I shall present myself as willing and devoted to your desires and requests, appearing humble with a spirit of no small readiness, rather than pleasing you with a refined, clear, and lovely eloquence.

I shall therefore begin to weave the tale of my ancient and most venerable genealogy and lineage, and my fated love. Since I am already here in your venerable, sisterly presence, and seeing myself barren and fasting of eloquence before such an outstanding and divine assembly of you, O Nymphs—diligent handmaidens of burning Cupid—and in such a kind, delightful, and sacred place, breathed upon by pure breezes and flower-bearing winds: I am fitly compelled to assume a venerable daring and a tranquil fear of speaking. Therefore, before all else, grant pardon, O most beautiful and blessed Nymphs, to this babbling of mine and to my lowly, earth-born, and puny efforts, if it should happen that in any part I incautiously

One, therefore, descending from this ancient and honored **Lineage**, named **Lelio Syliro** by the holy Senate—it would be a long story to give the most powerful reason—was sent and designated as Consul in the region and **March of Treviso** <note>original: "Marchia Taurisana," referring to the territory surrounding the city of Treviso, anciently associated with the "Tauri" or "Taurini" peoples</note>, named after the high mountain. He gave his outstanding daughter in solemn, just, and untainted marriage. They were joined then, joyfully, she being a maiden endowed with prudence and distinguished by an extraordinary nature and matronly gravity, beyond her conspicuous beauty and the flowing abundance of her worldly goods. She was well-born and noble, of manifold virtue and illustrious and most decorous learning, practically nurtured in royal delights and fatherly discipline; she was named **Trivia Calardia Pia**. Her mother was named **Rhoa Pia**. She was amply endowed with an inheritance from her father, who gave her a great part of the tenth region, **Venetia**: a flat homeland enclosed by the lofty and conspicuous peaks of imminent, distinguished, and notable mountains, rich in springs, brooks, and the courses of rivers, wooded and abundant with harmless animals.

The most magnificent **Hymeneal rites** <note>wedding ceremonies</note> having been celebrated, and the **Herculean knot** <note>a complex knot on the bride's belt which only the husband was to untie</note> dissolved, and the holy **Cinxia** <note>a Roman epithet for Juno as the goddess who presided over the "girding" and ungirding of the bride</note> having been religiously invoked to fulfill the matrimonial laws, with the divine **Zygia Lucina** <note>titles for Juno and Diana as goddesses of marriage and childbirth</note> showing favor, they had a most noble offspring and a copious birth, taking up many children, male and female alternately. Of these, the first-born was **Lelio Maurio**, nicknamed for his dark color. The second, **Lelio Halcioneo**. The third, **L. Tipula**. The fourth, **L. Narbonio**. The fifth, **L. Musilistre**. In the daughters, nature, seconding the superior virtues, conferred upon them such beauty and grace that they would never be thought of as conceived by human conception. The first was named **Murgania**, and the second **Una Quintia**. The third **Septimia**. The fourth **Alimbrica**. The fifth **Astorgia**. The sixth **Melmia**. To speak briefly, the parents, unmindful of the fruitful blessing from the patroness of childbirth, and boasting of their elegant progeny, presumed them to be born of their own virtue. Alas, who can ever escape the fatal difficulty and the inconstant, fallacious, and mobile fortune unharmed? For to them it happened, through the demerit of such a divine gift—not otherwise than to **Atalanta** and **Hippomenes** <note>In myth, these lovers were turned into lions for desecrating a temple</note>—and beyond this, comparing themselves wickedly in beauty and worthiness to our mistress, the **Cyprian Mother** <note>Venus</note>, the mother of our arrow-bearing Lord <note>Cupid</note>. Oh, evil and nefarious deed, and rash daring! ...denying that **Murgania** was anything but **Venus** herself. Therefore, they built a **Shrine** <note>original: "Sacello"</note> in the suburban areas. From this, she took her name among the people even until today, known as **Fairy Morgana** <note>original: "Phada Murgania," a reference to the legendary figure Fata Morgana</note>. And the place still preserves the memorial name **Murganio**.

Because of this unjust and enormous matter, and cruel human impiety—daring, greedy, ambitious, proud, and wicked—the gods, who do not bear mortal offenses unpunished nor allow any insolence to increase, grew wrathful. They said that these earth-born creatures wished, through usurpation, to illicitly liken themselves to the high gods. The most holy mother of our dreaded lord <note>Polia likely refers to Venus, the mother of Cupid (Love), who is offended that a mortal has usurped her name</note>—whom we now most deservedly serve—showed herself as a fierce avenger (no differently than **Juno** toward **Antigone**, and the indignant **Eriboea** toward **Isis**). And likewise **Quintia** and **Septimia**, sisters fleeing not far from Murgania, were also transformed into ritual springs. And **Allymbrica** was turned to ash, not far from the others, by the terrifying lightning-bolts of the great native and thunder-bearing **Jove**; and all the palace and royal mansion, built in that place for pleasure, were all converted into coals, and the place was called **Carbuncularia** <note>The Place of Charcoal</note>. From there, it later trickled into a small stream. And **Astorchia**, a fugitive weeping over the miserable events, she too flowed into her father as a little river. And likewise **Melmia**. They gave their perpetual names to those places, their lapping waves embracing their sweet father, **Lelio Siliro**. And he, transmuted into liquid matter, increased by his dear daughters, became a celebrated river of the purest ritual waters, which is still seen flowing very freshly in that pleasant region. From his shortened name, it is called the **Sili** <note>The Sile River, which flows through the city of Treviso</note>. And his wife, struck by lightning and weeping for the miserable and horrendous events, was transformed into a notable fountain, called by her surname the **Calardia Fountain**, near her beloved father **Tito Butanichio**, who had been made into a liquid river, weeping for the hard and cruel fate of his lineage mixed within him. And her mother **Rhoa**, flowing between her husband and her most beloved brother **Caliano**, derives into her sweetest son, the Sili.

No male was left unpunished by the celestial wrath and just vengeance. These, not submerging themselves in their father's bosom, always remain with him as creatures of the river.

A iii

Therefore, from this tearful and pitiable disaster, the only survivor to escape was the firstborn, **Lelio Mauro**. During his childhood, he had been invited by his relatives, the lords of the **Altinati** <note>the people of the ancient Roman city of Altinum</note>, to a solemn funeral anniversary outside the **Mania Gate**, at the place named **To the Spirits of the Dead** <note>original Latin: "ad Manes"</note>. In that place, the bodies of the entire city were buried, and even with the word now corrupted, the site is still called "The Mani." Once the pompous obsequies were performed with ancient rites and in the patrician manner, he remained behind to walk with some other youths. It happened that as they were in those maritime places near the watchtower or lighthouse of the port of **Altino**—which was named **Turricella** <note>literally "Small Tower"</note> and from which the noble town of **Turricello** founded there currently takes its name—they were captured in their youth by invading pirates. From there, he was led by force among the ancient **Bruttian** people <note>an ancient tribe in Southern Italy, modern-day Calabria</note> to a famous city that is now called **Teramo**. Because of his noble character, he was adopted by a magnificent and noble man named **Theodorus**, and he grew up living like a patrician. After receiving a sufficient education in literature, he devoted himself strenuously and assiduously to military exercises.

When he reached manhood, and as time progressed, he achieved various victories through his excellent deeds and his brave, lofty, generous, and robust spirit, performing all his military duties with great constancy. Just as **Bellerophon** <note>a hero of Greek mythology</note> was exalted by **Heurie** <note>likely a reference to a mythological purifier or a specific regional legend</note>, for similar reasons he was no longer called **Lelio Mauro**, but due to his excellent condition and outstanding deeds, he was named **Calo Maurio** <note>the name combines the Greek "Kalos" (beautiful/noble) with his family name to distance him from his family's cursed past</note>, so as to extinguish that ill-omened name with his exceptional virtues.

Because of all these things, he was appointed by the most holy Roman Senate to a military prefecture and invested with the **general's cloak** <note>original: "paludamento," the ceremonial cloak worn by Roman commanders</note>. He happened to be sent to reside and serve in the very place where he was born and originated, keeping his homeland safe and protected from barbarian invasions. Finding a site with most pleasing shade and breezes, made beautiful by rivers and springs, he named it **Calo Mario** after himself. He did this so that, by the benefit of the site's beauty, he might occasionally find delight and respite from the heavy and constant harassment of the enemy; the area was truly green and clothed in herbs and flowers.

Once he was established there as the **City-Guardian** <note>original: "Poliucho," from the Greek "polioukhos," a deity or hero who protects a city</note>, he built a noble and great city for the local people as an eternal monument to the cherished memory of his dear mother. It was located near the **Bull's Neck** <note>original: "collo Tauri"</note>, a place most rich and pleasant for both literary study and military exercise, hosting ancient worship and the truest sanctity and religion. It sat above the rushing and swift **Father Sile** <note>the river Sile</note>, and he gave it the name of his pious mother, **Trevisia**. From this, it retains its maternal name even to this day <note>referring to the city of Treviso</note>.

He ruled there happily for a long time, and the city possessed a favorable increase, with abundance, the peace of the **civilian toga** <note>original: "togate pace," referring to peace time when the military cloak is set aside</note>, and social alliances with its neighbors. And his successors inherited it from him...

For which reason I was deserted and left by everyone, except by my merciful and excellent **Nurse** <note>original: "Altrice" – a term for a wet-nurse or foster mother, implying a deep, maternal bond</note>, who remained to help and to witness the last breath and departure of my spirit. And having been many times entangled by the **heavy disease**, I returned to myself only fitfully, uttering rambling words, frequent laments, and little whimpers, wandering and wavering in my mind. And there, as best as I could and knew how, I sincerely invoked help from the **Divine Diana**. For at that time I had no knowledge or worship of other deities except for this Goddess. And with multiplied prayers, with a trembling voice, purely entreating, I sought her protection. To her holy and cold rites of **chastity** <note>original: "castimonie"</note>, while the grave illness tormented me, I vowed myself as a suppliant, promising to serve religiously and forever in her sacred temples with steadfast purity, if she, taking pity on me, would free me from the deadly contagion and disease. This I did with a firm and persevering purpose in my mind. And I did so with all the better hope because I remembered the benign favor that the said Goddess showed to **Iphigenia** <note>In Greek mythology, King Agamemnon was forced to sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia, but Diana/Artemis saved her at the last moment, replacing her with a deer.</note>. While **Agamemnon**, by the warning of Apollo, wished to immolate her in sacrifice, and her pious parents were harshly weeping together, the Goddess—moved by this and taking pity—interposed a smoke-filled cloud, and saving Iphigenia, a **doe** was found in her place. Therefore, by such a similarity, I felt almost secure, hoping for her holy help and protection. And thus there was no delay of time before I was cured, and miraculously regaining strength, my former health was restored.

Consequently, bound by these high and spontaneous promises and solemn obligations, I intently applied myself to their execution, and was diligent in fulfilling my professed vows. I had no less a purpose to keep myself unsullied than the **Matrons during the Thesmophoria** <note>An ancient Greek festival in honor of Demeter; participants practiced ritual celibacy</note>, sleeping upon beds made of the leaves of the **Chaste Tree** <term>Agno arbore (Vitex agnus-castus), a willow-like shrub believed in antiquity to suppress sexual desire</term>. Nor did I have less devotion and religion than **Cleobis and Biton** <note>Brothers famous for their filial piety who died peacefully after performing a great labor for their mother, a priestess</note>. And having been introduced into the holy temple, and received into the comforting convent and solitude of many other virgin girls who served that modest Goddess in purity, I began diligently to visit the **Dianic Altars** with them and to venerate them humbly. 

Wherefore, consuming the most beautiful part of my flowering girlhood and pleasant age in those chaste chills, it happened that our **Poliphilo**, fervently and wildly in love, remained wretched, discontented, and in heartache during this whole intervening time, which was a year and more. From my heart every thought of this Poliphilo had been erased and wiped clean. It was as if I had drunk the waters of **Lethe**, son of **Phlegethon** <note>In classical mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness. At this solemnity, it is customary for the bold and youthful crowd to greedily gather for the sacred spectacles. And having clearly caught sight of me, he was totally lost. From that moment on, he affectionately hoped that he had found (persuading his own inflamed heart) an immediate and opportune remedy; yet he was ignorant of what he should do, except to gaze and gaze again with the most intent stares at my most pleasing head, adorned with golden tresses. Upon which adornment he had supremely and solidly placed and built every one of his pleasant and delicious pleasures, his happy contentment, and his determined and fixed thoughts. 

But because from then on I had bound myself with a devoted heart to my betrothed vows, I never, or only very rarely, allowed myself to be seen by any man. Instead, hidden and with my veiled face covered, with the most secret departures and entries to the holy temple, and remaining almost unknown for a long stretch of time, I strove to keep myself inconspicuous. 

Poor lover Poliphilo, who no longer valued gracious life more than terrifying death, counting a day as a year because of the long delay in being able to see me again, was all anxious and perplexed. Yet with a constant and persistent spirit, and a little astuteness, and with provident and sleepless investigation and diligence—(like a man bound and thrust into a horrific **prison** <note>original: "ergastulo" – a Roman term for a private dungeon</note> who is only intent on breaking out to flee, or like a sick man desiring health who intends on escape)—he knew how to search and explore every corner so thoroughly. 

And perhaps directed by flying **Love** <note>original: "Amore" – referring to Cupid</note> to such a sleepless watch, he found me in the temple one day, where I remained alone to pray. He, blinded by excessive love and deprived of reason by fiery desire—(like an animal without reason that does not consider the end of its fleeting appetite)—approached, half-dead. 

Whereupon, no sooner did I see him before me than my ill-disposed heart was quickly contaminated; like cold **Adamant** <note>original: "Adamante" – a legendary stone of extreme hardness, often identified with diamond, believed to be resistant to fire</note> which does not change in fire, it froze and stiffened, becoming colder than **Porphyry** stone <note>original: "petra Porphirica" – a hard, purple-red rock used by the Romans for imperial monuments, symbolizing cold permanence here</note>. And with a harsh and fierce spirit, all pity having been rejected and stunned, I turned my soul toward him in great hatred. Perhaps even darker...

And so I would more gladly expose myself to a quick death than to live such a harmful life miserably without your most desired affection; for a swift end is better than dying slowly. And if by chance some Deity presses me with inexorable cruelty, let it at least be permitted for me to die by your hand, if I am not permitted to live sweetly. Because when your angelic and venerated presence is removed from my eyes, that true, unique, and consoling delight—which I, greedy and never satiated, took from it—is stolen and gone.

And therefore, I no longer hoped to be able to obtain an opportune remedy for these bitter and insupportable languors, except for when the kind heavens might grant that I see you again. Otherwise, I saw the harsh ruins of my tedious life threatening to invade. And therefore, like a condemned man awaiting the inevitable capital blow, almost without grieving, I gave and delivered my miserable life into the hands of the terrifying sisters <note>The Fates, who spin and cut the thread of life</note>. <meta>This page continues Poliphilo’s direct address to Polia. He is describing the agony of his unrequited love and his physical and emotional state during her long absence, using classical metaphors and natural paradoxes to express his devotion.</meta>

And the urgent fires bubbling in the depths of my heart exacerbated me so much, having no other good to hope for or desire except for you alone, Polia, my chief and most powerful medicine. And I was unaware of you, deprived of you, abandoned by you. And the more I thought upon the ungrateful absence of your outstanding form and celestial beauty, your most decorous face, and the elegant sum of your exquisite virtues, the more my pain and bitterness grew, since I could not enjoy them. For these reasons, O wretched lover that I am, with such impetus—ill-advised and headlong—I accepted these horrific injuries, these false blandishments, and the subtle allurements of love, veiling and hiding the bitterness and most restless agitation that I was bound to suffer from them many times, or rather, most of the time, in an invasive way. 

And therefore, having purely and with such tolerance voluntarily accepted these most bitter snares for your sake, my sweetest Lady Polia, they have since unjustly left me—alas, wretched me!—for so long a time without seeing you again, my total good, all my hope, all my consolation; you, the solacing prison <term>original: "ergastulo"; a Roman term for a private prison or workhouse, here used as a metaphor for being held captive by love</term> of my heart. I have been without the spectacle of the exquisite and venerable adornment of this, your most beautiful head, and without the sight of this so gracious appearance and remarkable, wondrous image. 

Just as the Arbonian lake <note>A legendary lake in Africa mentioned by ancient geographers, said to boil when the sun sets and freeze when the sun is at its height</note> in Africa, when the Sun is absent, its waters boil fervently, and in its presence at midday, they grow cold and freeze; so I, in your absence, Polia, my most radiant Sun, was all scorched and burning, melting away like liquefying wax. And now, in your sunny presence, I freeze with horror <note>Poliphilo refers to "horror" in the classical sense of shivering or trembling with awe</note>. 

Think a little upon this, Polia, my delight and my pillar, that for such a long stretch of time I have found myself in supreme anguish and formidable dangers to my life. Which life, for your love and perpetual service, I willingly preserved at greater risk than the blonde and mature crops in the spacious fields remain at risk from the crackling lightning, the flashing thunder, the rushing rains, and the blowing winds. 

And just like the serpent-like and unruly ivy embracing the old poplar tree, if it is uprooted and torn away from there, it cannot thereafter climb by itself, but falls to the damp earth, lying soft and weak and lingering. And just like a precarious vine without its support and propping pole, or prostrate without its beloved **ELM** <note>original: "ULMO"; in antiquity, vines were often grown up elm trees, a poetic symbol of a perfect marriage or partnership</note>, it sinks down. So it is with me, no differently, without you, my firmest column and pillar, my support and most constant pier, upon which I had lovingly and inflexibly leaned my life with an obstinate purpose. Your absence, therefore, is the cause that finds me fallen and thus abandoned to death. For this reason, my passion had expanded so much that it did not permit me to feel even a tiny bit of the heavy pain; rather, I was more sharply agitated and stung by anxious love...

Truly, **POLIA** having reached this point in her story, could not moderate or contain herself without sighing somewhat piteously. And several times as she spoke, tears were drawn to her amorous eyes and her rosy cheeks became somewhat wet, moving and likewise provoking the surrounding **Nymphs** to compassion for the sorrowful lover **Poliphilo**, who had perished so sadly through vehement love and excessive pain. They drew amorous sighs from the depths of their tender hearts because of this. And turning their placid and moist eyes benignly toward me, they condemned **Polia** as if she were a criminal. But they were all the more eager to hear the end of such an unjust matter. And after a very short pause <note>original: "morula"; a brief delay or pause.</note>, they urged her to continue her gracious speech. At this, **Polia** modestly took the fine handkerchief <note>original: "sudariolo"; a small cloth used for wiping the face, often associated with mourning or perspiration in classical texts.</note> that hung from her white shoulders, wiped her tear-stained eyes, and dried her deep-purple cheeks. Having checked her warm sighs and steadied her sweet voice, she continued with matronly gestures in this manner:

"Most blessed **Nymphs**, hear of a great cruelty <note>original: "seuitia"; Latin for fierce cruelty or savagery.</note>, such that I know not what gentle and pious soul would not now be justly angered against me. Where was the divine vengeance <note>original: "ultione"; meaning retribution or punishment.</note> hidden then? That through my wicked obstinacy and hard stubbornness, my beloved **Poliphilo** should die so unworthily. O celestial vengeance, why were you so slow to act? Why did you not rightfully extinguish me for my iniquitous and perfidious soul at that very moment? But indeed, it was not long before I clearly saw the kindled wrath of the offended Goddess <note>Refers to Venus, the goddess of love.</note> and her arrow-shooting son <note>Refers to Cupid.</note>, had I not expiated my crude iniquity, and had my freezing and stiff heart not begun to glow and devoutly appease that Most Holy Deity—and if my mind had not been opportunely freed from my persistent resolve, from those false, sweet, and vain thoughts, and from fallacious and subtle opinions..."

Therefore, taking only a secret flight, while my heart remained somewhat hard and then intractable, my mind insuperable, and my will harsh and savage—more cruel than **Phineus** <note>original: "Phinao"; a king of Thrace famous in mythology for his cruelty toward his own children.</note> or **Harpalyce** <note>A legendary Thracian princess known for her feral upbringing and ferocity.</note>—having my breast frozen most coldly, more than the hard crystal of the northern Alps, and more rigid than Jet <note>original: "Gagite"; a black gemstone believed in antiquity to have protective properties, sometimes said to be found in eagle nests.</note>, which protects the eagle’s egg. But I was inexorable toward his torments, despite his sweetest supplications, heartfelt entreaties, and amorous prayers. And remaining untainted by any of his anguish, spurning and refusing all humanity and resisting any consent, there was no way nor path that he, in that unspeakable moment, could even slightly tame or move that rigid and tiger-like breast—far more than was fitting for one so unyielding and cursed. Love could in no way adhere to it, nor even approach it. His power, which so differently governs and applies itself to human hearts, was spurned and stupefied. Just as wax, however sticky <note>original: "viscabile"; meaning adhesive or viscous.</note>, cannot be fixed to bare rock when pushed and compressed. 

O too fearful and bitter case! By which I was not terrified, and even less was I moved. In it, he could not break the reins of my imprisoned pity. They were incessantly goaded by a **flame-breathing** <note>original: "isfiammabondo"</note>, immeasurably furious, and implacable youth <note>This is Cupid, transformed from a sweet boy into a terrifying executioner.</note>. With beast-like rage and fury, and with a whip made of sinew and fire, he fiercely struck them, pitilessly goading the shackled girls. He acted with even greater vengeance than **Zethus and Amphion** took against their stepmother **Dirce** <note>In Greek myth, these brothers punished Dirce for her cruelty by tying her to the horns of a wild bull to be dragged to death.</note>.

These women, wandering and distraught, intent on fleeing through trackless and pathless places, were forced to pass through dense thorns. Because of the mangled and mortal breaking of their limbs and the heat of the **burning chariot** <note>original: "infocato carro"</note>, they often went off the path, trampling through the small shrubs. Torn from head to foot, blood rained from their shattered limbs and their lacerated flesh. And I saw the vermilion and smoking blood spreading copiously over the prickly briars and upon the earth. In total disorder, through the thick and pointed brambles, driven by a furious rage, now here, now there, they wretchedly dragged the burning and heavy chariot, which further cruelly scorched their soft and delicate flesh. This flesh was not only cooked by the heat but cracked like parched leather. And if they were not crying out "Alas!" and "Woe!" in miserable affliction, they were uttering loud shouts, weeping, and miserable wailing, driven into a fury greater than that of **Orestes** <note>original: "Oreste"; a Greek mythological figure driven to madness and pursued by the Furies as punishment for the murder of his mother.</note>.

Thus the rough and heavily wooded place resounded entirely with their piteous cries; and now, as their jaws began to tighten and their tired and spent voices grew hoarse, the sorrowful, lifeless women could no longer endure. After a short hour, many most cruel beasts beset them. And the **executioner** <note>original: "carnifice"</note> and pitiless boy, after the long and bloody slaughter and cruelty inflicted upon the unfortunate and wretched **young women** <note>original: "adulescentule"</note>—he who was bloodthirsty and practiced in such butcheries—suddenly descended from the burning vehicle. With a **Rhomphaia** <note>original: "Romphea"; an ancient Thracian sword with a long, sharp blade, often used as a symbol of divine or cruel execution.</note> made entirely of iron and sharply whetted, he approached them once they were released from the troublesome yoke and the heavy pulling. He, stripped of any mercy or compassion, with rigid and uncorrupted severity, suddenly pierced them through the middle of their beating hearts.

As for me (imagine, piteous **Nymphs** <note>Polia addresses her audience of nymphs as she recounts her dream.</note>), terrified by the sight of such evil and bloody inhumanity, I found myself devoid of any counsel, and greatly terrified, and frightened beyond belief. I stayed hidden and concealed within a biting thicket entangled with thorny briars and wild roses, and with stinging weeds and the harsh buckthorn with its strong thorns. 

And under this broken density and woodland shadow, staying thus covered, I hesitated, terrified without measure by such a vision. It put me in greater fear than the horrible ghost of **Clytemnestra** appearing to the matricide **Orestes** <note>In Greek myth, Orestes was haunted by the ghost of his mother, Clytemnestra, after he killed her to avenge his father.</note>, armed with serpents and burning fire. Without hope of help, I feared they might perform a similar tearing upon me. 

And trembling, I said to myself: "Woe is me, would I ever be like **Iphigenia** <note>The daughter of Agamemnon, often depicted as a tragic sacrificial victim in Greek mythology.</note>, brought here by the winds as a stranger among the most cruel Taurians to be made a victim?"

Woe is me! What Caucasus, what Hyrcania, what interior Libya or **Agisymba** <note>original: "Agisinua"; an ancient geographical term for a land in central Africa, considered the limit of the known world.</note> could nourish such immense, such bloody beasts? What could equal such incredible cruelty? Woe is me, this exceeded beyond measure the atrocity and rage of all wild beasts, for those most savage animals were tearing apart the fallen prey, limb by limb, stripping the flesh from the bone.

## POLIA RELATES HOW THE WISE NURSE, THROUGH VARIOUS EXAMPLES AND PARADIGMS, WARNED HER TO AVOID ANGER AND ESCAPE THE WRATH OF THE GODS, AND HOW A WOMAN KILLED HERSELF IN DESPAIR DUE TO UNRESTRAINED LOVE. NOT WITHOUT SUPREME EFFORT and great labor, divine and piteous Nymphs, can a mind already disposed and inclined toward one purpose be drawn back—especially when it has been made difficult by obstinacy and hardened by time, and even more so while it still finds some delightful pastime and reward in that state. To wish, on the contrary, to adapt and turn back a mind that is entirely alienated by a false persistence proves to be extremely difficult. And this is not at all surprising if the senses are sometimes depraved, distorted, and corrupt; then, things of a sweet nature usually appear ungrateful, unpleasant, contemptible, and bitter. It presents itself as even less marvelous, most excellent Nymphs, if whiteness appears black and offensive to eyes that are sick, impure, and bleary <note>original: "lippi" — referring to eyes inflamed or running with humor, a common metaphor for spiritual or intellectual blindness</note>. If glowing things seem covered in a livid coating, and those shining with whiteness and reflecting splendor appear stained, sprinkled with rust, covered in darkness, drenched in the ink of the cuttlefish <note>original: "uomicione ſepiale" — the dark, defensive discharge of a squid or cuttlefish</note>, and darkened with black ink—this is undoubtedly not due to a defect in the object itself, but because of a sensory illness. Just so, and not otherwise, was it with me. She began to claw and scratch her face and beat her breast with her cruel palms, all hope severed, dissolving into a flood of tears. Her ready eyes turned into tears more bitter than those of Egeria <note>In Roman myth, Egeria was a nymph who wept so much at the death of her husband Numa Pompilius that she was turned into a fountain</note>. Nothing was pleasing, nothing desirable; everything was tasteless to her except wicked death, and she longed for the swift end that Iphis <note>A youth in Greek mythology who hanged himself after being rejected by the cold-hearted Anaxarete</note> met. From this was born a rabid fury; becoming her own lover <note>original: *morosa*</note> and cruelest executioner, she secretly took—on a dark day, while her husband was unaware—a sharp, knife-edged blade. Like a wicked accomplice, unable to satisfy her desires, and with all confidence shattered, she became her own mortal enemy. Committed to her furious plan, she exacted a horrendous and terrifying vengeance. And crowned with mournful Smilax <note>A plant associated with unrequited love and grief</note> and the leaves of the Ostrya <note>The hop-hornbeam, a tree often associated with sadness or misfortune</note>, she called upon the infernal and mourning-bringing Furies. Then (O unheard-of crime!), she impiously drove the harmful blade right through the center of her sorrowful heart.

Because afterward, arriving at uncomfortable old age, we still skillfully want to lie about our past youth. And we are consumed above all by gnawing, continuous, and unending pain in our hearts, sighing and weeping for the past delicious, amorous, and comforting time. And for the contempt shown toward that repudiated age, and for the rare, much-desired look now forbidden to us by the fleeing youths; because age requires a parity of likeness <note>The Nurse argues that the young seek the young, and the old are left alone</note>. And commemorating the lost loves and the lovable sweetnesses, we greedily desire to live more than we did in the time of our flowering youth—the end of which was then unrecognized. But as deprivation approaches, the appetite for living urges us, as if it were possible to have the years of Nestor, and of Priam, and the years of the Sibyl <note>All figures famous for their extreme longevity in classical myth</note>.

She having left the room, I remained alone. And there I scrupulously re-examined, ruminating upon the useful words, the heated and weighed-out warnings, and the clear and terrifying examples. She had perfectly touched upon that part of the argument which directly condemned me as stubborn and a cruel rebel, deserving of sharp punishment by celestial wraths. Terrified by these things, and wishing with all my power to avoid and flee from them, and to escape free from this anxiety, there came to my mind (I know not by what celestial care I was led) my lover Poliphilo. I knew that because of my impious cruelty, he had miserably despoiled himself of his gracious life in the sacred Temple <note>This refers to an earlier scene where Poliphilo appeared to die of grief in a temple after Polia rejected him</note>. Love, that master craftsman, finding in this first movement a small point of entry, together with some burning sighs, little by little began to penetrate the forbidden place. And with his first sweet little torches, nesting themselves quietly in my hard and torpid heart, he took his place. And already feeling a pleasant little flame course through and spread into the parts of my heart, reaching even to the innermost base of my inexperienced soul, and beginning to nourish itself upon my consent, there grew an incentive and a sweet desire to enter, vigorous and intrepid, under the amorous laws of the solacing Cupid. And I no longer wished to offer any obstacle or resistance to the amorous arrows.

And being now in prompt deliberation, I thought with uncertainty on the various occurrences and dispositions of shifting fate, and the manifold ends brought about solely by this sweet Love. Through this, my industrious and tenacious memory caused the fearful vengeances of Juno <note>The queen of the gods, often depicted as a punisher of those who offended her or her marriage laws</note> to bubble up in my mind, representing things that terrified me greatly. It grew with a gradual increase, and with a sweet little throbbing and a divine impulse, spreading itself diffusely through my whole being and successively altering me, fruitfully scattering a deadly anguish of new love, often sobbed out, and without delay or intervening pause, with a widening spread. 

It was just as when the Lernean poison from the blood of the Centaur Nessus <note>original: "Niso"</note> dissolved through the most robust body of Hercules while he was sacrificing. My wavering and unruly mind, withdrawing from those seething and empty thoughts and frivolous opinions and vain frustrations, was artfully led astray. And being totally wrenched from them, with my whole soul already suborned by amorous suggestions, I returned to the perished Poliphilo, desiring him willingly in his original essence. 

I was beyond measure sorrowful for his death. And after many various, oblique, ambiguous, and troublesome thoughts, and two-fold terrors, I showed myself bold and yielding enough to go and see him again; and to wish to show respect to him when dead, whom I would not look upon when living because of my hostile malice. REVEREND AND HOLY PRIESTESS, it is a virtue to know how to preserve oneself amidst arduous and deadly labors, turbulent inconveniences, and ungrateful loss; and with persuasive hope, to place a bridle and moderation upon the intemperate soul with probity and skillful manner, and not to fall headlong or fail impatiently and without counsel, but rather, by suffering with perseverance, to stand ready for the undertaking. However narrow and difficult it may be, one must yield with concealment <note>original: "dissimulamento"</note> to volatile and obstinate fate, its mockery, and its insidious cunning. For victory is won not with brute strength, but with virtue and wit. Just as the persevering Bellerophon <note>A Greek hero who, through great trials, tamed Pegasus and defeated the Chimera</note> succeeded in glory. For the strenuous soldier places glory before all wages and rewards.

Wishing, therefore, to legitimately attain the honorarium <note>original: "honorio," the reward or honor</note>, which is the debt and expected prize of my amorous struggle <note>original: "Agone," from the Greek for a contest or athletic struggle</note>, I firmly and bravely disposed myself to remain a target, so that violent Cupid <note>original: "Cupidine"</note> might find in me a disdain for shameful inconstancy. I judged it madness and levity for a timid and cowardly man to approach the fight, for nothing presents itself as more powerful than strength of soul. Considerable shame and modesty persuade me that it is becoming for a soldier to face forward; for to turn one's back <note>original: "tergauertire"</note> and show one's shoulders in a contest once begun is disgraceful. But above all, it never belongs to a soldier to despair, nor to fail in a fight once initiated; for it is better not to begin at all than, having begun, to abandon the undertaking. 

In this regard, if I do not err, it seems to me that one cannot truly be called happy if they have not somewhat sustained their opposite. From this, insolence is born and over-confidence is generated, from which an unhappy end proceeds—as it did for Polycrates <note>A tyrant of Samos whose legendary good luck eventually led to his downfall and execution</note>. Therefore, the perfection of a test is felt all the better through its contrary, just as on the touchstone <note>original: "indice," literally an indicator; here referring to the legend of Battus from Ovid, who was turned into a touchstone</note> of Battus it is clearly understood.

Being thus variously rapt, maddened, and absorbed in these feigned and so delicious thoughts, and in the enjoyment of such an image from hour to hour and moment to moment, the accidental and blind wounds grew fertile within my consenting soul. And Cupid, having seized the jurisdiction, tyranny, and licensed power over me entirely, directed me toward this affectionate mystery. This alone I desired above all else: Oh, if only I could open and discover my soul to her and indicate my intrinsic desires. With the Socratic affection <note>A reference to the philosopher Momus's wish that humans had windows in their chests so their hearts could be seen</note>, to put a window in my breast and show her the strike of the amorous wound, and the immoderate love that I bear for her, and tell her of my pressing snare and the urgent flame by which my melted heart is consumed, and show her the dissipation of my life of love. And to tell her with piteous and mild words, and moaning laments, of the extreme pain I sustain in loving her. And so, with a wandering, unruly, lost, and roaming mind, I languished supremely from intemperate heat; at times sighing, and at times happy; now placid, quiet, and tranquil; at other times indignant, hesitating without hope, and discontented. That sacred and celebrated little day was consumed with these mixed and inverted accidents, esteemed as shorter than a single atom of time, or a fleeting moment.

And already the ruby-red Sun, sinking into the greenery at the furthest reaches of Hesperia <note>original: "Hesperia"; the West, often referring to Italy or the setting sun's destination</note>, signaled a coming day of clear skies. From the sacred oracle, the delicate, noble, and assorted women took their departure and leave. And they brought an end to the solemn offices and ceremonial observances. These were not like those the Egyptians perform for Isis and Osiris with wailing; nor like the barbarians with the noise of cymbal-players, drummers, and flute-players for the dancers. Rather, they were like the Greeks with choral dances and melodic songs, or the Latin rites of consecrated young virgins, performed with devotion and the greatest joy.

Then, as her extraordinary and more-than-human image was separated and withdrawn from my hungering eyes and wavering senses, I found myself scorched and burned by a fierce love, crackling like salt thrown on a fire. With eyes dazed by her illustrious beauty, her brightness, and the noble refinement of her elegant form, I saluted her again with a few clever words, saying to myself: "Farewell, farewell, little thief and plunderer of all my well-being." And secretly repeating "farewell" many times with the tiny bit of heart she permitted to remain in me at her departure, feeling my soul being snatched and carried away with her, I too took my leave, most painfully and with sobbing.

She made her milky and shining white breast a high trophy of my spoils and a delicious storehouse. Not otherwise—alas for me!—did the grieving Laodamia <note>In Greek mythology, she was so devastated when her husband Protesilaus left for the Trojan War that she died of grief</note> look upon the departure of her beloved Protesilaus with eyes that followed him longingly. And, more wretched still, when she could no longer see him, she fell upon the shore near death, weeping from mortal grief and repeatedly calling for her Protesilaus.

Thus I, grieving with the sweetest little tears flowing abundantly like drops of rain, called, invoked, and shouted for Polia. O wretched Ariadne, did you find yourself so desolate of all hope, not seeing your treacherous deceiver Theseus? Scattering his name, calling out uselessly and in vain through the vast caves and hollowed rocks of the deserted Dia <note>An ancient name for the island of Naxos, where Theseus abandoned Ariadne</note>, calling him to no avail. Nothing appeared before your tear-blurred eyes except the reddened cliffs, the rigid mountains of <term>Murex</term> <note>original: "Murice"; likely referring to purple-tinted rocks or jagged limestone</note>, the wild shrubs of <term>Prini</term> <note>original: "Prini"; holm-oaks or prickly shrubs</note>, the harshest shores, and the curves of the banks, with foam-covered waves and rushing, roaring floods. 

How am I now, wretch that I am, abandoned by my found delight, by my only good and most effective remedy, in such lamentable anguish and bitter torment? With the rekindling of a more ferocious love? And thus burdened with every sorrow? From this, I feel myself fainting. For I felt the alleviation of my distress only while gazing upon her. I am not convinced, therefore, that you, O unfortunate Io, daughter of the famous Inachus, saw yourself as afflicted as I when your form was changed, and your once-golden tresses became harmful and rigid horns. And your human voice thundered out in lowing, and the green meadows became an unusual food...

I remained no less full of lament, disconsolate and dismayed, because my pleasures had been transformed into the heaviest penalties; from my eyes, raining with tears, that illustrious light had been withdrawn and taken away. I was left without that illuminating and celestial torch, which most effectively guided my dark thoughts. O splendid light of my blind mind! Mistress of my life! Lady of my will! Queen of my heart! In no other way was my soul, caught and enclosed in my furnace-like chest, consumed by parched and burning love. ## THE FIRST LETTER, WHICH POLIPHILO RECORDS HAVING WRITTEN TO HIS POLIA; AND AS SHE WAS NOT MOVED IN THE SLIGHTEST, HE SENT HER THE SECOND.

MOST EAGER AND SUPREMELY DESIROUS to reveal, even a little, the significant flame of my impatient Heart—which, by your noble and singular love, is so powerfully and validly set ablaze that it consumes itself in languishing—O noble and most worthy Nymph, one who is venerated and a unique, marvelous, and perfect exemplar of beauty on this earth. With these words—no, not words, but profuse and unhindered little tears <note>original: "lachrymule"; a Latinate diminutive used to express the intimacy and pathos of his weeping</note> staining <note>original: "liturando"; from the Latin *liturare*, meaning to smear or smudge, suggesting the ink is running from his tears</note> this present paper, I have taken this tolerable and honest daring. It is not out of rashness, but driven beyond belief by the constant stimulus and the troublesome persistence of a hostile love, that I disclose and declare my incredible passion and the sincere affection I bear for you and toward you, my sweet good, my sweet hope, and the only relief for my unknown troubles and for the languors you have not yet considered. To you, with a piteous voice, reverent words, and humble prayer, I commend my state which is in peril <note>original: "in discrimine"</note>; and from my arrow-struck and wounded heart, I supplicate for help to moderate this disordered fire.

Having found a convenient way to write, after a few days—carefully and intently setting aside my health—I sent her this second little letter to read:

"If my torment were less harsh than your accustomed cruelty, O most beautiful Nymph—and Polia, endowed with virtue <note>original: "macta uirtute"; a Latin expression of praise</note>—to my long afflictions, with coaxing hope, I would persuade myself to be patient. But clearly now I know (by my wicked and unfavorable star) that your crude severity and wildness surpass and exceed any of my burning martyrdom. Therefore, what does it help, what is it worth for love to increase and grow every hour in my already consumed little heart <note>original: "corculo"</note>, such a sweet fire, if you always show yourself more atrocious and freezing than frozen ice? And your breast is more cold-producing than the springs of Dirce and Neome <note>Fountains in Greek mythology known for their cold or sacred waters.</note>, and colder than the salamander <note>According to medieval lore, the salamander was so cold it could extinguish fire on contact.</note> which extinguishes fire with its touch, in the face of my handmaid-like and servile patience, and my notified vows and indicated affection. My passion is all the more inflamed the more it is opposed by your unpleasantness.

Nevertheless, I cannot unbind the lingering and solid chain that holds me laboriously under such a soft and pressing yoke. Indeed, the more I kick back, the more I involve myself, caught and captive in this amorous snare <note>original: "Naſſa"; a wicker trap used for catching fish.</note>, like a fly <note>original: "muſcula"</note> entangled in the inextricable work of Arachne <note>A reference to the spider's web, from the myth of the weaver turned into a spider.</note>. And thus strictly bound, and enslaved and captive, neither strong nor fit for flight, I am constrained to bow down and incline myself toward you. For in you alone consists my precious liberty and all my necessary good. Wherefore, if you clearly understood, my Lady, such sincere and consummate delight, and such voluntary subjection, and such active and industrious love, why then will you not freely accept these things given to you? Offered along with my whole life, which hangs perilously in your delicate hands? 

Alas, sweetest and most beautiful Polia, I pray you, help me! Allow and concede that these words of mine (not proud, not arrogant, but devout) may penetrate a little way into your heart. And stir up in yourself some small measure of compassion. Receive these hot sighs, listen to my intimate and familiar laments, recognize my heartfelt benevolence, and attend to such a faithful and gentle subject. For I am greedily dying, I am consuming myself, from your immoderate love. So much so that the whole world could not withdraw me from this, nor move me (being more steadfast than Milo <note>Milo of Croton, an ancient Greek athlete famous for his incredible strength and endurance.</note>), from loving you excessively above every other precious thing, and from cherishing and revering you, and from prostrating myself to adore you, O fashioned and true image of a Goddess. Represented before my eyes, and my public gaze, so conspicuously and remarkably—in whom I see most clearly depicted all my salvation, and expressed all my peace, delight, and contentment."

Now, my hope, do not deny me—who am entirely yours—that which I so piously beg of you: pity and a tempering of my urgent fire. For without it, I do not know how to live, nor can I; and even if I could, I would not wish to. I surely hope to find help at some time in that angelic countenance, in those most modest and adorned manners, and in that graceful and illustrious aspect. These are, without doubt, the principal and most excellent evidence that the supreme Jupiter, with exquisite and highest diligence, has fashioned you as a miraculous display, polished with every excellent beauty. These beauties undoubtedly transcend those of all the excellent young ladies of the world, and are found perfectly united in you alone. For this reason, I do not doubt even for a moment that that same Creator, if he has shaped such goodness and celestial gifts in you, has also kindly concealed within you a fragment of his own likeness. 

Therefore, I hold the certain opinion that he has likewise placed some fragment of mercy within your human heart. He did not create you among the Hyperborean Gryphons <note>Gryphons of the far North, legendary for their ferocity and guarding gold.</note>, nor did you spring from mother Niobe <note>A queen in Greek myth who was turned to stone by grief; here used to signify hardness of heart.</note>, nor from a wild and rough Apulian father, nor were you sired by the cruel Thracian Diomedes <note>A king who fed his horses on the flesh of strangers.</note>, nor the furious Orestes, nor the malignant Phaedra. Instead, you come from most humane parents, and perhaps even from those beyond this world. This thought is what principally preserves and sustains me in such gnawing <note>original: "rosulento"</note> and fluid heat. Otherwise, my charred heart <note>original: "carbunculato"; like a glowing coal</note> and indignant soul would have surely fled by now. 

Succor me then, you who are help-bringing and health-giving! For I do not beg for the insolent desire of Midas <note>The king whose touch turned everything to gold, representing greed.</note>, nor that of Pygmalion <note>A sculptor who fell in love with a statue he created.</note>, but only that you, being propitious, may quickly grant me favor. Help me in my need, show yourself pious, placate your anger, soothe your spirit, calm your mind, soften your heart, and embrace this amorous affection. Rule over him who wishes to be your most faithful servant, serving you eternally as a slave. Farewell.

### E iii

...pleasing you—that which happens most often when loving without premeditation—he whom one intensely loves. In the present, wishing to persuade you that perseverance is both timely and useful, you will understand that she was no more moved or turned by my aforementioned letters than **Mount Olympus** <note>original: "monte Olympo"; the legendary home of the Greek gods, used here to represent immovability.</note> is shaken by the loose and unbridled winds. But for all that, not ceasing what I could not leave—the **Contest** <note>original: "Agone"; implying a struggle or athletic competition of the heart.</note> I had begun—I sent her yet a third letter, making a diligent search of what she held in her soul: whether her heart was a **touchstone** <note>original: "petra cotica"; a hard stone used to test precious metals.</note> or composed of human matter. All the while, ever-watchful **Love** <note>original: "Amore"</note> was assiduously prodding me, and my insolent appetite was smeared and anointed only with soothing hope. I wrote to her in this tenor:

I would sooner wear out my tongue, noble and most high-born maiden, than ever be able to express upon the white paper how laborious, how heavy, and how bitter is my sharp pain. Day and night, it increases, redoubled within my languishing heart without pause, seeing you so deaf and displeased. And only because I know that you are not yet content or even satisfied by my heavy torments—torments not a jot smaller, but rather excessively greater than those I have twice so sweetly written to you in a short time. 

But since fallacious, strained, savage, and painful **Love**, along with pitiless Fortune and my adversary star, necessarily constrain me to voluntarily slave for and serve you—a **Nymph** of admirable beauty beyond human reach, and most distinguished for your conspicuous and elegant form. But above all and anyone else I dare say, you are excessively pitiless and cruel, like a wild and untamed beast, more rigid and displeasing than the massive and famished **Lion of Androcles** <note>original: "Leone di Androdo"; a reference to the Roman story of Androcles and the Lion, though here emphasizing the beast's ferocity rather than its gratitude.</note>. These things belie your feminine humanity and that gentle and divine image of your shining, lovely countenance, darkening that celestial and rare creation. 

You are naked of humanity and rebellious toward the amorous fires of **Cytherea** <note>original: "Cytherea"; an epithet for Venus, goddess of love, who was said to have risen from the sea near the island of Cythera.</note>, and a scorner of the divine Empire of skillful Nature. For this reason, legal cause and hateful experience lead me to speak of so much precious time vainly consumed and fled with the greatest winged speed—loving you without measure, and day and night detained, occupied, and uselessly lost in that heat. Inflamed and parched, I love you, you who are the only one chosen to destroy my life, as I clearly see. For the more I love you, the more it seems I turn you to stone <note>original: "lapidifco"; literally 'I petrify' or 'I turn into stone'.</note> by my hardening. 

Ah, Polia, can it be that not an atom of piteous spirit can be found in you? That such a small and gracious hearing might be found for these little intermediary letters? Neither with clamorous sighs, nor with flowing and $sepiculate$ <note>original: "sepiculate"; likely meaning 'stinging' or 'pointed' like grains of grain, describing the sharpness of his tears.</note> little tears, steaming and anxiously dewing from my moist eyes, which weep at every hour...

Which eyes, with hasty desire and burning petulance, have been the cause and primary beginning of the ruin and captivity of my life. But my lovable Lady, if you saw me wasting away and languishing in your sight and presence, and all dissolving into tears, together with increasing sighs, and saw me sweetly working to bend your soul, and pleading for mercy, praying to you for peace and appeasement; and likewise, with all reverent and servant-like gentleness, telling of the incredible love I bear for you, and the bitterness of heart that I endure, and the weariness of my now hateful life, and that which I suffer miserably and continuously for you—woe is me <note>original: "Heu me"</note>, Illustrious Polia, beauty among the **Nymphs** <note>original: "Nymphe"; in this context, a term of high praise for a noble and beautiful young woman.</note>, I am certain that you would be moved to pity, and you would clearly recognize that I deserve to obtain favor and swift help from you. 

When you, persisting obstinately and impiously, refuse that help with resistance, and rejecting such a fervent and bold love, I can only guess that you are telling me to burst and die for you. In what way do you feel it a fitting cause to consent to such evil? What praise? What reward? What victory? What contentment could you ever derive from it? On the contrary: a most widespread infamy, noted for shameful cruelty. By this means, therefore, I gave diligent effort to reduce and humanize her, and to sweetly soothe her, and to mitigate the bitterness received from the arduous and dangerous work I had begun. But neither she, nor treacherous <gloss>perfidious</gloss> love, consented to my persuasive words, even though I showed her openly with high and sworn promises, by sign and expression, the sweetest flames of all my sweetness; she, in turn, failed to provide the required loving reciprocation <note>original: "reciprocatione amantime"; he desires her to return his love with equal fervor, but she remains cold.</note>. And with every industrious art and skillful thought, I strove to kindle her with that true, naked, simple, and excellent affection and amorous fire, in which, without any remedy, I continually nourished myself, wretched as I am, like a fire-dwelling moth <term>Pyraulo</term> <note>From the Greek 'pyrausta', a mythical insect believed to live in fire; a common Renaissance metaphor for a lover consumed by passion.</note>. More impious than Mithridates <term>Mitridate</term> <note>A king of Pontus known for his ruthlessness and his use of poisons.</note>, more savage than Alcmaeon <term>Alchameo</term> <note>A mythological figure who killed his own mother.</note>, and more ungrateful for such great love than Paris <term>Paride</term> was to Oenone <term>Oenone</term> <note>The first wife of Paris, whom he abandoned for Helen of Troy.</note> in the face of my prayers. Remove, then, these wicked rejections from your nymph-like heart, and this common coldness, and consent with pity to my suppliant petitions. Grant, my Lady, that I may obtain the desired peace; permit my agonizing little sighs to penetrate your hearing <note>original: "auditorio"</note>. Consent to my burning loves." And having performed many such complaints and urgings, it was not able to move the agitation of my continuous sorrow even a little bit. For this sorrow was so close within me, occupying all my vitals, and its most bitter roots have germinated so deeply in my heart, that I do not know, nor am I able, nor have the power to ever extirpate them by any other art, way, or means, except through your primary hope <note>original: "speranza precipua"</note>. And even less profitable were the groaning voices, vainly scattered around her proud palace, for she was more deaf than Icarus <term>Icaro</term> was to his father’s warnings, and more disdainful than Caunus <term>Cauno</term> was to the desperate Byblis <term>Biblide</term> <note>In Ovid's 'Metamorphoses', Byblis fell in love with her brother Caunus, who fled from her in horror.</note>. She was an abominator of sweet love, persisting in those false and customary opinions that are wont to harden in the tender and virginal age. And it is an arduous thing to let go of what is once impressed upon the soul; it cannot easily be weakened. From this, then, was the beginning and origin: that I was simply ensnared and tangled in these convoluted nets and deceitful traps, and enslaved by these subtle, fleeting, uncertain, fugitive, and momentary snares and amorous cleverness. So that, subjugated and destined <note>original: "candidato"</note> under this troublesome tyranny <term>Tyránide</term> and miserable servitude, I found only one pleasure and delight: to love her extremely and willingly. To whose allurements without delay disposing myself, I humbly accepted, and entirely dedicated myself as an untiring observer of his most turbulent, subtle, searching, unruly, and unbridled laws <note>original: "legule"; Poliphilo often uses legalistic language to describe the "rules" of love.</note>. Hoping reasonably that the archer Cupid, who had so excruciatingly wounded my sad heart within, might be legally—and toward my adverse love—a most safe protection, and toward those running into blind errors, an affable and remedial driver-away of pain, and a prosperous and pious aid, and a suitable tempering for the excessive burning and heat. Not expecting salutary help from anywhere else but from him. I hoped that he might likewise draw against her the hard and cruel bow with which he had so harshly drawn against me, and into my heart such a noxious arrow, injected without retreat, had wounded me. 

And in treating the old wound, he <note>Cupid</note> further exacerbated its bitterness and redoubled the wounding and mortal pain; but the hope of repairing the widened wound—always having in him unhesitating confidence, since I was his most devoted subject and little servant, and his rich prey, bond-slave, captive, spoils of war, and booty, and his abundant trophy—I hoped that same remedy which his most pious mother <note>Venus</note> and my Lady applied to the wounded Aeneas <note>Referring to the *Aeneid*, where Venus heals Aeneas with dittany.</note>, would also aid me, following that same maternal piety. 

And also being most dedicated to him, I hoped he might provide the same patronage that Holy Vesta benignly extended to her handmaid and subject Tuccia <note>Tuccia was a Vestal Virgin who proved her chastity by carrying water from the Tiber to the Temple of Vesta in a sieve without spilling a drop.</note>, when by the miracle of the sieve <term>cribro</term>, the committed fault being hidden, she was freed from public shame and infamous punishment. Wherefore, just as is often the case with lovers in many ways, being thus desperate in a heavy dispute without a judge or opposing party, I condemned both <note>Cupid and Polia</note> as conspirators in my fatal ruin, with plaintive laments weeping and accusing them as guilty and exquisite enemies of all pious humanity. 

Now joyful and festive, I revoked the sentence against myself. At other times aroused, like a rabid and impatient dog, biting at its restraining chain, I wanted to avoid and flee the hard knot of the amorous but troublesome snare <term>laqueo</term>, and unbind myself. Then, vainly imagining, I feigned many delightful solaces and pleasures: false vengeances, rash insults, troubling dangers, and undaunted death. Afterward, I found myself more strictly knotted and solidly armored <term>loricato</term> <note>Literally "wearing a lorica," a Roman breastplate; he is encased in his obsession.</note>.

...dismissed, I went alone, exploring with the utmost vigilance and frequency, minutely and searching into every corner to see if she could be found. It happened at last that Love and Fortune, being in a favorable alignment, were most kindly appeased. Suddenly they led me into the **Sacred Temple**, while she was unaware; she went there frequently <note>original: "sæpiculate"; a Latinism for "often."</note>, but in secret. And there, having found her alone, my heart quickly shook off all other desires. Like a fierce <term>Thracian lion</term> <note>original: "frameo Leone"; likely referring to a wild or spear-like ferocity.</note> leaping upon its prey, so, in no other manner, did I rush toward her, most fiercely invading her space. Having reached her and joined her side, I was suddenly melted—like wax near a flame—becoming breathless and overcome with consternation. Ignorant of what to do or say, I finally began to speak with a sorrowful and unpolished voice, saying most humbly:

With only a trembling voice and a tiny bit of spirit remaining from all my strength—as if my speech were forbidden within my afflicted throat, my eloquent tongue numbed by my grieving soul, and my sluggish limbs shaking throughout my whole body—I lamented:

"Alas for me, Polia! Golden and precious **Column** of my life, the only consoling hope for my afflictions! Many days have now passed since I have most fervently loved you alone. I have not only loved you, but have honored you as a Goddess, worshipping you even to the point of offending the other Gods. I have offered up my heart as a burnt sacrifice <note>original: "holocausto"; Poliphilo uses the language of ancient ritual sacrifice to describe his devotion.</note> with the burning flame of love, just as the priests used to do when sacrificing to **Bellona** <note>The Roman goddess of war.</note>. I have voluntarily surrendered my life to your judgment and will.

And yet, oh unhappy me, you have become undeservedly cruel toward me, and a most irritable driver-away of all my well-being. It is as if I had harmfully injured you, just as **Juno** persecuted the Trojans with great anger <note>A reference to Virgil’s Aeneid, where Juno’s grudge against Troy drives the plot.</note>. You are more harmfully hostile to me than British pebbles are to the honey-making bee <note>Based on a classical belief mentioned by Pliny that bees in high winds carry small stones as ballast to stay stable.</note>. You are more combatively contrary and different from my will than the hostile **Thetis** <note>A sea nymph representing water.</note> is to **Vulcan** <note>The god of fire.</note>. You are more troublesome than the flapping tail to the pike-fish, more harmful than weeds <note>original: "scandulace"; likely referring to darnel or tares.</note> to the crops, and more than the resounding hail to the most tender little leaves. You are more painful than the burning **Phoebus** <note>The sun god.</note> to the springtime flowers and the grassy meadows."

Finally, wishing with all the sweetness of my heart—with alluring and gentle speech—to soothe, appease, and propitiate her, and to move her from her harsh and obstinate purpose, I sought to turn back her dire and fierce will. I hoped to calm her many little disturbances <note>original: "turbelle."</note> and her unyielding and unseemly soul, and to turn her toward piety and mercy. ...with painful weeping and unbridled sighs, I diligently sought to diminish her rigid heart, and to suitably soften and relax its grip. Just as a tender twig or osier <note>original: "uinco"; a flexible willow branch used for weaving.</note>, no matter how fragile and dried out it presents itself, can still be twisted through the use of moisture, heat, and measure <note>original: "latice, & cum foculo, & modulo"; water, a small fire, and a shaping tool or rule.</note>, and be made into a bond for others. But she, although her fragile and delicate sex is naturally flexible and susceptible to love’s fire, was moved by nothing. Neither by my burning love, nor by my abundant tears—which the afflicted **Isis** did not weep so anxiously for her dear **Osiris** <note>Isis and Osiris are central figures in Egyptian mythology; Isis searched for and wept over her husband Osiris after he was murdered.</note>. Neither by my coaxing manner, nor by attempts to ignite, soften, or provoke her, could I move her to the sweet embrace of my most heartfelt love. She could not be swayed, nor would she change in any way, even though I offered her purely my most sincere heart—purged of all other loves <note>original: "examurcato"; a term derived from the processing of olive oil, meaning filtered or cleared of dregs.</note>—and a most shining affection. 

It was a love not like that which **Tiberius Gracchus** showed to his most beloved wife **Cornelia**, believing the omen of the two serpents <note>Tiberius Gracchus allegedly chose to die to save his wife after discovering two snakes in his house, following a prophecy.</note>. And beyond all comparison, it was greater than the love shown by her who, for her husband mourned and lamented at the burning pyre, wished to swallow glowing coals <note>This refers to Portia, the wife of Brutus, who according to legend committed suicide by swallowing hot coals.</note>. And greater than that of the most loving **Panthea** for her consort. And with a more friendly devotion than that of **Pylades** toward his **Orestes**.

Wishing at last to make her manageable, I persevered in trying to tame her wild and beast-like heart, and to domesticate it toward some humanity and sweetness. Yet it grew harder, remaining untainted, untamed, unmoved, and cruelly turning to stone. It was no different than if she were ignorant of gentleness and void of pity, as if she had been born in **Hyrcania** <note>A region near the Caspian Sea, famous in classical literature as the home of wild tigers.</note>, or in the forest of **Mount Ida** shrouded in shadows, among the rough and knotty oaks and sturdy trees. Or on **Mount Ismarus**, or originating among the **Anthropophagi** <note>Legendary man-eaters or cannibals.</note>. Or among the horrific furies of the **Cyclopes**, or raised as a foster-child in the hollowed cave of **Cacus** <note>A fire-breathing giant from Roman mythology who lived in a cave on the Aventine Hill.</note>, or among the **Syrtes** <note>Dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.</note>.

Because of this cruelty, while I constantly persevered in agonizing exasperation and unfeigned grief and sorrow, hoarse sighs began anew and more harmfully within my flaming breast—louder than the roaring of a starving or feverish **Lion** in a resonant and shadowy cavern or cave. Thinking back in vain on all my completed labor, and wickedly weighing her obstinacy—recognizing that an unperforated jar cannot be drained <note>original: "impforato dolio"; a metaphor for the futility of his efforts, likely referencing the myth of the Danaids who tried to fill leaking jars, though here it suggests Polia's heart has no opening through which to receive or release emotion.</note>—I was almost distrustful and desperate of such an arduous undertaking. ...was adorned with a **triumph** <note>original: "triumpho"; a ceremonial procession or grand victory celebration in the Roman style.</note>, much like our glorious one.
