Venerable and most distinguished and worthy Priestess <note>original: "Antista," a Latin term for a high priestess or overseer of a temple</note> of this Sacred Temple. Perchance it may appear incredible and beyond belief that no sooner had my soul finished its health-giving discourse than my desirable life returned to me. Suddenly, I found myself in the tight and locked embraces and the succulent and most flavorful kisses of this Nymph, a redolent virginal flower. And following the established order, which she has so gracefully and festively narrated, our love grew intimately with wondrous and amorous nurturing until this present moment. Therefore, being now before you, distinguished holy woman and president of this sacred place: to you belongs the duty to properly turn away, deflect, and avert evil; to foster good; to exalt humble and lowly things; to guide and support the wavering; to bring light to the obscure; and to amend and correct adversity. Therefore, we pray that you create an indissoluble bond <note>original: "illaqueatura," literally a snaring or entangling</note> and, by joining us, bind our souls in one harmonious will and one desire. Confirm and stabilize our united and solidified love, for we are perpetually disposed to yield and serve as handmaidens under the high Empire of the Divine Mother <note>Venus</note>. And here, Poliphilo fell silent.

The Divine Priestess, without a moment's delay, lovingly brought us together and said: "As it has pleased the immortal Gods, let it be no other way. Therefore, it seems right and just to me that you should depart from your former state to a more praiseworthy one. Be blessed by me. Live happily in love, and diligently visit this Holy Temple as your complete refuge and secure defense for your mutual love and equal affection. And whichever of you shall cause an impediment to this fated love, let that one be persecuted by the harmful and fearsome arrows and the hurled darts of Cupid. In whom I clearly see all my reviving and saving hope established and harmonized with adamantine snares and indissoluble chains, from which I cannot turn away, nor slant my eyes, but remain an unwearied spectator. 

And, longing to embrace me without wounding <note>original: "inuulnati amplexabonda"</note>, she pressed her milky and immaculate arms around my neck, sweetly nibbling <note>original: "mordicula"</note> with her coral-colored little mouth, kissing me. And I, hastening my little swollen tongue, playfully and most sugary-sweetly <note>original: "Zacharissimamente"</note>, tasted her, kissing her back until the ultimate end. And I, unruly, having collapsed into extreme sweetness, kissing her with a most honeyed little bite, was pressed even more tightly by her, who was further provoked; and in those amorously tightening embraces, I gazed upon a venerable rosy blush, naturally diffused in her snowy cheeks, with a staining Phoenician red <note>original: "punicanante"</note>, with the placid and ivory-like shine of her smooth skin, shining with the highest grace and adornment. And provoked by extreme sweetness, in her most shining eyes were little tears emulating clear crystal and most circular pearls—more beautiful than those of Euryalus <note>A reference to the youth Euryalus from Virgil's Aeneid, celebrated for his beauty</note>, and those of the dripping Aurora <note>The goddess of the Dawn</note> upon the dewy morning roses—sighing, that deified celestial image, like a smoky wand of musky and amber incense, seeking the most fragrant heavens. 

With no small delight for the celestial spirits, such an unexperienced and fragrant smoke-cloud redolent through the air, dissolving itself, as delightful sleep most quickly from my eyes—and with swift flight she took herself away, saying: "Poli—

->philo, my dear lover.<-

->Farewell.<-

<meta>This page concludes the dream of Poliphilo. It follows his final embrace with Polia, providing a bittersweet awakening that transitions the reader from the lush, architectural fantasy of the dream world back to the reality of 15th-century Treviso.</meta>

### HERE POLIPHILO ENDS HIS HYPNEROTOMACHIA,
### GRIEVING THAT HIS SLEEP WAS NOT
### LONGER, AND THAT THE SUN WAS ENVIOUS
### IN BRINGING THE DAY.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'T' set within a square border, intricately ornamented with Renaissance foliate and vine patterns.</image-desc>

SUCH UNEXPECTED DELIGHT having been snatched away, and that angelic spirit removed from my eyes, and the sweet and gentle sleep withdrawn from my slumbering limbs—waking me in that tiny instant—O me, Alas me, amorous readers! I was left all aching from the strong embrace of that blessed image and happy presence and venerable majesty, leaving me and deserting me between miraculous sweetness and intense bitterness. It was then that there departed from my sight that most joyful sleep, and that divine shadow was interrupted and dispersed, and that mysterious apparition taken away. By these I had been led and raised to such high, sublime, and penetrating thoughts. Whence, perhaps, the Sun—agitated by envy of such a blessed dream, and acting to plunder the glorious night like a public enemy and a slanderer <note>original: "Sycophanta"; here used in the classical sense of an informer or someone who exposes secrets, as the sun "exposes" the night</note> of the divine Mother <note>original: "diuina Matre"; referring to Night or perhaps Venus/Nature</note>—suddenly arrived with luminous splendors to paint the whitening Dawn with rosy color, having scattered the eternal night. And as the renewed day was illustrated and interposed, I remained packed and completely filled with a sweet and subtle deception.

Think, then, what livid envy the Sun would have felt then, if I had actually been enjoying the true and voluptuous delights of such a shapely and divine damsel and noble Nymph! For he could not bear—I judge because it is not permitted to be with a goddess—to grant me the long night (out of indignation) given to Alcmena <note>In Greek myth, Jupiter made the night three times longer so he could spend more time with Alcmena, the mother of Hercules</note>. Woe is me! Why did he not exchange a little of his speed for a small bit of sluggishness toward my brief rest, and pass over his decree for just a moment? And why was I not then granted the Stygian sleep from the casket of the curious Psyche? <note>Referring to the myth of Cupid and Psyche, where Psyche opens a box from the underworld and falls into a death-like "Stygian" sleep</note>

And here Philomela <note>The nightingale</note> before dawn, weeping, sang for me, hidden among the thorny brambles and among the thickets pressed with the dark foliage of little oaks, entwined by the winding honeysuckle <note>original: "Periclymeno"</note>, recounting the violences of the adulterous and wicked Tereus <note>In myth, Tereus raped Philomela and cut out her tongue; she was later turned into a nightingale</note>, saying with her musical chirping: "Tereus, Tereus, he violated me" <note>original Greek: "τηρηύς τηρηύς ἐμὲ ἐβιάσατο"</note>. Sighing, emerged and released from sweet sleep, I suddenly woke myself, saying: "Farewell then, Polia."

->At Treviso, while wretched Poliphilo was held by the most beautiful bonds of love for Polia.<-

->May 1, 1467.<-

<meta>This page contains the "Errata Corrige" or list of corrections for the first edition of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. It was common in early printing for a list of errors found after the pages were already printed to be added at the end. The printer, Aldus Manutius, was famous for his precision, but the complexity of this book—which mixes Italian, Latin, Greek, and invented words—led to many typographical slips.</meta>

**Physical Description of the Volume**

The book is protected by a sturdy binding of yellowish, aged <term>vellum</term><note>Parchment made from calfskin, common for durable bindings in the 15th through 17th centuries</note>. On the top of the spine, there is a small paper sticker with the number "536" handwritten or printed, likely a cataloging number from a previous library. At the base of the spine, the number "80" has been stamped.

The most striking feature of the spine is a dark leather title label. It is framed by elegant gold-tooled patterns at the top and bottom, which highlight the title and the historic date of 1499, both embossed in gold. The covers themselves are plain, showing the natural grain of the skin along with the stains and wear typical of a book that has been handled for over five centuries.
